This is why a real harmonic LPF after a transmitter PA is typically 5th or 7th order: the 2nd harmonic (at 2× the carrier frequency) needs to be 50 dB or more below the carrier, and a 1st-order filter cannot do that without also eating the carrier.
ch1_8.orderTradeoff: What does steeper cost? Three things, in this order. First, parts count and tuning work — a 7-pole LC filter has 7 elements that all need to land within tolerance. Second, passband loss — every real inductor and capacitor has loss, and 7 of them in cascade add up. Third, and least obvious, group delay and ringing — a steep filter rings on a transient, smearing the leading edge of fast signals. This is why CW operators and digital-mode users prefer narrower (sharper) filters, and SSB operators prefer wider (gentler) ones.
ch1_8.orderWidgetIntro: The plotter below shows the magnitude response of a low-pass or high-pass filter on the standard log-log axes. Drag the cutoff slider, toggle the order from 1 to 5, switch between low-pass and high-pass shapes — and watch how the −3 dB point stays put while the skirt steepens.
ch1_8.lcIntro: RC filters are the easiest filters to build, but they have a ceiling: a real RC always loses signal in its passband (the resistor is a real resistor, dissipating power), and its skirt is gentle. As soon as you need a sharper transition or low passband loss, the RC is replaced by an LC — one inductor and one capacitor working together. LC filters cost more in parts, are bulkier than RC, and need shielding against stray fields, but they buy three things: (1) low passband loss (an ideal LC has zero — you only see the loss in the inductor's winding resistance), (2) automatic 2nd-order roll-off at −40 dB/decade, and (3) resonance, which lets you build the band-pass and band-stop shapes you cannot make with an RC.
ch1_8.lcLpfRecap: You met an LC low-pass already in Chapter 1.6 — the textbook power-supply ripple filter. The series inductor opposes the AC ripple component while passing the DC current; the shunt capacitor short-circuits whatever ripple gets past the inductor down to ground. Same arrangement, scaled for higher frequencies, becomes the harmonic LPF sitting between every transmitter PA and antenna.
ch1_8.lcBandPassIntro: Series-LC band-pass. Wire L and C end-to-end in series with the signal path. From Chapter 1.7, a series LC presents a near-short at its resonant frequency f_{0} = 1 / (2π√(LC)) and rising impedance off-resonance. So the signal at f_{0} sails through; signals far from f_{0} see a high series impedance and are blocked. The bandwidth is set by Q (BW = f_{0} / Q), exactly as in Chapter 1.7.
ch1_8.lcNotchIntro: Series-LC notch — the trap. Take the same L and C from the band-pass, but wire them in series from the signal path down to ground — a series tuned circuit wired to ground. At its resonant frequency f_{0} the series pair is a near-short, so it dumps f_{0} straight to ground and the output collapses into a deep notch; every other frequency meets a high impedance and sails past untouched. This is the fact to internalise — schematic position sets the role. The same series LC in the line passes f_{0}; wired to ground it traps it. A parallel tank is the exact mirror: in the line it blocks f_{0} (band-stop), in shunt it passes it (band-pass).
ch1_8.sectionFamilies: Filter families — trade-offs in the response shape
ch1_8.familiesIntro: Take a 5th-order low-pass with a 1 kHz cutoff. There are infinitely many ways to assemble five poles to give that cutoff — and the choice between them is the choice of filter family. Each family optimises a different property and the others give worse:
ch1_8.familiesButter: Butterworth — maximally flat passband. The default if you have no strong reason to pick something else. The passband is monotonic and flat; the stopband rolls off cleanly at the order's nominal slope. The transient response is well-behaved without being especially fast. Almost every textbook filter response you have ever seen plotted is a Butterworth.
ch1_8.familiesCheby: Chebyshev — steepest skirt. Trades passband flatness for a sharper transition between passband and stopband. Comes in two variants — Type I ripples in the passband, Type II ripples in the stopband — both at the same nominal cutoff give a noticeably steeper skirt than Butterworth at the same order. Use when selectivity matters more than flatness — IF filters and the PA-output low-pass on a contest transmitter often run Chebyshev.
ch1_8.familiesBessel: Bessel — flat group delay. The opposite extreme: gives up steepness in exchange for the cleanest possible transient response. A square wave through a Bessel low-pass comes out the cleanest of any family at the same order — minimal ringing, minimal overshoot. Use anywhere the time-domain shape matters: digital-mode filters, anti-alias before a fast ADC, audio filters where phase distortion shows up as smearing.
ch1_8.familiesElliptic: Elliptic (Cauer) — steepest possible. Allows ripple in both the passband and the stopband, and pays for both with the steepest transition any filter family can give at a given order. The 2nd-order elliptic skirt is sharper than a 4th-order Butterworth. Used when nothing else is steep enough — narrow IF filters, harmonic-suppression LPFs at low order, and the brick-wall anti-alias filter ahead of a band-edge ADC.
ch1_8.familiesCallout: None of this matters for a beginner's lab. Build your first filter as a Butterworth — Elsie by Tonne Software (Windows or under Wine on macOS/Linux, free Student Edition) covers all four families, while the browser-based filter calculator at changpuak.ch (works on any OS, no install) covers Butterworth and Chebyshev for every topology — enough for any first lab. The other families are the tool you reach for when Butterworth is not steep enough, not flat enough in delay, or not ripple-tolerant in the passband. The order still sets the headline roll-off in dB/decade; the family only sets the shape of the transition between bands.
ch1_8.sectionVna: On the bench — sweeping a filter
ch1_8.vnaIntro: A VNA connected port-1 to filter-input and port-2 to filter-output measures <s21>S21</s21>, the forward transmission. Sweep the source across a frequency range that covers cutoff plus at least one decade on each side, and you read the filter's magnitude response straight off the screen — in decibels, on a log-frequency axis, exactly the Bode-plot format you just practised reading.
ch1_8.vnaCurves: Each of the four shapes traces a recognisable line. The low-pass starts flat at 0 dB and slides downward at the cutoff. The high-pass mirrors it, rising from the noise floor at the cutoff into a flat passband. The band-pass shows a peaked top with two skirts. The band-stop shows the inverse — a flat passband with one deep notch. The four shapes are visually distinct on the screen — once you've seen them once, you will never confuse them.
ch1_8.vnaMarkerHint: Tip. Drop a marker at the −3 dB point of the trace and the VNA reports f_{c} for you. For a band-pass, drop two markers at the −3 dB skirts and read off the bandwidth — that's the same definition as Chapter 1.7's f_{0} / Q. Marker math on the VNA is the fastest way to characterise an unknown filter.
ch1_8.sectionApplications: Where filters actually live in a radio
ch1_8.appsIntro: Every block in a <transceiver>transceiver</transceiver> is preceded or followed by a filter. Four canonical placements are worth knowing by name — they explain most of what filters do in practice:
ch1_8.appsHarmonicLpf: Harmonic low-pass after the transmitter PA. A class-AB or class-C amplifier driven hard generates strong 2nd, 3rd, 5th… harmonics of the carrier. The harmonic LPF — typically a 5- or 7-pole LC filter cut off just above the band edge — knocks them down by 50 dB or more before they reach the antenna. Without it, your 14 MHz transmission goes out partly on 28 MHz, 42 MHz, 70 MHz, etc. — straight into other amateur and broadcast bands. Every modern HF transmitter switches a different harmonic LPF in for each band.
ch1_8.appsIfFilter: IF filter in a superhet receiver. The selectivity of a superhet is set by one filter — the IF filter sitting at a fixed intermediate frequency between the mixer and the demodulator. Its bandwidth is matched to the mode: ≈ 2.4 kHz for SSB, ≈ 500 Hz for CW, ≈ 250 Hz for narrow data. A modern transceiver has multiple IF filters selectable from the front panel. The IF filter is also where most of the receiver's adjacent-signal rejection happens — the steeper its skirts, the closer in frequency a strong unwanted station can be without bleeding into the wanted one.
ch1_8.appsCrossover: Audio crossover. A two-way speaker has a tweeter (small, high-frequency) and a woofer (large, low-frequency). A crossover network sends each driver only the audio band it can handle — a low-pass to the woofer (typically 2 kHz cutoff, LC) and a high-pass to the tweeter. Same parts, same maths, same Bode plots — the only difference from an RF filter is the cutoff is in the audio range and the inductor is wound on a non-magnetic former for low distortion.
ch1_8.appsAntiAlias: Anti-alias before an ADC. Any sampling system needs an analogue low-pass ahead of the ADC, with a cutoff just below half the sample rate. Frequencies above that limit fold back into the baseband as aliases — false signals that cannot be undone in software. Modern SDR receivers use very steep elliptic anti-alias filters to use the maximum possible bandwidth without aliases creeping in.
ch1_8.keyTakeaway1: Four shapes. A filter is one of low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, or band-stop (notch). The shape determines what it keeps; the cutoff frequency determines where the line is drawn.
ch1_8.keyTakeaway2: The cutoff formula. For a first-order RC filter (the simplest there is), the cutoff is f_{c} = 1 / (2πRC). The same formula works for both low-pass and high-pass — only the topology (which component is in series with the signal, which is to ground) changes which side of f_{c} is the passband.
ch1_8.keyTakeaway3: Bode plot rules. At f_{c} the response is −3 dB (half power, 0.707 of input voltage). Far from f_{c} the response is a straight line on log-log axes with slope −20 dB per decade per pole. A 1st-order is −20, a 2nd-order is −40, etc.
ch1_8.keyTakeaway4: LC for sharper skirts. RC filters are easy but gentle and lossy. LC filters are sharper, lower-loss in the passband, and the only way to build resonant band-pass and band-stop shapes — straight extensions of the series and parallel LC topologies from Chapter 1.7.
ch1_8.keyTakeaway5: Family sets the transition shape. Order sets the headline roll-off; family (Butterworth, Chebyshev, Bessel, elliptic) sets the shape of the transition between bands and the time-domain behaviour. Default to Butterworth; reach for the others only when you have a specific reason.
ch1_8.labGoal: Build a first-order RC low-pass on a breadboard, sweep it on a VNA, and verify that the −3 dB point lands within tolerance of the calculated cutoff frequency.
ch1_8.labEquip1: VNA (a NanoVNA is sufficient — measurement range to at least 1 MHz)
ch1_8.labEquip2: <breadboard>Breadboard</breadboard> with two short jumper leads to the VNA's port-1 and port-2 <sma>SMA</sma> connectors
ch1_8.labEquip3: Multimeter (to verify component values before building)
ch1_8.labEquip4: A free filter-cutoff calculator (or a pen, paper, and the cutoff formula)
ch1_8.labComp1: One 1 kΩ resistor, ¼ W or larger, 5 % tolerance or better
ch1_8.labComp2: One 100 nF ceramic capacitor (marked «104» in the 3-digit code) — or any value between 10 nF and 1 µF
ch1_8.labComp3: One length of coax with two SMA-to-male-jumper adapters, or two short pigtails — for connecting the breadboard to the VNA ports
ch1_8.labStep1: Calculate the expected cutoff frequency for your component values: <nowrap><var>f_{c}</var> = 1 / (2π<var>R</var><var>C</var>)</nowrap>. With <nowrap><var>R</var> = 1 kΩ</nowrap> and <nowrap><var>C</var> = 100 nF</nowrap> you should get ≈ 1.59 kHz. Write the number down — you will check the bench measurement against it.
ch1_8.labStep2: Build the filter on the breadboard. R goes in series between the VNA port-1 hot lead and a node we will call OUT. C goes from OUT to ground. The VNA port-2 hot lead reads OUT. Both ground returns to the VNA share one ground rail on the breadboard. The schematic below labels the ports P1 and P2.
ch1_8.labStep3: Calibrate the VNA in transmission mode (S21) over a span that includes <var>f_{c}</var> with at least one decade on each side. For a 1.6 kHz cutoff, sweep from 100 Hz to 100 kHz — many bench VNAs cannot go that low; if so, swap the capacitor for 1 nF and aim for a 160 kHz cutoff, sweeping 10 kHz to 10 MHz.
ch1_8.labStep4: Connect the filter and read the trace. You should see a flat passband at low frequency, a smooth transition, and a downward skirt rolling off. Drop a marker at the −3 dB point and read the frequency.
ch1_8.labStep5: Compare the measured −3 dB point to the calculated <var>f_{c}</var>. With 5 % parts you should land within ±10 % of the prediction. If you are way off, suspect either a measurement issue (poor calibration, wrong sweep range) or a component issue (resistor or capacitor not what you think it is — measure with the meter).
ch1_8.labStep6: Optional: swap R and C on the board (capacitor in series, resistor to ground). The cutoff stays at the same frequency, but the trace now rises from low to high — you have built the high-pass. Same parts, same <var>f_{c}</var>, opposite role. This is the most concrete way to feel the duality.
ch1_8.labExpected: On the screen: a flat passband at 0 dB, a smooth knee centred near the calculated <var>f_{c}</var>, and a skirt sloping down at −20 dB per decade above cutoff. The −3 dB marker reads within ±10 % of the formula's answer.
ch1_8.labConnection: You have just measured the same filter that lives inside the audio path of every microphone preamp, the gate of every Arduino debouncer, and the input of every audio ADC. The decibel scale, the log-frequency sweep, and the −3 dB convention are not VNA-specific — they are the universal language for describing any filter, on any timescale, in any field of electronics.
ch1_8.labTrouble1: Skirt does not roll off cleanly. Likely a bad ground at the VNA-to-breadboard connection, or a stray inductance in long jumper leads. Shorten the leads, tie the grounds together at one point on the board.
ch1_8.labTrouble2: −3 dB point is far from the prediction. Measure the resistor and capacitor with the meter — capacitors especially can be 20 % off their marked value, and electrolytics often more. Trust the measurement, recalculate f_{c}, and check again.
ch1_8.labTrouble3: Trace looks flat at all frequencies. The filter is not in the path. Check that the VNA's port-2 lead is on the OUT node, not back on the input side of R, and that C is grounded.
ch1_8.quiz_q1: What is the gain of a first-order RC low-pass filter, in decibels, exactly at its cutoff frequency?
ch1_8.quiz_q1_explanation: By definition, the cutoff is the −3 dB point — half the input power makes it through, equivalent to <nowrap>1 / √2 ≈ 0.707</nowrap> of the input voltage.
ch1_8.quiz_q2: An RC low-pass with <nowrap><var>R</var> = 10 kΩ</nowrap> and <nowrap><var>C</var> = 100 nF</nowrap> has approximately what cutoff frequency?
ch1_8.quiz_q3: Which filter shape blocks DC but passes everything from a few hertz upward?
ch1_8.quiz_q3_explanation: A high-pass passes signals above its cutoff — and DC is the lowest frequency of all (0 Hz), so it is blocked. The same circuit is called a coupling capacitor when its job is to block DC supply voltage from a signal path.
ch1_8.quiz_q4: A first-order RC low-pass has a cutoff at 1 kHz. Approximately how much is the signal attenuated at 100 kHz, two decades above cutoff?
ch1_8.quiz_q4_explanation: First-order roll-off is −20 dB per decade. Two decades above cutoff means 2 × 20 = 40 dB of attenuation — that is a voltage ratio of 1:100, a power ratio of 1:10 000.
ch1_8.quiz_q5: A 5th-order low-pass filter rolls off at what nominal slope above its cutoff?
ch1_8.quiz_q5_explanation: −20 dB per decade per pole; 5 poles × 20 = 100 dB per decade. This is why harmonic LPFs in transmitters are typically 5th order or higher — anything weaker cannot push the harmonics far enough below the carrier.
ch1_8.quiz_q6: Which filter family gives the steepest possible roll-off at a given order?
ch1_8.quiz_q6_explanation: Elliptic (also called Cauer) accepts ripple in both the passband and stopband and gets the sharpest possible transition in return. Bessel is the gentlest; Butterworth is in the middle; Chebyshev sits between Butterworth and elliptic.
ch1_8.quiz_q7: Why does every transmitter PA need a harmonic low-pass filter at its output?
ch1_8.quiz_q7_c: To suppress harmonics generated by the non-linear amplifier so they don't radiate
ch1_8.quiz_q7_explanation: Class-AB and class-C amplifiers are non-linear — they generate strong 2nd, 3rd, 5th… harmonics of the carrier. Without a harmonic LPF, those harmonics would radiate and interfere with other services. Impedance matching is a separate concern handled by the <atu>antenna tuner</atu>, not the harmonic filter.
ch1_8.quiz_q8: An LC band-pass filter has a centre frequency of 14 MHz and a Q of 70. What is its −3 dB bandwidth?
ch1_8.quiz_q8_explanation: Same formula as Chapter 1.7: <nowrap>BW = <var>f_{0}</var> / Q = 14 000 / 70 = 200 kHz</nowrap>.
ch1_8.quiz_q9: On a Bode plot, the horizontal and vertical axes are both logarithmic because:
ch1_8.quiz_q9_a: Logarithms are easier to compute by hand than linear scales
ch1_8.quiz_q9_b: Linear axes can't show negative numbers
ch1_8.quiz_q9_c: Decibels are required by international convention for any plot
ch1_8.quiz_q9_d: Frequency-domain behaviour spans many decades and roll-off shows as a straight line on log-log axes
ch1_8.quiz_q9_explanation: Filter responses span many decades of frequency (Hz to MHz) and many decades of magnitude. Log-log axes compress that range into a readable rectangle, and the −20 dB/decade roll-off rule turns into a straight line — making it trivial to see filter order at a glance.
ch1_8.quiz_q10: An anti-alias filter ahead of an ADC sampling at 100 kSPS should have its cutoff:
ch1_8.quiz_q10_explanation: Nyquist's rule: a sampler at <var>f_{s}</var> can only represent frequencies below <var>f_{s}</var> / 2 unambiguously. Frequencies above that fold back into the baseband as aliases, which cannot be undone in software. The anti-alias filter must therefore stop everything above <var>f_{s}</var> / 2 — for a 100 kSPS ADC, just below 50 kHz.

cutoff.title: RC cutoff calculator
cutoff.description: Pick R and C to get the cutoff frequency of a first-order RC filter. Or pick a target cutoff and a value of one of the components — the calculator solves for the other.
cutoff.hint: The same calculator works for low-pass and high-pass — they share the cutoff formula. Only the schematic position of R and C changes which side of f_c is the passband.

bode.title: Interactive Bode plotter
bode.description: Magnitude response of a first- to fifth-order low-pass or high-pass filter, on log-frequency / dB-magnitude axes. Drag the cutoff to slide the curve left or right; toggle the order to steepen the skirt; switch between low-pass and high-pass to flip the curve's direction.
bode.ariaLabel: Bode plot showing magnitude in decibels versus frequency on a logarithmic axis. The cutoff frequency is marked with a vertical line; the −3 dB level is marked with a horizontal dashed line.
bode.hint: Slide the order up to 5 and watch the skirt steepen by 20 dB per decade per pole. The −3 dB point stays at f_c regardless of order — the skirt just gets sharper around it. Note also: only the magnitude is plotted; phase rotates by 90° per pole, but is hidden here for clarity.

vnaSweep.title: VNA sweep — the four filter shapes
vnaSweep.description: A simulated VNA showing the S21 magnitude trace for each of the four canonical filter shapes back to back. The shape is a tab; the cutoff (or centre, for band shapes) and the order are sliders. Each trace is annotated with its passband, stopband, and −3 dB markers.
vnaSweep.ariaLabel: Simulated VNA screen showing the magnitude transmission trace of one of the four filter shapes (low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, or band-stop). The vertical axis is S21 in decibels; the horizontal axis is frequency on a logarithmic scale.
vnaSweep.hint: Switch between the four shapes — the trace's silhouette is enough to identify the filter type at a glance, before you ever read a marker number. Real-world VNA traces look identical; the only difference is they have noise and a finite stopband floor (40–80 dB down, depending on the filter).

ch1_8.schematicRcLpfAria: Schematic of a first-order RC low-pass filter. A signal source on the left feeds a resistor R; after R the signal continues to the OUT terminal on the right; from the OUT node a capacitor C goes vertically down to a ground rail at the bottom.
ch1_8.schematicRcLpfCaption: RC low-pass. R in series with the signal, C from the output node to ground. R and C form a voltage divider — the output is taken across C. At low frequencies C's reactance is much larger than R, so almost all of V_{\mathrm{in}} drops across C: the signal reaches the output unattenuated. At high frequencies C's reactance falls to a near-short and the voltage drops across R instead, leaving the output near zero. The hinge between the two regimes is at f_{c} = 1 / (2πRC).
ch1_8.schematicRcLpfLabAria: Schematic showing how to wire an RC low-pass filter to the VNA on a breadboard. Port 1 hot lead connects through resistor R to a node labelled OUT; capacitor C connects from OUT to the ground rail; port 2 hot lead also connects to OUT; both VNA ground returns share one common ground rail.
ch1_8.schematicRcLpfLabCaption: RC LPF wired to the VNA on a breadboard. R goes in series between the port-1 hot lead and the node OUT; C goes from OUT to the ground rail. The port-2 hot lead reads OUT. Both VNA ground returns share one rail — without a common ground the S21 measurement is meaningless, because the two ports have no shared voltage reference.
ch1_8.schematicLcBpfAria: Schematic of a series-LC band-pass filter. A signal source on the left feeds an inductor L and a capacitor C wired end-to-end in series with the signal path; the output is taken across a load resistor connected from the output node to ground.
ch1_8.schematicLcBpfCaption: Series-LC band-pass. L and C are wired end-to-end in the signal path. R_{L} is the load — the next stage's input impedance or the antenna — not part of the filter itself: with an open-circuit output there is no band-pass shape at all. At f_{0} the series LC looks like a near-short, so almost all of V_{in} develops across R_{L}: V_{out} ≈ V_{in}. Off-resonance, the series impedance climbs and R_{L} sees less and less. The bandwidth follows the loaded-Q rule from Chapter 1.7 — a smaller R_{L} gives a lower Q and a wider passband.
ch1_8.schematicLcNotchAria: Schematic of a series-LC notch (band-stop) filter. The signal path runs from the input terminal through a series resistor (or source impedance) to the output terminal. From the signal node, an inductor L and a capacitor C in series drop to ground, shorting the resonant frequency away.
ch1_8.schematicLcNotchCaption: Series-LC notch (trap). A series LC — inductor and capacitor one after the other — hangs in shunt from the signal node to ground. R is the source's own internal resistance — not part of the filter itself: it is what V_{in} drops across once the pair shorts f_{0} to ground, and with an ideal source there would be no notch at all. At f_{0} the pair is a near-short and dumps f_{0} straight to ground, so the output collapses to a deep notch. Off-resonance the pair is high-impedance, draws almost no current, and everything else passes through untouched.
ch1_8.filterTypeGalleryAria: A 2×2 gallery of the four canonical filter shapes — low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, and band-stop. Each panel shows a small schematic on the left and the corresponding magnitude response curve on the right.
ch1_8.schematicRcHpfAria: Schematic of a first-order RC high-pass filter. A signal source on the left feeds a capacitor C in series; after C the signal continues to the OUT terminal on the right; from the C-output node a resistor R goes vertically down to a ground rail at the bottom.
ch1_8.schematicRcHpfCaption: RC high-pass. C in series with the signal, R from the output node to ground. R and C form a voltage divider — the output is taken at the junction between them. At low frequencies C's reactance is huge, almost all of V_{\mathrm{in}} drops across C, leaving V_{\mathrm{out}} near zero. At high frequencies C's reactance shrinks to a near-short, the voltage drops across R instead, and the output tracks the input. The hinge between the two regimes is at f_{c} = 1 / (2πRC).

bodeGuide.aria: Annotated Bode plot showing the magnitude response of a first-order low-pass filter on log-frequency / dB-magnitude axes. The cutoff frequency (letter f, lowered subscript c) is marked with a vertical line; a horizontal dashed line marks the −3 dB level; a thin diagonal line shows the −20 dB per decade asymptote in the stopband. Decade ticks on the frequency axis run from one hundredth to one hundred times the cutoff. Passband and stopband zones are labelled.

ch1_8.schematicLcLpfAria: Schematic of an LC low-pass filter. A series inductor L on the top rail, with a shunt capacitor C from the node after L down to a ground rail at the bottom. The input enters on the left; the output is taken on the top rail to the right of the L–C junction.
ch1_8.schematicLcLpfCaption: LC low-pass. Series inductor L in the signal path, shunt capacitor C from the output node to ground. The inductor opposes high-frequency current (its reactance grows with frequency); the capacitor shunts whatever high-frequency component remains down to ground. Together they roll off the signal at −40 dB per decade — twice as steep as the RC LPF, with much lower passband loss.
ch1_8.schematicCascadedRcAria: Schematic of two cascaded RC low-pass stages with an op-amp unity-gain buffer between them. First stage: input through R1 in series, then a node where C1 shunts down to ground. The node feeds the non-inverting input of the op-amp. The op-amp output feeds the second stage: R2 in series, then a node where C2 shunts down to ground; the same node is the output. A feedback wire connects the op-amp output back to its inverting input, configuring it as a unity-gain buffer.
ch1_8.schematicCascadedRcCaption: Two RC low-pass stages cascaded through a unity-gain buffer. Each individual stage is first-order; the buffer prevents stage 2 from loading stage 1 (without it, R2 and C2 would lower the effective impedance seen by C1, shifting both cutoffs). With the buffer, the two stages act independently and the overall response is truly second-order — −40 dB per decade above cutoff.
ch1_8.orderBufferAside: The triangle in the middle is an op-amp wired as a voltage follower (unity-gain buffer): it copies the voltage from its + input to its output unchanged. What makes it useful here: the input draws almost no current (so it doesn't load the first RC stage), and the output has very low impedance (so it can drive the second stage without sag). Together that keeps the two stages from affecting each other's cutoffs. Op-amp internals are out of scope for this section — we'll meet the op-amp properly later.

ch1_9.heroAriaLabel: Pen-and-ink sketch of a laminated-iron transformer: a rectangular core with two upright legs joined top and bottom by short cross-pieces. A coil winds around the left leg (primary) and a longer coil winds around the right leg (secondary), each drawn as a stack of small loops. A curved arrow loops around the inside of the core showing magnetic flux circulating from one leg to the other and back. Two leads come off the top and bottom of each coil, drawn as short stubs. Labels read «primary» on the left and «secondary» on the right.
ch1_9.intro: A transformer is two coils sharing a magnetic field. Pass changing current through the first coil; the changing field it makes cuts through the turns of the second coil; a voltage appears on the second coil. That's the entire idea — and it's the most useful trick in radio after Ohm's law. With it you can take 230 V from the wall and turn it into 12 V for your rig. You can take a 50 Ω antenna feedline and make it look like the 200 Ω your folded dipole actually wants. You can isolate one circuit's ground from another's so a fault in one can't hurt the other. All three jobs come from the same two coupled coils — only the turns ratio and the core change.
ch1_9.introPreview: We start with the seed of the idea: two coils, one driving, one listening, joined only by the magnetic field they share. Three formulas come straight out of that picture: voltage scales with the turns ratio, current scales with its inverse, and impedance — the punchline for radio — scales with the square of the turns ratio. Each one gets a worked example and an interactive widget. Then we look at why no real transformer matches those formulas exactly: magnetising current, leakage inductance, copper I^{2}R heating, and core losses from hysteresis and eddy currents. We tour the three core families you'll meet at the bench — laminated iron for power and audio, ferrite for broadband RF, and powdered iron for tuned RF. We meet the three topologies — the standard two-winding transformer, the single-winding autotransformer (think Variac), and the balun that connects a balanced antenna to coax. We close with where each kind shows up in a real radio, then wind a 4:1 step-up on a small toroid on the bench and measure it.
ch1_9.coupledRecap: From chapter 1.6, every coil with current flowing through it sets up a magnetic field. Inside the coil that field is concentrated; outside it spreads and weakens with distance. So far we treated the coil as a one-port component — current in, voltage across, end of story.
ch1_9.coupledIdea: Now place a second coil close to the first, oriented so the first coil's field passes through it. Nothing is wired between them. But Faraday's law says any change in the magnetic flux through a loop of wire induces a voltage in that loop — that's the rule that makes generators and microphones work. So when the first coil's current changes, its field changes, and a voltage appears across the second coil. Energy passes from the first circuit to the second through the magnetic field alone. No copper between them.
ch1_9.coupledOnlyAc: Notice the word change. A steady current makes a steady field, and a steady field induces nothing. That is why a transformer cannot pass DC. Hook a battery to the primary and the secondary is silent — except for one tiny blip at the instant you connect the battery, and another at the instant you disconnect it. Hook an AC source instead, and the field swings up and down 50 or 60 or a million times a second, and the secondary follows along.
ch1_9.coupledKeyCallout: That's the whole transformer. Two coils, one shared magnetic field, AC-only. Everything else in this chapter — turns ratios, impedance transformation, balun design, mains supplies — is bookkeeping on top of that one idea.
ch1_9.voltageIntuition: Each turn of wire that the changing flux passes through has the same voltage induced in it — call it one «volt-per-turn». A coil of N turns in series adds those volts up, so its terminal voltage is N times the volt-per-turn. Now we have a recipe for any voltage we like: pick the number of secondary turns so that N_{s} × (volts per turn) equals what we want. The volts-per-turn comes from the primary, so divide by N_{p} to get rid of it:
ch1_9.voltageFormulaIntro: The voltage on the secondary is the voltage on the primary multiplied by the turns ratio:
ch1_9.voltageStepUpDown: If the secondary has more turns than the primary, the voltage goes up — call it a step-up transformer. Fewer turns and the voltage goes down — a step-down. The same physical transformer can do either job: which winding you treat as the primary determines the direction. A 230 V → 12 V mains transformer used in reverse becomes a 12 V → 230 V step-up, with all the same windings — just driven from the other side.
ch1_9.voltageExample: Worked example. A small mains transformer has 920 turns on its primary and 48 turns on its secondary. Plug it into 230 V AC. The secondary voltage is 230 × 48 / 920 = 12 V — exactly what the rig wants on its 12 V input.
ch1_9.voltageWidgetIntro: Try it for yourself. Type any pair of turn counts (or nudge them with the spinner arrows); the voltage on the other side updates immediately, and the indicator tells you whether you've built a step-up or a step-down.
ch1_9.voltageGotcha: Step-up doesn't mean «free voltage». A 1:10 transformer hands you ten times the voltage with one tenth the current — power balances. We turn to that next.
ch1_9.currentConservation: A transformer cannot create energy. Whatever power flows in on the primary side has to flow out on the secondary side (minus losses, which we'll get to). Power is voltage times current — <nowrap><var>P</var> = <var>V</var><var>I</var></nowrap> — so if the secondary's voltage is ten times higher, its current must be one tenth, otherwise the books don't balance.
ch1_9.currentFormulaIntro: Current scales with the inverse of the turns ratio:
ch1_9.currentInverse: The transformer steps voltage and current in opposite directions. Step the voltage up by 10× and the current goes down by 10×. Step the voltage down by 4× and the current goes up by 4×. The product — power — stays the same on both sides.
ch1_9.currentExample: Worked example. The 230 V → 12 V transformer from before. Suppose the rig draws 5 A from the 12 V secondary. The primary current is 5 × 48 / 920 ≈ 0.26 A. The secondary's beefy 5 A doesn't show up on the AC line — only the gentler 0.26 A does, because the transformer trades current for voltage on the way through.
ch1_9.currentWireWidth: There's a practical clue you can read off any transformer by eye. The high-current side uses thicker wire. A 230 V → 12 V mains transformer has thin wire on the 230 V side (the primary, low current) and thick wire on the 12 V side (the secondary, high current). A microphone transformer in a tube amp does the opposite: thin wire on the secondary that drives the high-impedance grid, thick wire on the primary that carries the lower-impedance plate signal. The wire diameter is set by I^{2}R heating — too thin and the winding overheats and burns up.
ch1_9.currentCallout: Voltage and current trade places. The transformer is a lossless impedance transformer — and impedance is just the ratio of voltage to current. Which is the next section.
ch1_9.sectionImpedance: The impedance ratio — the punchline for radio
ch1_9.impedanceWhy: Most of what a transformer does for an amateur radio operator is match impedances. A transmitter is happiest delivering its rated power into a 50 Ω load. Many antennas are not 50 Ω — a folded dipole is around 200 Ω, a small loop antenna might be 5 Ω, a random wire could be 450 Ω. Connect any of those directly to the rig and the mismatch reflects a chunk of your power back at the PA, raises the SWR, and in extreme cases triggers the rig's foldback protection. A transformer with the right turns ratio can convert one impedance to another so the PA «sees» 50 Ω regardless of what hangs at the antenna feed point.
ch1_9.impedanceDerivation: Here's where the magic comes from. The impedance a circuit presents at its input is Z = V / I. We already know each side of a transformer: the voltage scales by the turns ratio, so V_{p} = V_{s} × N_{p} / N_{s}; the current scales by its inverse, so I_{p} = I_{s} × N_{s} / N_{p}. When we form the primary impedance Z_{p} = V_{p} / I_{p}, both factors land in the same ratio — N_{p} / N_{s} on top from the voltage, N_{s} / N_{p} on the bottom from the current — and dividing by the inverse is the same as multiplying. The two factors stack and we end up with the square of the turns ratio:
ch1_9.impedanceFormulaIntro: The primary impedance is the secondary load multiplied by the square of the turns ratio:
ch1_9.impedanceExample: Worked example. A 200 Ω folded dipole and a 50 Ω rig. We need a transformer that makes 200 Ω look like 50 Ω from the rig's side. Solve 50 = 200 × (N_{p}/N_{s})2 → (N_{p}/N_{s})2 = 1/4 → N_{p}/N_{s} = 1/2. A 1:2 turns ratio gives a 1:4 impedance ratio. That's exactly the spec for a 4:1 voltage balun — the most common antenna-feed transformer in the HF amateur shack.
ch1_9.impedanceWidgetIntro: Adjust the load impedance and the turns ratio; the widget shows what the source side sees, with a coloured indicator for whether the match is closer than 2:1 SWR.
ch1_9.impedanceCallout: The square is the whole point. A 2:1 turns ratio gives a 4:1 impedance ratio. A 3:1 turns ratio gives a 9:1 impedance ratio. A 7:1 turns ratio gives a 49:1 impedance ratio — the spec for a 49:1 unun on an end-fed half-wave antenna. Every common ratio you'll see in an antenna catalogue (4:1, 9:1, 16:1, 49:1) is a turns-ratio squared.
ch1_9.lossesIntro: The three formulas above describe an ideal transformer. Real transformers come close — power-mains units run 90–98% efficient, small RF ones a little less — but four loss mechanisms keep the actual numbers slightly off. None of them are showstoppers; you just need to know they're there.
ch1_9.lossesMagnetising: Magnetising current. This is the current the primary draws to maintain the changing magnetic flux in the core — and it flows whether or not the secondary is loaded. The reason: Faraday's law (V_{p} \approx N_{p} \cdot \frac{d\Phi}{dt}) ties the flux to the primary voltage itself, not to the load. The source forces a sinusoidal V_{p} across the primary; the flux has to change to match; so the primary keeps pulling enough current to build that flux up cycle after cycle. The magnetising current sits 90° behind the voltage: it is reactive. Physically: during one quarter of the cycle the source pushes energy into the magnetic field building up in the core; during the next quarter, as the field collapses, that same energy flows back out into the source. The net energy transfer per cycle is zero, so on its own this current doesn't dissipate as heat — the magnetic field is a temporary store, not a sink. A well-designed iron-core transformer with the secondary open draws 5–10% of its full-load primary current — almost all of it reactive. The small real fraction comes from the three other loss mechanisms covered below (core losses + winding resistance) and is what keeps an idle mains transformer warm to the touch.
ch1_9.lossesLeakage: Leakage inductance. Not every line of flux generated by the primary actually reaches the secondary; a small fraction takes a shortcut through the air. From the secondary's point of view that flux is missing, so the induced voltage is slightly low — and the «missing» flux acts like a tiny inductor in series with each winding. Loaded transformers droop a few percent at full current because of this, and the droop gets worse at higher frequencies.
ch1_9.leakageDiagramAria: Transformer cross-section with a rectangular iron core; primary winding on the left limb, secondary on the right. A bold blue arrow traces the main flux looping through the iron and threading both windings. A thin dashed orange loop in the window represents leakage flux that closes back on the primary through air, never reaching the secondary.
ch1_9.leakageDiagramCaption: The main flux <var>Φ_{m}</var> closes through the iron and threads both windings — this is what carries power across. The leakage flux <var>Φ_{l}</var> takes a shortcut through air and never reaches the secondary, so it behaves like a tiny inductor in series with each winding.
ch1_9.lossesCopper: Copper losses (I^{2}R). The wire used for the windings has resistance. Current through resistance dissipates as heat. The bigger the load, the bigger the current, the worse the heating — and unlike the other three losses, this one scales with the square of the load current.
ch1_9.lossesCore: Core losses. The core itself absorbs some energy from each AC cycle. Hysteresis loss — the magnetic domains in the iron resist flipping back and forth, and that resistance shows up as heat. Eddy currents — the changing flux induces little circulating currents inside the core itself, just like in any conductor sitting in a changing field. Lamination of iron cores into thin insulated sheets breaks up the eddy-current paths, which is why every cheap mains transformer has those visible stripes on its sides. Ferrite cores are non-conductive, so they sidestep the eddy problem entirely.
ch1_9.lossesEfficiencyCallout: Practical efficiency. A small mains transformer at full load: 80–90%. A large one: 95–98%. A small RF broadband transformer on a ferrite toroid: 80–95%. The other 2–20% becomes heat. None of the four losses scale with what you wish they would: leakage gets worse with frequency, copper gets worse with current, core gets worse with flux density. Real-world transformer ratings come with both a power limit and a frequency range — exceed either and one of the losses catches up to you.
ch1_9.sectionCores: The cores you'll meet at the bench
ch1_9.coresIntro: Three core families dominate radio work. They behave so differently that the «right» one depends entirely on what frequency you're working at and what shape the signal is.
ch1_9.coresIron: Laminated iron (silicon steel). The classic mains-transformer brick. Made of thin iron-alloy sheets stacked into E and I shapes (you can see the edges if you peer at any 50 Hz / 60 Hz transformer). High permeability — a small number of turns gives a big inductance. But iron's electrical conductivity means eddy currents are a problem above audio, so iron-core transformers are limited to roughly 50 Hz – 20 kHz. Used for: mains step-down power supplies, audio output transformers in tube amps, microphone matching transformers.
ch1_9.coresFerrite: Ferrite. A non-conductive ceramic of iron oxide. Because it doesn't conduct, eddy currents are negligible and ferrite cores work all the way up into the GHz range. The «mix» numbers identify the frequency band: mix #43 for 1 MHz to 30 MHz (HF amateur work), mix #61 for 30 MHz to 300 MHz (VHF), mix #31 for low-frequency common-mode chokes. Most ferrite cores are shaped as toroids (donuts) — winding self-shielded, almost no leakage flux. Used for: broadband RF transformers, baluns and ununs, switching power supplies, EMI suppression chokes.
ch1_9.coresPowderedIron: Powdered iron. Iron particles bound in an insulating matrix. Lower permeability than ferrite but much more stable with temperature and current. Lower core loss too, which means higher Q in tuned circuits. Colour-coded by mix: T-50-2 «red» for 1–30 MHz, T-50-6 «yellow» for 10–50 MHz. Used for: tuned RF transformers, traps, narrow-band matching networks where Q matters more than bandwidth.
ch1_9.coresAir: Air core. No core at all — just a coil wound on a cardboard or plastic former. Low coupling between windings (the field spreads), so the simple turns-ratio formulas don't apply cleanly. But there's no core to saturate, no hysteresis, no temperature dependence. Used for: VHF / UHF tuned transformers, high-Q resonant circuits, very-high-power circuits where any core would saturate or burn.
ch1_9.coresGalleryAria: Side-by-side gallery of three transformer cores. Left: a rectangular laminated iron core in E-I shape with two coil windings on its central leg, drawn with stripes to show the laminations. Middle: a circular ferrite toroid drawn as a dark ring, with a coil wound around its body in a continuous helix. Right: a powdered-iron toroid, drawn the same shape as the ferrite but with a redder colour to indicate the iron-powder material.
ch1_9.coresGalleryCaption: The three core families used in radio. Each suits a different frequency range and use case: laminated iron for low-frequency power, ferrite for broadband RF, powdered iron for tuned RF.
ch1_9.topologyTwoWinding: Two-winding (isolated). The textbook transformer: primary and secondary are separate windings sharing only the core. No copper connects them — a fault on one side cannot pass DC or low-impedance leakage to the other. This galvanic isolation is the reason every safety-critical mains transformer is two-winding. Every example we worked above is a two-winding transformer.
ch1_9.topologyAuto: Autotransformer. A single winding with a tap partway along — part of the winding serves as both primary and secondary. Cheaper, smaller, lighter than a two-winding transformer of the same rating, because each turn does double duty. The catch: no isolation. A fault on one side reaches the other through the shared winding. Common as a Variac (a continuously adjustable autotransformer used to set output mains voltage on a test bench), and inside some power supplies where isolation is provided elsewhere. Same turns-ratio formulas apply — the «turns ratio» is just the ratio of the full winding to the tapped portion.
ch1_9.topologyBalun: Balun. Short for «BALanced–UNbalanced». A specialised transformer that connects a balanced source (two equal-and-opposite signals, like a dipole's two halves) to an unbalanced load (one signal plus ground, like coaxial cable). At the same time, a balun can transform impedance — the most common amateur balun is 4:1 (2:1 turns ratio, squared = 4:1 impedance), used to match a 200 Ω folded dipole to a 50 Ω coax feedline. Baluns are nearly always wound on ferrite toroids using bifilar (two parallel wires) windings. The full balun treatment lives in chapter 3.3 with antennas; here you just need to know one exists and what it does.
ch1_9.topologyCallout: The same physics drives all three. Voltage scales with the turns ratio, current with its inverse, impedance with the square. The differences are practical — isolation, cost, balanced-vs-unbalanced — not in the underlying behaviour.
ch1_9.sectionApplications: Where transformers live in a radio
ch1_9.appsPowerSupply: The mains supply. Every mains-powered radio has a step-down transformer somewhere — typically a laminated-iron-core transformer running at mains frequency (50 / 60 Hz), bringing 230 V or 120 V down to whatever DC rail the rig actually runs on (usually 12 V or 13.8 V). The transformer also gives you safety isolation between the mains and the chassis the user touches.
ch1_9.appsAudio: Audio output transformers. Tube amplifiers run their output stages at 3–5 kΩ plate impedance; a typical loudspeaker is 4–8 Ω. An audio transformer with a roughly 25:1 turns ratio (~600:1 impedance) bridges the two. Solid-state power amps don't need the matching transformer — modern transistors deliver enough current at low voltage to drive a speaker directly — but the audio transformer survives in tube gear, broadcast equipment, and high-end studio kit.
ch1_9.appsRfMatching: RF impedance matching. Inside an HF transceiver, broadband ferrite transformers appear at every stage transition where the impedance changes — between the mixer and the IF amplifier, between the IF and the audio detector, between the PA's output and the antenna jack. A typical solid-state HF rig uses two or three of these on the signal path.
ch1_9.appsBalun: Antenna feed (balun / unun). Between the coax coming out of your rig and the wire antenna in the air. A balun if the antenna is balanced (dipole, folded dipole), an unun if both sides are unbalanced (random wire, end-fed half wave). Common ratios — 1:1, 4:1, 9:1, 49:1 — all squared turns ratios.
ch1_9.keyTakeaway1: A transformer is two coils sharing a magnetic field. Energy crosses from one circuit to the other through that field — no copper between them. Only AC: a static current makes a static field, and a static field induces nothing.
ch1_9.keyTakeaway2: Voltage scales with the turns ratio. V_{s} / V_{p} = N_{s} / N_{p}. More turns on the secondary → step-up. Fewer → step-down.
ch1_9.keyTakeaway3: Current scales with the inverse turns ratio. I_{p} / I_{s} = N_{s} / N_{p}. Voltage and current trade places — the high-voltage side carries less current, and vice versa.
ch1_9.keyTakeaway4: Impedance scales with the SQUARE of the turns ratio. Z_{p} / Z_{s} = (N_{p} / N_{s})2. This is the punchline for radio: a 2:1 turns ratio gives a 4:1 impedance ratio — that's the 4:1 balun; a 7:1 turns ratio gives a 49:1 impedance ratio — the 49:1 EFHW unun.
ch1_9.keyTakeaway5: Real transformers lose 2–20% to four mechanisms: magnetising current, leakage inductance, copper I^{2}R heating, and core losses (hysteresis + eddy currents). None big enough to spoil the formulas; all big enough to matter when you want a precise calibration.
ch1_9.keyTakeaway6: Three core families: laminated iron for power and audio (50 Hz – 20 kHz), ferrite for broadband RF (1 MHz – 1 GHz), powdered iron for tuned RF (1 – 50 MHz, higher Q). Pick by the frequency you're working at, not by what's in the parts bin.
ch1_9.schematicVoltageDemoAria: Schematic of a basic two-winding transformer with an AC source on the primary and a load resistor on the secondary. Left side: a sine-wave voltage source labelled V-sub-p drives the primary winding through two leads. Right side: a resistor R-sub-load is connected across the secondary winding, with one secondary lead labelled V-sub-s. The transformer in the middle has a ratio label of 1 to N reading from primary to secondary, and an iron core is implied by two short vertical lines between the two coils.
ch1_9.schematicVoltageDemoCaption: The basic two-winding transformer. AC source on the primary, load on the secondary. The ratio label «1:N» reads primary turns : secondary turns. N greater than 1 makes a step-up; N less than 1 makes a step-down.
ch1_9.schematicImpedanceMatchAria: Schematic of a transformer used to match impedances. On the primary side, a source labelled «50 Ω rig» drives the primary through a coax-style two-wire connection. On the secondary side, a load labelled «200 Ω antenna» is connected across the secondary. The transformer carries a ratio label of 1:2 between primary and secondary.
ch1_9.schematicImpedanceMatchCaption: 4:1 impedance match using a 2:1 turns ratio (the schematic itself labels the transformer «1:2» — the same ratio written from primary to secondary). The 200 Ω load on the secondary appears as 50 Ω at the primary because the impedance ratio is the SQUARE of the turns ratio. The rig sees a clean 50 Ω match instead of the raw 200 Ω antenna.
ch1_9.schematicAutoAria: Schematic of an autotransformer: a single inductor winding with a tap partway up. The full winding goes between two terminals at the top and bottom, and a third terminal — the tap — connects to a point inside the winding, dividing it into an upper portion and a lower portion. An AC source connects across the full winding; a load connects between the tap and the bottom terminal.
ch1_9.schematicAutoCaption: Autotransformer. A single winding with a tap. The source drives the full winding (top to bottom); the load sees only the lower portion (tap to bottom). The turns ratio is the full-winding turns divided by the tapped-portion turns. No isolation — the load shares the bottom terminal with the source.
ch1_9.schematicBalunAria: Schematic of a 4:1 voltage balun. On the unbalanced side, a 50 Ω coaxial feedline brings the signal in: the inner conductor goes to the balun's primary winding, the outer shield goes to ground. On the balanced side, the secondary's two terminals connect symmetrically to the two halves of an antenna, with no ground reference between them. The balun core is drawn as a ferrite toroid surrounding both windings.
ch1_9.schematicBalunCaption: 4:1 voltage balun. Converts an unbalanced 50 Ω coax feedline (inner conductor + grounded shield) into a balanced 200 Ω antenna feed (two symmetric terminals, no ground). The 4:1 impedance ratio comes from the 2:1 turns ratio (squared). The schematic itself labels the transformer «1:2» — the same ratio written from primary to secondary.
ch1_9.schematicLabAria: Schematic of the lab activity: an Arduino board labelled with the digital pin used as a PWM source connects to one end of the primary winding of a hand-wound toroid transformer. The other primary lead returns to the Arduino's GND pin. On the secondary side, a multimeter set to AC volts is connected across the two secondary leads. The toroid is drawn as a circle representing the ferrite core.
ch1_9.schematicLabCaption: The lab build. Arduino PWM drives the 10-turn primary; the multimeter on AC reads the 40-turn secondary. Expected ratio: 4× the primary RMS voltage.
ch1_9.labGoal: Wind a 4:1 step-up transformer on a small ferrite toroid, drive it with the Arduino as a <square>square-wave</square> source, and verify that the secondary voltage and current match the predicted turns-ratio scaling.
ch1_9.labEquip1: One ferrite toroid — FT-37-43 or FT-50-43 (mix #43, suitable for 1–30 MHz). Any small ferrite donut from a junk-box motherboard or USB-cable lump will work for the demonstration; brand-new toroids are about 1–2 € each from any electronics supplier.
ch1_9.labEquip2: About 60 cm of 0.3–0.5 mm enamelled (magnet) wire — two colours if you can get them, so you can tell primary from secondary apart. Salvaged from a small 5 V transformer or bought new on a small spool.
ch1_9.labEquip3: True-RMS multimeter with an AC voltage range that goes down to ~1 V full scale (most do).
ch1_9.labEquip4: Arduino Uno (or any board with a PWM pin) and a USB cable. We use it as a square-wave source — no clever code required.
ch1_9.labComp1: Transformer (you wind it): 10-turn primary + 40-turn secondary on the toroid. Each «turn» is one full pass of the wire through the centre hole.
ch1_9.labComp2: Resistor: 1 kΩ, 1/4 W, for the loaded test in step 5.
ch1_9.labComp3: Wire: two short jumper leads (5–10 cm) to connect the primary to the Arduino's PWM pin and GND.
ch1_9.labStep1: Wind the primary first: 10 turns of one colour. Pass the wire through the toroid hole, around the outside, back through the hole — that's one turn. Space the turns evenly around the ring. Leave 5 cm of lead at each end. Strip the enamel off the last 1 cm of each lead with sandpaper or a sharp knife; enamel is invisible, but it's an insulator and will block contact with the multimeter probes if you don't.
ch1_9.labStep2: Wind the secondary on top of the primary: 40 turns of the other colour, in the same direction as the primary, spread evenly around the same toroid. Same lead length, same enamel-stripping.
ch1_9.labStep3: Upload the standard «Blink» sketch to the Arduino, but change the pin to one of the PWM pins (3, 5, 6, 9, 10, or 11) and the delays to 1 ms on / 1 ms off. That gives you a 500 Hz square wave — well inside the audio range where the toroid behaves as an ordinary transformer. (If you'd rather use analogWrite, set the PWM pin to a 50% duty cycle — same result.)
ch1_9.labStep4: Connect the primary leads: one to the chosen PWM pin, the other to the Arduino's GND pin. Power the Arduino over USB.
ch1_9.labStep5: Set the multimeter to AC volts, lowest range that goes above 5 V (most have a 20 V AC range). Touch the probes to the secondary leads. Expected reading: about 4 V AC. The Arduino's 5 V square wave has an RMS of about 2.5 V on a 50% duty cycle, scaled by the 4:1 turns ratio gives 10 V — but the meter reads peak-rectified rather than true RMS on a square wave unless yours is true-RMS, so cheaper meters land in the 4–8 V range. The exact number depends on the meter; the ratio compared to the primary voltage is what matters.
ch1_9.labStep6: Optional load test: clip the 1 kΩ resistor across the secondary leads. The secondary voltage will drop a bit (the leakage inductance and copper resistance kick in under load). The Arduino's current draw will rise — measure with a USB power monitor if you have one — confirming that current on the primary side scales up when current on the secondary side scales up.
ch1_9.labExpected: Without load on the secondary: secondary AC reading ≈ 4 × primary AC reading (matching the 4:1 turns ratio). With the 1 kΩ load: secondary voltage drops ~10–20% but the ratio still hovers near 3.5×–4×; primary current rises in compensation.
ch1_9.labConnection: What you just built is a tiny version of the broadband ferrite transformer used in every HF transmitter to match between IF and PA stages. The ratio formulas you measured at audio frequencies behave identically at HF — the ferrite mix and core size set the operating range, but the underlying physics is the same one we'll use in chapter 3.3 to design a 4:1 antenna balun.
ch1_9.labTrouble1: No reading on the secondary. The most likely culprit is enamel still on the leads — the wire looks bare but isn't. Re-strip the last 1 cm of each lead and re-test. Second culprit: a broken solder-style twist on the multimeter probes; touch the probes together and confirm continuity beep first.
ch1_9.labTrouble2: Reading jumps around. 500 Hz is at the very low end of cheap multimeters' AC bandwidth; some auto-range slowly. Switch to manual range, give it a couple of seconds to settle. If it still won't lock, raise the PWM frequency by changing the delays to 0.5 ms / 0.5 ms (1 kHz) — most multimeters are happy there.
ch1_9.labTrouble3: Reading is much lower than 4×. Either the secondary turns count is off (re-count by tracing the wire through the hole — a half-turn is easy to miscount), or the turns are wound in opposite directions. The second case still works as a transformer — but the polarity is flipped and you'll see the same magnitude as expected; if you're seeing < 1× it's almost certainly a turn-count miscount.
ch1_9.quiz_q1: Which of the following will not work as a transformer's input?
ch1_9.quiz_q1_b: A 5 V square wave from an Arduino
ch1_9.quiz_q1_explanation: A transformer needs a changing magnetic field to induce a voltage on the secondary. A DC battery delivers a steady current, which makes a steady field, which induces nothing. The other three sources are all AC or pulsed, so they all work.
ch1_9.quiz_q2: A transformer has 100 turns on its primary and 25 turns on its secondary. You apply 240 V AC to the primary. What voltage appears on the secondary?
ch1_9.quiz_q2_explanation: <nowrap><var>V_{s}</var> = <var>V_{p}</var> × <var>N_{s}</var> / <var>N_{p}</var></nowrap> = <nowrap>240 × 25 / 100 = 60 V</nowrap>. Fewer turns on the secondary means a step-down in voltage.
ch1_9.quiz_q3: The same transformer (100:25 turns) drives a load drawing 4 A on the secondary. What current flows in the primary?
ch1_9.quiz_q3_explanation: Current scales with the inverse turns ratio. I_{p} = I_{s} × N_{s} / N_{p} = 4 × 25 / 100 = 1 A. The voltage stepped down 4×, so the current must step up 4× to keep power constant — but on the primary side, where the voltage is higher, the current is correspondingly lower.
ch1_9.quiz_q4: A 200 Ω antenna is connected to the secondary of a 1:2 turns-ratio transformer. What impedance does the source on the primary side see?
ch1_9.quiz_q4_explanation: Impedance scales with the square of the turns ratio. Z_{p} = Z_{s} × (N_{p} / N_{s})2 = 200 × (1/2)2 = 200 × 1/4 = 50 Ω. This is exactly the 4:1 balun used to match a folded dipole to coax.
ch1_9.quiz_q5: You want a transformer that converts a 50 Ω feedline to a 450 Ω random-wire antenna. What turns ratio do you need?
ch1_9.quiz_q5_explanation: Impedance ratio = 450 / 50 = 9, so the turns ratio is <nowrap>√9 = 3</nowrap>. The primary (50 Ω side) has fewer turns, the secondary (450 Ω side) has more, so the ratio reads 1:3 from primary to secondary. The full transformer is a 9:1 unun.
ch1_9.quiz_q6: Which loss mechanism scales with the square of the load current?
ch1_9.quiz_q6_explanation: Power dissipated in resistance is P = I^{2}R — the square of current times the resistance. This is why winding wire is sized for the worst-case current, and why mains transformers get noticeably hotter at full load than at half load even though the field is the same.
ch1_9.quiz_q7: Which core type is the right choice for a broadband HF transformer covering 1.8 MHz to 30 MHz?
ch1_9.quiz_q7_explanation: Mix #43 ferrite is the standard for HF broadband transformers. Laminated iron is too lossy above audio. Powdered iron has lower loss but is for narrow-band tuned circuits, not broadband. Air core has too little permeability for compact broadband transformers.
ch1_9.quiz_q8: What is the main advantage of an autotransformer over a two-winding transformer of the same rating?
ch1_9.quiz_q8_a: It is smaller, lighter, and cheaper
ch1_9.quiz_q8_d: It works on DC as well as AC
ch1_9.quiz_q8_explanation: An autotransformer reuses one winding for both primary and secondary, so it needs less copper and a smaller core for the same VA rating. The trade-off: no isolation — primary and secondary share copper, so a fault on one side reaches the other directly. (None of the other answers is correct: an autotransformer is worse for isolation, has comparable magnetising current, and like every transformer cannot pass DC.)
ch1_9.quiz_q9: Why are iron-core transformer cores built from thin laminated sheets rather than from a single solid block?
ch1_9.quiz_q9_a: Laminations make the transformer cheaper to manufacture
ch1_9.quiz_q9_b: Laminations break up eddy-current paths in the core
ch1_9.quiz_q9_c: Laminations increase the core's magnetic permeability
ch1_9.quiz_q9_explanation: The changing magnetic field in the core induces circulating currents in the iron itself — eddy currents — which heat the core and waste energy. Stacking thin insulated sheets breaks up the conducting paths into small isolated loops, which can carry far less current. Ferrite cores sidestep the issue entirely because ferrite doesn't conduct.
ch1_9.quiz_q10: A balun on a folded-dipole antenna feed has a 4:1 impedance ratio. What turns ratio does that imply?
ch1_9.quiz_q10_explanation: Impedance ratio is the square of the turns ratio: 4 = (turns ratio)2 → turns ratio = √4 = 2, written as 1:2 from primary to secondary. The 4:1 voltage balun is the most common one in the HF amateur shack — used to feed a folded dipole (≈ 200 Ω) from 50 Ω coax.

magCurrent.title: Magnetising current over time
magCurrent.description: Drag the phase slider to see how primary voltage, magnetising current, and stored field energy line up across one full cycle. The play button animates the cycle.
magCurrent.ariaLabel: Plot of normalised primary voltage (sine) and magnetising current (cosine, lagging by 90°) over one full cycle
magCurrent.hint: Notice: when the voltage hits its peak, the current is crossing zero — and vice versa. That's the 90° lag: the two are never both large at the same instant, so the average power V·I over a full cycle is zero.

turnsRatio.title: Turns ratio calculator
turnsRatio.description: Set the primary and secondary turn counts and the primary voltage. The widget gives the secondary voltage and current, and tells you whether you've built a step-up or a step-down.
turnsRatio.hint: The current side is calculated by treating the transformer as ideal — power in equals power out. Real transformers lose 2–20% along the way.

impedance.title: Impedance transformer
impedance.description: Set the load impedance on the secondary and the turns ratio. The widget gives the impedance the source on the primary side actually sees.
impedance.hint: Common antenna impedances: 50 Ω (most rigs), 75 Ω (TV coax), 200 Ω (folded dipole), 450 Ω (random wire), 2450 Ω (end-fed half wave).

ch1_10.heroAriaLabel: Pen-and-ink sketch of a glass-bodied through-hole diode on the left, with its schematic-symbol counterpart on the right; a small pair of arrows between them shows that the part on the workbench and the triangle-and-bar in a circuit diagram are the same object.
ch1_10.intro1: Every component you have met so far — resistors, capacitors, inductors, transformers — is linear: double the voltage across it, double the current through it. The diode is the first deliberately non-linear component in this course. It conducts current in one direction and blocks it in the other. That single property — «one-way valve for electrons» — is enough to turn AC into DC, protect a circuit from an accidentally reversed battery, hold a steady reference voltage, and catch the inductive kick that would otherwise destroy a transistor when a relay opens.
ch1_10.intro2: In this chapter we meet the diode as a circuit element: what its symbol says, what its current–voltage curve looks like, and the four jobs it does in almost every piece of radio equipment ever built — rectification, voltage regulation, flyback protection, and signal detection. Transistors come next chapter; everything they do depends on understanding diodes first.
ch1_10.symbolIntro: A diode has two terminals: the anode (positive side, the «entrance») and the cathode (negative side, the «exit»). Conventional current flows easily from anode to cathode and is blocked from cathode to anode — like a one-way mechanical check valve in a water pipe. The schematic symbol shows this directly: the triangle is an arrow that points the way current is allowed to flow, and the bar at the tip is a wall that stops current trying to flow the other way.
ch1_10.symbolKey: On a real diode, the cathode is marked by a painted band on the body — same end as the bar in the schematic symbol. Get this end right when you put the part in a circuit, or it will simply not conduct.
ch1_10.sectionIv: The I–V curve and the forward voltage drop
ch1_10.ivIntro: Resistors obey Ohm's law: double the voltage, double the current. A diode does not. Below a certain «knee voltage», almost no current flows. Above the knee, current rises so rapidly that doubling the voltage can multiply current by a million. The graph below makes this concrete.
ch1_10.ivCurveExplain: Try this: pick a diode, then drag the V slider. Notice how, below the knee, the current readout reads «≈ 0» on a 25-mA scale (it is actually flowing — just nanoamps, far too small to see). Push past the knee and the curve goes nearly vertical: roughly another 100 mV across the diode multiplies current by ten. That ten-per-100-mV blow-up is what makes diodes useful as switches: in a circuit driving them past the knee, they look like a low-resistance wire; below it, they look like an open switch.
ch1_10.ivKnee: The voltage at which the curve takes off is the forward voltage drop, written V_F. It is set by the semiconductor material: silicon diodes have V_F ≈ 0.6–0.7 V; Schottky diodes (a metal-semiconductor junction instead of silicon-silicon) have V_F ≈ 0.2–0.3 V; LEDs have V_F set by the colour — red ≈ 1.8 V, green ≈ 2.1 V, blue and white ≈ 3.0 V. The wider the semiconductor's band gap (the energy interval an electron has to «jump» to release a photon), the bluer the light and the higher V_F.
ch1_10.ivRule: Rule of thumb when designing. A conducting silicon diode drops ≈ 0.7 V across itself, almost regardless of the current flowing through it (this is the «vertical-curve past the knee» fact you saw in the widget above). By Kirchhoff's voltage law the drops around a series loop have to sum to the source voltage, so if 5 V drives a series diode + resistor, the resistor takes whatever is left over: 5 − 0.7 = 4.3 V. Pick the resistor accordingly. For a Schottky use 0.3 V; for a red LED, 1.8 V.
ch1_10.ivCalloutExperiment: On the bench you can measure V_F directly with most multimeters' diode-test mode. The meter pushes ≈ 1 mA through the part and reads the voltage that develops across it. Anode on red probe, cathode on black: a working silicon diode reads ≈ 0.6 V; reverse the leads and it reads «OL» (open-loop). Measuring an LED this way also lights it dimly — handy for distinguishing red, green, and blue LEDs in an unmarked drawer.
ch1_10.sectionHalfWave: Half-wave rectifier — the simplest AC-to-DC converter
ch1_10.halfWaveIntro: Now use the «one-way valve» to do a job. The mains and the wall-wart in your house are <ac>AC</ac>; almost every electronic device runs on <dc>DC</dc>. Somewhere in between sits a <rect>rectifier</rect>: a diode (or four) that turns the alternating waveform into a one-direction one. The simplest version is a single diode in series with the load:
ch1_10.halfWaveSchematicCaption: Half-wave rectifier. The diode D blocks negative half-cycles of V_{\mathrm{in}}; the load R_L sees only the positive halves.
ch1_10.halfWaveExplain: When the AC source's anode-end is positive (top of the cycle), the diode conducts: current flows through <var>R_L</var>. When the source reverses (bottom of the cycle), the diode is reverse-biased and blocks: no current, no output voltage. The load sees a series of positive half-sine bumps with zero gaps between them — half-wave rectified output. This is the shape of <var>V_{\mathrm{out}}</var> in the picture below.
ch1_10.halfWaveWaveformCaption: Top: input <var>V_{\mathrm{in}}</var> swings ±<var>V_{\mathrm{peak}}</var>. Bottom: output <var>V_{\mathrm{out}}</var> across the load — only the positive halves get through, dropped slightly by the diode's <var>V_F</var>.
ch1_10.halfWaveWaveformAria: Two stacked plots over a shared time axis. The top plot is a sine wave swinging between positive and negative peak voltage. The bottom plot shows half-cycle bumps separated by flat zero-voltage gaps — only the positive halves of the input pass through.
ch1_10.halfWaveCaution: Half-wave rectification has two flaws: only half the input energy reaches the load (the other half is wasted as the diode blocks it), and the gap between bumps is as long as a bump itself, so the output is more zero than not. Useful for low-current battery chargers and signal detection; not useful when you actually want a steady DC supply. The fix — bridge rectifier + smoothing capacitor — is next.
ch1_10.sectionBridge: Bridge rectifier and the smoothing capacitor
ch1_10.bridgeIntro: Four diodes in a bridge use both halves of the AC cycle. When the AC source is positive on one node, two of the diodes conduct (one on the way out, one on the way back); when it reverses, the other two conduct. Either way, current through the load goes the same direction. The output is now twice as many bumps with no flat gaps — full-wave rectification.
ch1_10.bridgeSchematicCaption: Bridge rectifier with DC+ and DC− output terminals. On the positive half-cycle of V_{\mathrm{in}}, current flows AC+ → D1 → DC+ → R_L → DC− → D3 → AC−. On the negative half-cycle the diagonally-opposite pair D2 + D4 takes over, and current through R_L still flows in the same direction. Note the clockwise numbering D1 → D2 → D3 → D4: the diodes that conduct together are always the two opposite corners of the diamond.
ch1_10.bridgeAfter: The output is still pulsating, not smooth: voltage drops to zero at every zero-crossing of the input. To turn the bumps into a near-flat DC rail you add a smoothing capacitor across the load. The cap charges fast on the way up to each peak (the diodes conduct), then discharges slowly through the load between peaks (diodes blocked). What you read on the load is now the cap's voltage, which only sags a little between peaks. The «sag» is the ripple voltage — and the bigger the cap, the smaller the ripple:
ch1_10.rippleCalloutMath: Ripple sizing rule. Peak-to-peak ripple voltage ΔV ≈ I_{\mathrm{load}} · t_{\mathrm{period}} / C. For 50 Hz mains after a bridge, t_{\mathrm{period}} = 10 ms (100 Hz ripple). So a 100 mA load with a 470 µF capacitor has a peak-to-peak ripple of ≈ 0.1 × 0.01 / 470·10⁻⁶ ≈ 2 V. Want it down to 200 mV? You need 4700 µF.
ch1_10.bridgeNote: Almost every wall-wart, bench supply, and amateur-radio power supply uses this circuit (or a switching variant of it) as its first stage. After the cap comes a regulator — a Zener for low currents, a three-terminal regulator for medium loads, a switching regulator for high efficiency. The regulator turns the still-rippling rail into a clean fixed voltage, and the next section meets the simplest version of one.

diodeIv.title: Diode I–V curve
diodeIv.description: Pick a diode family, drag the voltage slider, and watch the current explode past the knee. The three curves have the same shape — only the knee position differs.
diodeIv.ariaLabel: Plot of diode current versus voltage for three diode families. Below the knee voltage of each, the curve is flat at zero; above the knee, the curve rises near-vertically as the Shockley exponential takes over.
diodeIv.readoutLead: At V = {{voltage}} the active diode passes I = {{current}}.

silicon.name: Silicon (1N4148)
silicon.note: Knee at ≈ 0.6 V — the workhorse small-signal silicon diode. The 1N4148 is the cheapest and most common signal diode in any hobby kit.

schottky.name: Schottky (1N5819)
schottky.note: Knee at ≈ 0.3 V — half the silicon drop, so much less power wasted in low-voltage rectifiers and detectors. The trade-off is higher reverse leakage current.

ledRed.name: Red LED
ledRed.note: Knee at ≈ 1.8 V — well above silicon. The semiconductor material (GaAsP) has a wider band-gap, which is also what makes it emit red light. Bluer LEDs need wider gaps still: green ≈ 2.1 V, blue/white ≈ 3.0 V.

ripple.title: Smoothing capacitor and ripple
ripple.description: Drag the capacitor value and watch the rectified bumps turn into a near-flat DC rail. Bigger cap → smaller ripple, but a bigger inrush surge at switch-on.
ripple.ariaLabel: Plot of the rectified bridge output (light grey bumps) with the smoothed capacitor output (orange) overlaid. As C increases, the orange trace flattens out toward peak voltage.
ripple.readoutLead: With C = {{cap}}, peak-to-peak ripple ΔV ≈ {{ripple}} and average DC ≈ {{avg}}.
ripple.readoutFormula: ΔV ≈ I_load · t_period / C = (V_peak / R_load) · (1 / (2·f_mains)) / C

zenerRegulator.title: Zener regulator — schematic, I–V curve, and load line
zenerRegulator.description: Drag <var>V_{\mathrm{in}}</var>, <var>R_s</var>, <var>R_L</var>, or pick a different Zener. Watch the <ll>load line</ll> slide horizontally on the I–V chart and the operating point ride the near-vertical Zener curve. The schematic on the left labels each component with its live value (the supply voltage, the voltage drop across <var>R_s</var>, the regulated voltage across the Zener) — every reading updates as you move the sliders.
zenerRegulator.ariaLabelSchematic: Schematic of a Zener voltage regulator built from circuit primitives: a battery, a series resistor, a Zener diode, and an optional load resistor. Each component carries a live numeric label that updates as the user drags the sliders.
zenerRegulator.ariaLabelChart: Plot of the Zener I–V curve in the regulating region. A dashed load line shows the constraint imposed by the supply and the series resistor; the open circle at their intersection marks the operating point.
zenerRegulator.readoutLead: At V_in = {{v_in}} the Zener clamps the output at V_Z = {{v_z}}; current through the loop is I = {{i_z}}, leaving V_Rs = {{v_rs}} dropped across the series resistor.
zenerRegulator.warningDropout: V_in is below the Zener's nominal {{v_z0}} — there is not enough headroom to keep it in breakdown. The output is now whatever the R_s / R_L voltage divider returns, NOT a regulated reference.
zenerRegulator.warningPower: Zener is dissipating {{p_z}}, past its {{p_max}} rating — in real hardware it would overheat. Either raise R_s to limit the current, or use a higher-power Zener.
zenerRegulator.warningKnee: Zener current is only {{i_z}} — close to the «knee» of the I–V curve where r_z grows and regulation gets sloppy. Datasheets typically spec a minimum I_Z of 5–10 mA for clean regulation.

ch1_10.sectionZener: Zener diode and the simple voltage reference
ch1_10.zenerIntro: Reverse-bias an ordinary diode hard enough and it eventually breaks down — passes a large current and (usually) destroys itself. A Zener diode is a diode engineered so that the breakdown is sharp, predictable, and non-destructive: at a specific reverse voltage V_Z, it conducts cleanly. Below V_Z it looks like an open switch; above V_Z it clamps the voltage almost perfectly. That sharp clamp is what makes a Zener useful as a cheap voltage reference.
ch1_10.zenerHowSlope: Wait — the breakdown region on the I–V curve is not truly vertical: voltage does creep upward as current grows. So how is this «stabilization»? Two things hide behind that picture. First, the slope is much smaller than it looks. A typical 5.1 V Zener has a dynamic resistance r_z ≈ 5–15 Ω, so a 10 mA change in current shifts the voltage by only ~100 mV. The visible tilt on the plot comes from how the current axis is scaled — at equal axis scales the breakdown line would read as nearly vertical.
ch1_10.zenerHowModel: A handy mental model of a Zener in regulating mode: an ideal «battery» with voltage V_Z, in series with a small resistor r_z. The voltage between the two terminals is then V = V_Z + I × r_z. The first term (e.g. 5.1 V) is a constant the current cannot affect; the second is the small rise in voltage with current that gives the curve its tilt. The word «dynamic» in the name of r_z does not mean «varying» — it means «describing the response to a change in current»: r_z = ΔV / ΔI is the slope of the curve, not the ratio V/I. For a plain resistor those two numbers coincide; for a non-linear element like a Zener in breakdown they do not — and the slope, not the ratio, is what matters. Across the regulating region r_z is approximately constant.
ch1_10.zenerHowCircuit: Second — and this is the key — a Zener does not stabilize voltage on its own. Stabilization happens only inside the circuit <nowrap><var>V_{\mathrm{in}}</var> → <var>R_s</var> → Zener → GND</nowrap>, with <var>V_{\mathrm{in}}</var> always larger than <var>V_Z</var>. The series resistor <var>R_s</var> does the heavy lifting: it absorbs the difference between <var>V_{\mathrm{in}}</var> and <var>V_Z</var>. When <var>V_{\mathrm{in}}</var> fluctuates, that variation is dropped almost entirely across <var>R_s</var> rather than the Zener — because <var>R_s</var> is much larger than <var>r_z</var> (typically 1 kΩ vs 10 Ω), the <vd>voltage divider</vd> strongly favours <var>R_s</var> as the absorber.
ch1_10.zenerHowExample: Numerical check. Take V_{\mathrm{in}} = 9 V, R_s = 1 kΩ, a 5.1 V Zener with r_z = 10 Ω. Step 1 — Kirchhoff’s voltage law. In a series loop the source voltage divides between R_s and the Zener; the Zener holds its share at V_Z, so R_s takes the rest: V_{\mathrm{in}} − V_Z = 9 − 5.1 = 3.9 V drops across R_s. Step 2 — Ohm’s law on R_s. With 3.9 V across a 1 kΩ resistor: I = 3.9 V / 1 kΩ = 3.9 mA — the same current flows through the Zener (series loop). Step 3 — small r_z correction on the Zener voltage. The «V_Z = 5.1 V» on the datasheet is the value at some reference current; the actual voltage on the Zener depends slightly on the current passing through it, via r_z. So V_Z = 5.1 + I × r_z = 5.1 + 3.9 mA × 10 Ω ≈ 5.14 V. (Step 1 used 5.1 V as a 1 % simplification — the 40 mV refinement here is exactly what makes the next part interesting.) Now bump V_{\mathrm{in}} to 12 V: R_s now takes 6.9 V, so I ≈ 6.9 mA, and by Step 3 V_Z ≈ 5.1 + 6.9 mA × 10 Ω ≈ 5.17 V. V_{\mathrm{in}} changed by 3 V (33 %); V_Z changed by 30 mV (0.6 %). That 30 mV is just r_z × ΔI = 10 Ω × 3 mA — Step 3 applied to the change. The 100× attenuation of supply variation equals the 100× ratio between R_s (1 kΩ) and r_z (10 Ω).
ch1_10.zenerHowAnalogy: Overflow-pipe analogy. Picture a pool with an overflow drain at a fixed height on its side wall.
