At the low end sit the very-low, low, and medium-frequency bands; then come <hf>HF</hf> (high frequency, 3–30 MHz — the long-distance workhorse), <vhf>VHF</vhf>, <uhf>UHF</uhf>, and up. Amateurs get slices throughout — the bands the converter named above — and each behaves differently, which is the whole subject of the propagation chapter later. For now, the takeaway is one picture:

polar.caption: Polarisation seen end-on, as the wave travels toward you. The orange arrow is the electric field; its orientation is the polarisation.
polar.ariaLabel: Three end-on views of a wave coming toward the viewer, showing the electric field oriented vertically, horizontally, and rotating for circular polarisation.

spectrum.caption: The electromagnetic spectrum on a logarithmic scale. Radio is just one slice; the same fields at higher frequencies become light and beyond.
spectrum.ariaLabel: A logarithmic frequency axis from kilohertz up to 10 to the 21 hertz, showing the radio, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma-ray regions, with a bracket marking the amateur radio bands.

ch2_1.keyTakeaway1: A radio wave is a self-sustaining disturbance of linked electric and magnetic fields, launched when an alternating current wiggles in a wire — an antenna.
ch2_1.keyTakeaway2: The electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular and in phase — two faces of one wave, not two separate things.
ch2_1.keyTakeaway3: Every electromagnetic wave travels at the speed of light, c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s, no matter its frequency.
ch2_1.keyTakeaway4: Wavelength and frequency are tied by λ = c / f — or, for radio, the shortcut λ in metres = 300 / f in MHz.
ch2_1.keyTakeaway5: Polarisation is the orientation of the electric field, set by the transmitting antenna — the receiving antenna must match it, or much of the signal is lost.
ch2_1.keyTakeaway6: Radio is just the low-frequency end of one continuous electromagnetic spectrum — infrared, visible light, and X-rays are the same kind of wave at higher frequencies.
ch2_1.labGoal: Show that an alternating current in one wire induces a voltage in a nearby wire with nothing connecting them — the bare principle behind every antenna.
ch2_1.labComp1: Two pieces of wire, about 30 cm each
ch2_1.labStep1: Connect Arduino pin 9 to a 30 cm wire — the «transmitting» antenna — and leave its far end free.
ch2_1.labStep2: Load a sketch that toggles pin 9 as fast as the board can — tens of kHz from a simple loop, or up to a few MHz with advanced direct-port tricks. The faster it switches, the stronger the effect.
ch2_1.labStep3: Suspend the second 30 cm wire a few centimetres away, connected only to the oscilloscope probe — probe tip to the wire, ground clip to the Arduino GND.
ch2_1.labStep4: Watch the oscilloscope. With the receive wire close, a small wiggle should appear in step with the transmitted signal — energy crossing the gap with no electrical connection at all.
ch2_1.labStep5: Slowly move the receive wire away. The induced signal shrinks fast; bring it back and it returns.
ch2_1.labExpected: A few to a few tens of millivolts of induced signal at close range, dropping off quickly with distance. It is not a clean radio link — Arduino clock speeds sit far below the ham bands and the power is tiny — but it is unmistakable proof that a wiggling current in one wire reaches another across empty space.
ch2_1.labConnection: What you just built is a scaled-down version of what an <ant>antenna</ant> does. The changing current in the transmitting wire set up a changing field that reached across the gap and induced a current in the receive wire — energy crossing empty space with no connection between them. A real antenna does the same thing, but runs fast and large enough to launch that field as a self-sustaining wave that travels far beyond the bench.
ch2_1.labTrouble1: Nothing at all on the scope: make sure the oscilloscope ground clip goes to the Arduino GND. Without a shared ground reference the scope cannot read the signal.
ch2_1.labTrouble2: The signal does not change as you move the wire: you may be seeing mains hum or coupling through the bench, not your transmitter. Unplug the Arduino for a moment — if the «signal» stays, it is not coming from your wire.
ch2_1.labTrouble3: Very weak even up close: raise the toggling frequency and narrow the gap between the wires. Radiated coupling climbs steeply with frequency.
ch2_1.quiz_q1: What is a radio wave actually made of?
ch2_1.quiz_q1_a: A stream of fast electrons flying through the open air
ch2_1.quiz_q1_b: Vibrating air, just like sound but travelling faster
ch2_1.quiz_q1_c: Linked electric and magnetic fields renewing each other
ch2_1.quiz_q1_d: An electric current flowing along an invisible wire in space
ch2_1.quiz_q1_explanation: A radio wave is a self-sustaining disturbance of electric and magnetic fields — nothing physically travels across the gap, and no medium such as air is needed. It is not sound: sound is moving air and dies in a vacuum, while radio waves cross empty space happily.
ch2_1.quiz_q2: How are the electric and magnetic fields arranged inside an electromagnetic wave?
ch2_1.quiz_q2_a: At right angles, both peaking at the same instant
ch2_1.quiz_q2_b: Parallel to each other, pointing the very same way
ch2_1.quiz_q2_c: At right angles, but one peaks when the other is zero
ch2_1.quiz_q2_d: Randomly, changing direction from moment to moment
ch2_1.quiz_q2_explanation: The two fields sit at a perfect right angle and rise and fall together — they are two aspects of one wave, not separate things. The right-angle direction between them also points the way the wave travels.
ch2_1.quiz_q3: A 2 MHz wave and a 2 GHz wave both leave an antenna. Which one travels faster through space?
ch2_1.quiz_q3_a: The 2 GHz wave — a higher frequency means a higher speed
ch2_1.quiz_q3_b: The 2 MHz wave — lower frequencies travel more easily
ch2_1.quiz_q3_c: It depends on the transmitter's output power
ch2_1.quiz_q3_d: Both travel at the same speed — the speed of light
ch2_1.quiz_q3_explanation: Every electromagnetic wave travels at <var>c</var> ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s regardless of frequency. Frequency sets the wavelength, not the speed.
ch2_1.quiz_q4: Using <var>λ</var> = <var>c</var> / <var>f</var> (shortcut: 300 / <var>f</var> in MHz), what is the wavelength of a 150 MHz signal?
ch2_1.quiz_q4_explanation: 300 / 150 = 2 metres — which is why 150 MHz sits in the «2-metre» region. Higher frequency, shorter wave.
ch2_1.quiz_q5: A wave has a wavelength of 3 metres. What is its frequency?
ch2_1.quiz_q5_explanation: Rearrange the shortcut: <var>f</var> in MHz = 300 / <var>λ</var> in metres = 300 / 3 = 100 MHz.
ch2_1.quiz_q6: What determines the polarisation of a radio wave?
ch2_1.quiz_q6_a: The orientation of its electric field
ch2_1.quiz_q6_c: The frequency the wave was transmitted at
ch2_1.quiz_q6_d: The total distance the wave has travelled
ch2_1.quiz_q6_explanation: Polarisation is simply which way the electric field oscillates — vertical, horizontal, or rotating. A vertical antenna radiates a vertically polarised wave; a horizontal one radiates horizontal.
ch2_1.quiz_q7: Why does receiving a horizontally polarised signal with a vertical antenna give a weak result?
ch2_1.quiz_q7_a: Vertical antennas only work for nearby local signals
ch2_1.quiz_q7_c: Horizontally polarised waves travel noticeably slower
ch2_1.quiz_q7_d: It makes no difference — an antenna catches every polarisation
ch2_1.quiz_q7_explanation: When the antenna does not match the wave's polarisation, far less of the field pushes on its electrons. A 90° mismatch — cross-polarisation — can cut the received signal by more than 20 dB, over 99 % of the power.
ch2_1.quiz_q8: Where does radio sit in the electromagnetic spectrum?
ch2_1.quiz_q8_a: It is a completely separate phenomenon from light
ch2_1.quiz_q8_b: At the high-frequency end, above the gamma rays
ch2_1.quiz_q8_c: At the low-frequency end of one continuous spectrum
ch2_1.quiz_q8_d: Only radio is electromagnetic; the rest are particle streams
ch2_1.quiz_q8_explanation: Radio (about 3 kHz to 300 GHz) is the low-frequency slice of one continuous spectrum. Infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are electromagnetic waves too — same linked fields, same speed, only higher frequencies.

ch2_2.heroAriaLabel: A slow audio waveform on the left feeding into a fast carrier sine, whose peaks swell and shrink to trace the audio — an amplitude-modulated radio wave leaving an antenna on the right.
ch2_2.intro1: In Chapter 2.1 you learned what a radio wave is and that it flies at the speed of light. But a bare wave — a pure, unchanging sine — barely says anything. Switch it on and the only message the world receives is «I am here». This chapter is about the next step: loading real information onto that wave, so it can carry your voice, your Morse, or a stream of data across the planet.
ch2_2.intro2: The craft of doing that is called <mod>modulation</mod>. We will follow one signal all the way through: a voice, turned into electricity by a microphone, gently altering a high-frequency <car>carrier</car> so it can fly. Along the way we will meet the three classic ways radio carries a voice — <am>AM</am>, <ssb>SSB</ssb>, and <fm>FM</fm> — and see why each one occupies the slice of spectrum it does.
ch2_2.sectionMessage: The message: audio and digital signals
ch2_2.messageP1: Start with the thing you actually want to send. Sound is moving air — pressure rising and falling against your eardrum. A microphone is a tiny generator that turns those pressure waves into a voltage that rises and falls in exact step. Plot that voltage against time and you get the wiggly trace you see in any voice-memo app: an audio signal. Human speech lives almost entirely between about 300 Hz and 3 kHz — slow and low compared with the radio frequencies to come.
ch2_2.messageP2: Messages come in two flavours. Some vary smoothly through every in-between value — a voice, music. We call these analog. Others have only a few fixed states — on or off, 1 or 0. We call these digital. Morse code is the original digital signal: the key is either down or up, with nothing in between. Whichever kind it is, this raw, low-frequency information — before it touches a radio — is the baseband signal.
ch2_2.messageP3: On an oscilloscope the two look quite different — one a smooth wiggle, the other a staircase of flat steps:

audioDigital.caption: An analog signal (top) varies smoothly through every value; a digital signal (bottom) jumps between a few fixed levels. Both are «baseband» — the raw message, before modulation.
audioDigital.ariaLabel: Two stacked plots over a shared time axis: the top is a smooth wiggly analog waveform, the bottom is a square digital waveform switching between a low and a high level.

ch2_2.sectionWhy: Why a voice can't fly on its own
ch2_2.whyP1: Here is the obvious question: if the microphone already hands us an electrical signal, why not push it straight into an antenna and be done? Two reasons, and both are fatal.
ch2_2.whyP2: First, antenna size. In Chapter 2.1 we saw that an antenna must be a sizeable fraction of a wavelength to radiate well, and that wavelength is λ = c / f. Put a 3 kHz audio tone through that: λ = 300 000 000 / 3000 = 100 000 m — a wavelength of 100 km. A useful antenna would be a quarter of that, twenty-five kilometres of vertical wire. Nobody is building that.
ch2_2.whyP3: Second, everyone at once. Every human voice occupies the same band, roughly 300 Hz to 3 kHz. Wire them all straight to antennas and every station on Earth would pile into that one narrow sliver of spectrum — a single unintelligible roar, with room for just one conversation on the whole planet.

antennaSize.caption: An antenna must be a fraction of a wavelength. At an audio frequency the wavelength is tens of kilometres; shift the signal up to a radio carrier and the antenna shrinks to something you can hold.
antennaSize.ariaLabel: A size comparison: a 3 kilohertz audio signal needs a 25 kilometre antenna shown next to a tiny human figure, while a 145 megahertz radio carrier needs only a half-metre whip.

ch2_2.whyP4: The fix solves both problems at once. Pick a steady, high-frequency sine — a carrier — high enough that its antenna is a sensible size, and let the voice ride on it by gently altering the carrier in step with the speech. Give each station its own carrier frequency and they stop colliding: tune to 7.10 MHz for one conversation, 7.12 MHz for the next. That deliberate altering of a carrier to make it carry information is exactly what modulation means.
ch2_2.sectionCarrier: The carrier and its three knobs
ch2_2.carrierP1: A carrier is the simplest signal there is: a pure sine wave at one fixed frequency — say 7.1 MHz — with nothing else going on. By itself it carries a single bit of information: present or absent. Switch it on and off in a rhythm and you have Morse code (the mode hams call CW). To send a voice we must do better — we must change the carrier continuously, in step with the speech.
ch2_2.carrierP2: A sine wave gives you exactly three things you can change: its amplitude (how tall it is), its frequency (how tightly its cycles are packed), and its phase (the timing of where a cycle begins). Vary the amplitude in time with the message and you have amplitude modulation (AM). Vary the frequency and you have frequency modulation (FM). Phase modulation, the third, is FM's close cousin and turns up mostly in digital modes — we will meet it later. The diagram shows one carrier modulated all three ways:

carrierKnobs.caption: The same carrier, modulated three ways. AM changes the height, FM changes the spacing of the cycles, PM nudges their timing. The grey line is the message driving each one.
carrierKnobs.ariaLabel: Four stacked waveforms: the message signal on top, then the carrier modulated in amplitude, in frequency, and in phase.

ch2_2.amP1: AM is the oldest and simplest method, and the easiest to picture. Imagine your hand on the volume knob of that steady carrier, turning it up and down in perfect time with your voice. A loud syllable swells the carrier; a quiet moment shrinks it. The outline traced by the carrier's peaks — its <env>envelope</env> — becomes a copy of your speech, riding on the fast carrier underneath.
ch2_2.amP2: We can make that precise without any heavy maths. Write the carrier's height as C and the message as m — a number swinging between −1 and +1 as you speak. AM simply multiplies them: the carrier's height becomes C × (1 + m). That multiplying is not just on paper — in the transmitter a real circuit, the modulator, does it (you will build a crude one in this chapter's lab; full transmitters come in Part III). When you are silent, m = 0 and the carrier sits at its steady height C; speak, and the height breathes up and down. Drag the slider below to drive it harder or softer and watch the envelope:

amExplorer.title: AM modulation explorer
amExplorer.description: Set how hard the message drives the carrier (the modulation index). Watch the envelope breathe in the time view, and the carrier-plus-two-sidebands appear in the frequency view.
amExplorer.indexHint: 0 = unmodulated carrier · 1 = 100 % modulation (envelope just touches zero) · above 1 = overmodulation
amExplorer.overmodWarn: Overmodulated — the envelope is tearing, splattering energy into neighbouring channels.

beat.title: Two tones, one beating wave
beat.description: Each tone below is perfectly pure — its amplitude never changes. Yet their sum has an amplitude that rises and falls: a beat. Slide the tones apart and together. Then read it backwards — a wave whose amplitude wobbles can only be built from more than one frequency.
beat.stateNone: The two tones are identical, so their sum is just one louder tone — no wobble at all.
beat.stateSlow: The tones are close together, so the sum wobbles slowly. That slow rise and fall is the beat.
beat.stateFast: The tones are far apart, so the sum wobbles quickly — a fast beat.

ch2_2.amP3: Something surprising happens if we look at the same signal in the frequency domain instead of in time — that is, a view of how much energy sits at each frequency, the picture a spectrum analyser draws. Multiplying a carrier at frequency f_{C} (C for carrier) by a single audio tone at frequency f_{M} (M for the message) does not just jiggle one frequency — as a plain fact of the arithmetic, it produces three: the carrier itself, unchanged, plus two new tones — one at f_{C} + f_{M} and one at f_{C} − f_{M}. Those two new tones are the sidebands, upper and lower — your audio shifted up and down to sit beside the carrier. All of your voice lives in the sidebands; the carrier sitting between them carries none of it.
ch2_2.amWhence: But that should nag at you: we changed the carrier's amplitude, not its frequency — so how can two brand-new frequencies appear? The answer is hidden in what «a frequency» really means. A pure tone has a single frequency only because its amplitude never changes — it holds the same height forever. The moment that height starts to rise and fall, the wave is no longer one pure tone, and rebuilding it takes more than one. You can hear this for yourself: strike two tuning forks tuned close together — say 440 Hz and 444 Hz — and you hear not two notes but a single note whose loudness throbs. A steady tone cannot throb, so a throbbing loudness is always the fingerprint of two or more frequencies beating against one another — an effect called a beat. Slide the two tones below apart and together, and watch how the amplitude of their sum rises and falls — the very throb you would hear from the forks:
ch2_2.amWhenceClose: That breathing sum is exactly the upper and lower sidebands of an AM signal, on their own — the same two tones, with no carrier between them yet. Notice that the two are different frequencies — one on each side of the centre — even though they carry the same information; that sameness is exactly why SSB (single sideband) will later be able to throw one away and lose nothing. The audio tone itself is never sent on its own — its pitch is carried by how far apart the two sidebands sit, the spacing the slider sets above: the higher the tone, the wider they spread, and the faster their sum throbs. Now add one more tone in the middle — on the spectrum its spike stands taller than the other two, because it carries more energy — that is the carrier, and you have full AM. So the sidebands were never made by a separate step: a carrier whose amplitude breathes simply is several frequencies added together. The breathing envelope (the time view) and the cluster of spikes (the frequency view) are two pictures of one and the same signal.
ch2_2.amP4: How hard you drive the carrier is the modulation index — the largest value m reaches as you speak, or equally the message height divided by the carrier height, from 0 (no modulation) up to 1 (100 %, where the envelope just kisses zero at the quietest instant). Push past 100 % and the envelope tries to go negative, flattening and tearing — overmodulation. The torn waveform sprays energy far outside its own channel — out-of-band emissions, or «splatter» — interfering with everyone nearby.
ch2_2.calloutOvermod: More is not louder. Cranking the microphone gain past 100 % modulation does not make you louder — it distorts your audio and splatters interference across the band. A clean signal at 90 % beats a torn one at 130 % every time.

amPower.title: AM power and bandwidth calculator
amPower.description: An ordinary AM signal sends its carrier in full — and that carrier carries no information at all. See how the watts split, and how wide the signal sits.
amPower.hint: At 100 % modulation each sideband reaches half the carrier's amplitude; and since power goes as amplitude squared, each one carries only a quarter of the carrier's power. The two together make half the carrier's power — which is one-third of the total (carrier plus the two sidebands). Those wasted two-thirds sitting in the carrier are exactly what SSB removes.

ch2_2.ssbP1: AM works, but it is wasteful — and the spectrum is crowded real estate. Look again at what AM actually transmits: a carrier that carries no information, plus two <sb>sidebands</sb> that are mirror-image copies of each other. You are paying to send the very same thing three times over.
ch2_2.ssbP2: SSB — single sideband — is the ruthless edit. First throw away the carrier; it carried nothing. That alone leaves double-sideband (DSB) — both sidebands, no carrier. Then throw away one of the two identical sidebands; the other already says everything. What remains is a single sideband, and every watt of transmitter power now goes into the one piece that actually carries your voice. Keep the upper copy and it is upper sideband (USB); keep the lower and it is lower sideband (LSB).

ssbSpectrum.caption: From full AM to SSB. Full-carrier AM (left) wastes power on the carrier and sends both sidebands; removing the carrier gives DSB; removing one sideband too leaves SSB — the same voice in under half the room.
ssbSpectrum.ariaLabel: Three frequency spectra side by side: full AM with a tall carrier spike and two sidebands; double-sideband suppressed carrier with two sidebands and no carrier; single sideband with just one sideband.

ch2_2.ssbP3: The payoff is efficiency. Dropping the carrier alone saves two-thirds of the power; dropping a sideband halves the bandwidth, from about 6 kHz down to roughly 2.7 kHz. With no carrier, and no power wasted during the pauses between words, SSB wrings the most distance out of every watt — which is why it is the workhorse voice mode on the long-distance HF bands. The price is at the receiver: it must rebuild the missing carrier to make sense of the signal — the carrier set the reference frequency the sidebands are measured against, so without it the recovered tones come out shifted. That shift is why an off-tune SSB station sounds like quacking ducks until you zero it in.
ch2_2.calloutSsbTip: By long-standing convention, amateurs use lower sideband (LSB) below 10 MHz (so on 80 m and 40 m) and upper sideband (USB) above 10 MHz and on VHF/UHF. Nothing in the physics picks a side — the two sidebands carry identical information. In Ukraine, though, that 10 MHz split is not left to convention at all: the Regulations of the Amateur Radio Service require the lower sideband below 10 MHz and the upper one above it. Follow it either way, or everyone you call will sound like ducks.
ch2_2.fmP1: AM rides on the carrier's height; <fm>FM</fm> leaves the height untouched and rides on its <freq>frequency</freq> instead. Swap the volume knob for the tuning knob: nudge the carrier slightly higher in frequency on a loud sound and slightly lower on a quiet one, many times a second, in step with the voice. The carrier's height never changes — only how tightly its cycles are packed.
ch2_2.fmP2: The amount the frequency shifts away from its resting point is the frequency deviation. A loud sound pushes the frequency further from centre; a soft sound barely moves it. (The speed of the wobble follows the pitch of the sound; the size of the swing follows its loudness.) On the 2-metre and 70-centimetre bands, amateur FM typically swings about ±5 kHz at full volume, while narrowband channels use about ±2.5 kHz. Drag the deviation below and watch the cycles bunch and stretch:

fmExplorer.title: FM modulation explorer
fmExplorer.description: Set the frequency deviation — how far the carrier swings from its rest frequency. Watch the cycles bunch up and spread out, while the height stays perfectly constant.
fmExplorer.deviationHint: Larger deviation means a wider swing and a wider signal. Narrowband FM uses a small deviation; wideband FM (and broadcast) uses a large one.

ch2_2.fmP3: Because the message lives in the frequency and not the height, an FM receiver can simply ignore amplitude — and most natural noise (lightning crashes, ignition sparks, motor hiss) arrives as amplitude spikes. The receiver clips the signal flat, throwing those spikes away, and recovers clean audio. That is why FM hisses into silence between stations and why it carries broadcast music. It also brings a neat quirk, the capture effect: when two signals share a frequency, the stronger one completely silences the weaker, instead of the two garbling together as they would on AM.
ch2_2.calloutArmstrong: FM was invented by Edwin Armstrong in 1933 — the same engineer who gave us the superheterodyne receiver you will meet in Part III. He spent years insisting FM's noise immunity was real while the industry, invested in AM, ignored him.
ch2_2.sectionBandwidth: Bandwidth: how much room each mode needs
ch2_2.bwP1: Every mode we have met pays rent in the spectrum, and the rent is <bw>bandwidth</bw> — the width of frequencies the signal actually occupies. The numbers were hiding in plain sight all along: an AM voice spreads its two <sb>sidebands</sb> across about 6 kHz; SSB, with a single sideband, about 2.7 kHz; a <cw>CW</cw> (Morse) signal, barely switching on and off, only a couple of hundred hertz. Narrower modes pack more conversations into the same band.
ch2_2.bwP2: FM is the spendthrift. Its frequency is forever swinging, so it throws off not two sidebands but a whole series of them, and its signal is wider than the deviation alone. A handy estimate is <carson>Carson's rule</carson>: bandwidth ≈ 2 × (<dev>deviation</dev> + highest audio frequency). A 2-metre FM signal with ±5 kHz deviation and 3 kHz audio needs about 2 × (5 kHz + 3 kHz) = 16 kHz — nearly six SSB conversations' worth. (The 5 kHz here is the one-sided ±5 kHz deviation, not the full swing.) That width is the price FM pays for its noise immunity. Compare the modes side by side:

bandwidth.title: Bandwidth visualiser
bandwidth.description: Pick a mode and see how much spectrum it occupies — and how many fit in a slice of band. For FM, adjust the deviation and audio and watch Carson's rule respond.
bandwidth.hint: CW sips spectrum; SSB is the efficient voice mode; AM doubles it; FM trades width for noise immunity. This is why crowded HF bands run SSB and CW, while spacious VHF/UHF can afford FM.
bandwidth.deviationOnly: Deviation and audio only apply to the FM modes.

ch2_2.keyTakeaway1: A carrier is a bare sine wave at one frequency; modulation loads information onto it by varying one of its three properties — amplitude (AM), frequency (FM), or phase (PM).
ch2_2.keyTakeaway2: Audio cannot be radiated directly: its wavelength would demand an impossible antenna, and every voice would crowd the same band. A high-frequency carrier fixes both at once.
ch2_2.keyTakeaway3: AM varies the carrier's amplitude, producing a carrier plus two sidebands at f_{C} ± f_{M}. The information lives in the sidebands; the carrier carries none of it.
ch2_2.keyTakeaway4: SSB deletes the carrier and one redundant sideband — the same voice in about 2.7 kHz instead of 6 kHz, with every watt doing useful work. It is the HF voice workhorse.
ch2_2.keyTakeaway5: FM varies the carrier's frequency by the deviation; its constant amplitude lets the receiver discard noise spikes (and gives the capture effect). It is standard on VHF/UHF.
ch2_2.keyTakeaway6: Bandwidth is the spectrum a signal occupies: ≈ 200 Hz for CW, ≈ 2.7 kHz for SSB, ≈ 6 kHz for AM, ≈ 16 kHz for narrowband FM (Carson's rule: 2 × (deviation + audio)).
ch2_2.labGoal: Generate an amplitude-modulated waveform and see its envelope on the oscilloscope — the very outline an AM receiver's detector reads to recover the sound.
ch2_2.labStep1: Load a sketch that drives two pins: pin 9 as a fast «carrier» (the Arduino's default PWM, ~490 Hz) and pin 6 as a very slow «audio» tone, around 10 Hz. The slow tone stands in for a voice, slowed right down so the envelope is easy to see.
ch2_2.labStep2: Mix them: run pin 6 through one 10 kΩ <res>resistor</res> and pin 9 through the other, joining both at a single point. This crude two-resistor mixer makes the fast carrier ride up and down on the slow tone.
ch2_2.labStep3: Probe that joined point with the oscilloscope — tip to the node, ground clip to the Arduino GND. Set the timebase slow enough to see several slow cycles across the screen.
ch2_2.labStep4: Watch the trace: the fast carrier should swell and shrink about ten times a second, its peaks tracing the slow «audio». That breathing outline is amplitude modulation.
ch2_2.labStep5: For a cleaner demo, replace the slow tone with a function generator, or build a proper analog multiplier around an MC1496 or AD633 chip — the two-resistor mix is illustrative, not a true multiplier.
ch2_2.labExpected: The fast trace's height rising and falling in step with the slow tone — a textbook AM envelope. It is not a clean broadcast signal (the «carrier» is audio-rate, not RF, and the mixer is crude) but the shape is exactly right.
ch2_2.labConnection: The envelope you are watching is precisely what an AM receiver's detector pulls out: strip away the fast carrier and the slow outline left behind is the recovered «audio». Looking at AM on a scope is the same view your radio has of the signal.
ch2_2.labTrouble1: Flat carrier, no breathing: check that pin 6 is really running the slow tone, and that both resistors actually meet at the same node.
ch2_2.labTrouble2: Nothing on the scope at all: send the ground clip to the Arduino GND, and make sure the timebase is not so fast that you only see a single carrier cycle.
ch2_2.labTrouble3: Envelope too subtle to see: keep the two resistors equal, or lower the «audio» resistor a little so the slow tone has more say.
ch2_2.quiz_q1: Why can't a microphone's audio signal be fed straight to an antenna and broadcast?
ch2_2.quiz_q1_a: Its wavelength is far too long for any practical antenna
ch2_2.quiz_q1_b: Audio is too weak to push any current into an antenna
ch2_2.quiz_q1_c: Antennas can only radiate digital, not analogue, signals
ch2_2.quiz_q1_d: Air strongly absorbs every frequency below about 1 MHz
ch2_2.quiz_q1_explanation: A 3 kHz tone has a wavelength of about 100 km, so a useful antenna would be tens of kilometres long — impossible. And every human voice sits in the same 300 Hz–3 kHz band, so they would all collide. Modulation lifts the audio onto a high-frequency carrier, shrinking the antenna and giving each station its own slot.
ch2_2.quiz_q2_a: The metal wire that carries current up to the antenna
ch2_2.quiz_q2_b: A steady sine wave at a single fixed frequency
ch2_2.quiz_q2_c: The raw audio signal coming straight out of the microphone
ch2_2.quiz_q2_d: The battery supply that powers the whole transmitter
ch2_2.quiz_q2_explanation: A carrier is a pure single-frequency sine. On its own it says only «present or absent»; modulation makes it carry real information by varying its amplitude, frequency, or phase.
ch2_2.quiz_q3: In AM, what does the transmitter vary in time with the voice?
ch2_2.quiz_q3_explanation: AM is amplitude modulation: the carrier's height swells and shrinks with the message, tracing an «envelope» that is a copy of the audio. FM varies frequency instead.
ch2_2.quiz_q4: An AM transmitter sends a carrier at <var>f_{C}</var> modulated by a single tone at <var>f_{M}</var>. What appears in the spectrum?
ch2_2.quiz_q4_a: Just the original carrier at <var>f_{C}</var>, unchanged
ch2_2.quiz_q4_c: The carrier plus a sideband on each side of it
ch2_2.quiz_q4_d: A continuous smear of energy across the whole band
ch2_2.quiz_q4_explanation: Multiplying a carrier by a tone produces three frequencies: the carrier, an upper sideband at <var>f_{C}</var> + <var>f_{M}</var>, and a lower sideband at <var>f_{C}</var> − <var>f_{M}</var>. The information lives in the two sidebands.
ch2_2.quiz_q5: In a full-carrier AM signal, where is the information actually carried?
ch2_2.quiz_q5_c: Split evenly between carrier and sidebands
ch2_2.quiz_q5_d: In the tiny gaps between the cycles
ch2_2.quiz_q5_explanation: The carrier is a fixed, unchanging sine — it holds no information at all. Everything you say is in the sidebands. That is why SSB can throw the carrier away and lose nothing.
ch2_2.quiz_q6: How does SSB use roughly half the bandwidth and far less power than AM?
ch2_2.quiz_q6_a: It digitally compresses the audio before transmitting
ch2_2.quiz_q6_b: It transmits the audio in short rapid bursts
ch2_2.quiz_q6_c: It drops the carrier and one redundant sideband
ch2_2.quiz_q6_d: It uses a much higher carrier frequency
ch2_2.quiz_q6_explanation: The two AM sidebands are mirror copies and the carrier carries no information, so SSB keeps just one sideband. Bandwidth drops from about 6 kHz to about 2.7 kHz, and every watt goes into useful signal.
ch2_2.quiz_q7: Why does FM reject noise better than AM?
ch2_2.quiz_q7_a: FM signals are simply always stronger than any noise
ch2_2.quiz_q7_b: Noise cannot reach the VHF frequencies FM uses
ch2_2.quiz_q7_c: FM uses a lower band that natural noise tends to avoid
ch2_2.quiz_q7_d: Its information is in the frequency, not the amplitude
ch2_2.quiz_q7_explanation: Most natural noise rides on amplitude. Since FM carries its message in the frequency and keeps amplitude constant, the receiver clips the signal flat — discarding the noise spikes — and still recovers the audio.
ch2_2.quiz_q8: Using Carson's rule, what is the approximate bandwidth of an FM signal with ±5 kHz deviation and 3 kHz audio?
ch2_2.quiz_q8_explanation: Carson's rule: bandwidth ≈ 2 × (deviation + highest audio) = 2 × (5 + 3) = 16 kHz. That is why FM, despite its noise immunity, is too wide for the crowded HF bands and lives mostly on VHF/UHF.
ch2_2.compareIntro: No mode wins at everything — each buys one strength with a weakness. Set <am>AM</am>, <ssb>SSB</ssb> and <fm>FM</fm> side by side and the right choice for a given band or job becomes clear.
ch2_2.compareCaption: AM, SSB and FM at a glance. SSB is the narrowest and most power-efficient; FM shrugs off noise; AM is the simplest to receive. Which one to use depends on the band and the task.
ch2_2.cmpAmPower: Low — two-thirds wasted in the carrier
ch2_2.cmpSsbPower: High — every watt carries the voice
ch2_2.cmpSsbRx: Fussy — must reinsert the carrier and tune precisely
ch2_2.cmpFmRx: Moderate — clips the signal flat, then reads its frequency
ch2_2.cmpAmUse: Broadcast and legacy; rare in ham voice today

ch2_3.heroAriaLabel: A thick arrow of DC power flowing into a transmitter block; out of it, a thin beam becomes a radio wave leaving an antenna while a much wider glow radiates away as heat from a finned heatsink.
ch2_3.intro1: You call it a «100-watt» radio. But trace the power through it and that single number splits in two. On one side a DC power supply pushes current into the set — power going in. On the other side an antenna flings a radio wave into the sky — power coming out. Those are never the same number, and the gap between them is what this chapter is about.
ch2_3.intro2: Three questions follow from that gap, and they are the whole chapter. How much power actually goes in, and how much comes out? Why is the output always smaller — where do the missing watts go? And when the signal is an <ssb>SSB</ssb> voice that swells and collapses with every word, never holding still for an instant, what does «100 watts» even mean? The three answers are <eff>efficiency</eff>, heat, and a careful way of measuring called <pep>peak envelope power</pep>.
ch2_3.sectionTwoPowers: Two powers: what goes in, what comes out
ch2_3.twoP1: Recall from Chapter 1.2 that electrical power is voltage times current: <var>P</var> = <var>V</var> × <var>I</var>, measured in watts. That one formula does double duty here, because there are two quite different powers to track — measured with different instruments, at two different points in the station.
ch2_3.twoP2: The first is the DC input power: what the power supply delivers. A typical home or mobile radio runs from a 13.8 V supply. Key it up at full output and it draws something like 21 A. Multiply them and you get the input power: P_{DC} = 13.8 V × 21 A ≈ 290 W. You measure it with the two DC instruments from Chapter 0.2 — a voltmeter across the supply, and an ammeter in series with the supply lead.
ch2_3.twoP3: The second is the radio-frequency (RF) output power: what actually leaves the radio and travels down the feedline toward the antenna. For that same radio the figure on the box is «100 W». An ordinary DC meter cannot read it, because it is a fast radio-frequency wave (here, perhaps 14 MHz on the 20-metre band) rather than a steady voltage — you need an RF power meter, or an oscilloscope across a dummy load (the lab at the end does exactly that). Two numbers, two instruments, two points in the circuit:

powerFlow.caption: The two powers of a transmitter, measured at two points. DC input power (supply voltage × current) goes in at the left; RF output power leaves toward the antenna at the right. They are never equal.
powerFlow.ariaLabel: A block diagram: a 13.8 volt DC supply feeds a transmitter block, which feeds an antenna. The supply side is labelled DC input power measured with a voltmeter and ammeter; the antenna side is labelled RF output power measured with an RF power meter.
powerFlow.gap: 290 W in, 100 W out — the difference becomes heat

ch2_3.twoP4: The puzzle is right there in the numbers: 290 watts go in, 100 watts come out. The radio is not broken — no radio turns all of its DC power into radio waves. The question is where the other 190 watts went, and the answer has a name.
ch2_3.sectionEfficiency: Efficiency: where the missing watts go
ch2_3.effP1: <eff>Efficiency</eff> is simply the fraction of the input power that comes out as signal. We write it with the Greek letter <var>η</var> (eta): <var>η</var> = <var>P_{RF}</var> / <var>P_{DC}</var>. For our radio that is 100 / 290 ≈ 0.34, or 34 %. About a third of the DC power becomes radio wave; two-thirds does not.
ch2_3.effP2: So where do the other two-thirds go? Energy is never destroyed — it cannot simply vanish. Every watt that does not leave as radio wave is turned into heat inside the radio, almost all of it in the final amplifier: the transistor (or tube) that boosts the weak signal up to full power. The missing watts are the warmth in the heatsink and the breeze from the cooling fan.
ch2_3.effP3: The bookkeeping is exact: <var>P_{heat}</var> = <var>P_{DC}</var> − <var>P_{RF}</var>. Our radio sheds 290 − 100 = 190 W as heat the whole time you transmit. That is why power transistors are bolted to finned aluminium, and why amplifiers have fans — the heatsink's only job is to carry that heat away before the device cooks itself.

powerSplit.caption: Where the DC input power goes. A third becomes the RF signal that leaves the antenna; the other two-thirds become heat in the final amplifier. The widths are drawn to scale — heat is the big stream, not the signal.
powerSplit.ariaLabel: A flow diagram: a wide stream of 290 watts of DC input splits into a narrow 100-watt stream of RF output and a wide 190-watt stream of heat.

ch2_3.calloutEnergy: Nothing is lost — it is converted. Efficiency does not measure how much power «disappears»; it measures how much of the input becomes signal. The rest becomes heat, with every watt accounted for: P_{DC} = P_{RF} + P_{heat}.

efficiency.title: Efficiency calculator
efficiency.description: Enter what the supply delivers and what the radio puts out. See the efficiency, and the heat the final amplifier must shed.
efficiency.hint: DC input is supply voltage × current. Efficiency is RF output ÷ DC input. Whatever is left over — usually the larger share — leaves as heat in the final amplifier. An efficiency above 100 % is impossible; if you reach it, a measurement is wrong.

ch2_3.effP4: Efficiency is not a fixed property of «radios» in general. It is mostly decided by one design choice inside that final amplifier: how the amplifying device is run. That choice is called the amplifier's class, and it forces a trade-off that runs through the whole of radio.
ch2_3.sectionClasses: The amplifier's bargain: linearity versus efficiency
ch2_3.classP1: Picture the final <tr>transistor</tr> as a tap that the incoming weak signal opens and closes, letting a strong current through from the power supply. Where you set that tap's resting point decides everything. Leave it half-open all the time and it can follow the signal up and down perfectly — but a half-open tap is always wasting power as heat, always warm, even when nothing useful is happening. Snap it fully shut for part of every cycle and it wastes nothing while shut — but now it passes only part of the wave, and the output is a distorted copy of the input.
ch2_3.classP2: That is the entire bargain: the more time the device spends fully off (or fully on), the less heat it wastes — and the worse it reproduces the input's shape. Engineers label points along this trade-off as classes, set by how much of each cycle the device conducts — measured as the conduction angle, where 360° is the whole cycle and 180° is exactly half (its half-angle is what classic texts call the «cutoff angle»). The four you will meet, from most faithful to most efficient:

classChart.caption: Each panel is one cycle of the drive signal (the thin curve). The device conducts only while the signal rises above the dashed threshold — that shaded slice is the conduction angle. A narrower slice wastes less power (higher efficiency), but Class C conducts so briefly it mangles the wave shape, so it can carry only modes with no information in their amplitude. The efficiencies are best-case; real amplifiers fall short.
classChart.ariaLabel: Four panels, each showing one cycle of a signal as a thin curve with a dashed conduction-threshold line. The slice where the signal rises above the threshold is shaded: Class A across the whole cycle, Class AB a little over half, Class B exactly half, Class C only a brief slice. Below each panel is its efficiency and whether it is linear.

ch2_3.classP3: Class A conducts for the entire cycle — the tap never fully closes. It is the most faithful and the most linear, and the least efficient: even in theory it cannot beat 50 %, and real Class-A stages manage only 25–30 %. Class B conducts for half of each cycle; a single Class-B device would pass only half the wave, so two are paired — one handling the positive half, one the negative — a «push-pull» stage that rebuilds the whole wave at up to about 78 %. Class AB sits between them, conducting a little over half the cycle, and is the everyday choice for clean voice amplifiers. Class C conducts for well under half the cycle and is the most efficient of all — climbing past 80 % — but it badly distorts the wave's shape. (These are best-case figures; every real amplifier falls a little short.)
ch2_3.classP4: Here is why that bargain matters so much on the air. A linear amplifier hands back exactly the input's shape, only bigger — and you need that whenever the information lives in the amplitude. SSB and AM carry your voice in the swelling and shrinking of the wave (Chapter 2.2), so they must use a linear class — A, AB, or B — and pay the efficiency penalty. But FM and CW carry no information in their amplitude at all: an FM wave's height never changes, and CW is simply on or off. There is no envelope shape to protect, so they can use ruthless, efficient Class C and keep most of the power.
ch2_3.calloutClassC: This is why an FM handheld sips its battery while an SSB rig gulps. A constant-amplitude mode (FM, CW) can run a Class-C amplifier near 70–80 % efficiency; a voice mode that rides on amplitude (SSB, AM) is stuck with a linear amplifier at roughly half that. Same output power, very different heat — and very different talk-time per charge.

conduction.title: Amplifier class explorer
conduction.description: Drag the conduction angle — how much of each cycle the device is switched on. Watch the class, the best-case efficiency, and which modes it can carry.
conduction.linearUse: any mode — SSB, AM, FM, CW
conduction.hint: Efficiency shown is the theoretical best case for an ideal device — real amplifiers fall short because of losses. Conducting less of the cycle raises efficiency but distorts the wave: below half a cycle (180°) the amplifier is nonlinear and can only carry modes whose information is not in the amplitude.

ch2_3.sectionPep: PEP: measuring a signal that won't hold still
ch2_3.pepP1: One loose end remains. Measuring power is easy when the signal holds steady — a CW carrier keyed down, an FM transmission, or a dead carrier into a dummy load all sit at one level you can read off a meter. But an SSB voice never holds still. It has no carrier, so between words it falls to nothing; on a loud vowel it leaps to full power; an instant later it is small again. Point a power meter at it and the needle dances. So which reading is «the» power?
ch2_3.pepP2: Radio answers with two honest numbers, and you need both. The first is <pep>peak envelope power</pep> (PEP): the power in the single biggest RF cycle — the crest of the loudest peak. Formally it is «the average power over one RF cycle at the crest of the <mod>modulation</mod> <env>envelope</env>». It is the highest power the signal ever reaches, and it is what matters for not splattering onto your neighbours, so it is the number the rules limit (often 1.5 kW PEP) and the number radios are rated at («100 W PEP»).
ch2_3.pepP3: The second is the average power: the power averaged over time, gaps and peaks together. This is the number that heats your amplifier and that a lamp would glow from. For an SSB voice it is surprisingly small — ordinary speech is mostly quiet gaps and low-level sounds, so the average works out to only about a fifth of the PEP. A 100 W PEP SSB signal pushes barely 20 W on average. Two special cases pin the idea down: a steady carrier (FM, or a tuning carrier) has average power equal to its PEP — it is always at its peak — while the standard two-tone test (feeding the transmitter two equal audio tones at once, the bench-standard way to check a linear amplifier) averages exactly half its PEP.

pepEnvelope.caption: An SSB voice over a few seconds. PEP is the height of the single loudest peak; the average power (dashed) is far lower, because speech is mostly gaps and quiet moments. The radio is rated by the peak but heated by the average.
pepEnvelope.ariaLabel: A radio-frequency envelope that swells and collapses with speech, dropping to zero in the gaps between words. The tallest peak is marked PEP; a much lower dashed line marks the average power.

pep.title: PEP and average power calculator
pep.description: Set a peak envelope power and a mode, and see the average power — the number that actually heats the amplifier.
pep.hint: A steady carrier sits at its peak the whole time, so its average equals its PEP. The two-tone test averages exactly half. An SSB voice, mostly gaps and low levels, averages only about a fifth — which is why a voice rig runs cool while a continuous carrier of the same PEP runs hot.

ch2_3.pepP4: Put the two numbers together and a practical rule falls out. Your radio's heat comes from the average power, not the peak. During an SSB chat the average is low, so the amplifier coasts and stays cool. But switch to a mode that sends a full, continuous carrier — FM, RTTY (radioteletype), FT8 (a digital mode), or just holding the TUNE button (which keys a steady carrier so you can tune the antenna) — none of which fall silent between sounds the way speech does, so the average power jumps up to equal the PEP. Now the amplifier runs flat out the whole time, and many radios must be turned down to perhaps half their rated output power to keep from overheating. The mode's duty cycle — the fraction of the time it transmits full power — decides whether your finals survive, not the PEP rating alone.
ch2_3.calloutHistory: For decades the rules took the other end of this chapter's two numbers: they limited the DC input power to the final stage (the old «1000 watts DC input» limit), because that was easy to measure with a voltmeter and an ammeter. Modern rules switched to PEP output — it is what actually reaches the air and causes, or avoids, interference. This whole chapter — DC in versus RF out — is the story of that change.
ch2_3.calloutDuty: Mind the mode’s duty cycle before you key a continuous mode. A 100 W SSB rig is happy on voice, where the average power is low. The same rig on FM, RTTY, or a long FT8 transmission runs at full average power continuously — read the manual and turn the rated output power down if it asks you to. Holding the tune button at full power is the classic way to cook a finals transistor.
ch2_3.keyTakeaway1: Two powers, two places: DC input (P_{DC} = V × I, what the supply delivers) and RF output (P_{RF}, what reaches the antenna). They are never equal.
ch2_3.keyTakeaway2: Efficiency η = P_{RF} / P_{DC} is the fraction that becomes signal. The rest is heat: P_{heat} = P_{DC} − P_{RF}. Energy is converted, never lost.
ch2_3.keyTakeaway3: The final amplifier's class sets its efficiency, which rises as the device conducts less of each cycle: Class A (≤ 50 %, fully linear) → AB → B (≈ 78 %) → Class C (the highest, but nonlinear). Less conduction means more efficiency and more distortion.
ch2_3.keyTakeaway4: Amplitude-carrying modes (SSB, AM) need a linear amplifier and pay in efficiency; constant-amplitude modes (FM, CW) can use an efficient Class-C amplifier.
ch2_3.keyTakeaway5: PEP is the power at the crest of the loudest peak — the rated and regulated number. Average power, which heats the radio, is much lower for SSB voice: about a fifth of the PEP.
ch2_3.keyTakeaway6: Heat follows the average power and the mode's duty cycle: SSB voice runs cool, while a continuous carrier (FM, RTTY, tuning) runs the finals flat out and may need the power turned down.
ch2_3.labGoal: Measure the DC input power and the RF output power of a real low-power transmitter, work out its efficiency, then feel the missing watts as heat.
ch2_3.labComp1: A low-power transmitter — a QRP (low-power) rig, a handheld, or an Arduino RF experiment
ch2_3.labComp2: 50 Ω dummy load (four 200 Ω 1 W resistors in parallel make 50 Ω rated for 4 W)
ch2_3.labStep1: Connect the transmitter to the dummy load — never to a real antenna for this test, and never key up without a load on the output. Transmit a steady, constant-amplitude carrier — CW with the key held down, FM, or the rig's TUNE/carrier mode — not SSB voice, whose level never holds still long enough to read. Keep each transmission short so the finals do not overheat.
ch2_3.labStep2: Measure the DC input. Put the multimeter on DC volts across the supply terminals while transmitting, and read the current with the meter in series with the supply lead (or from the supply's own display). Multiply: <var>P_{DC}</var> = <var>V</var> × <var>I</var>.
ch2_3.labStep3: Measure the RF output. With an RF power meter, read it directly. With an oscilloscope across the dummy load, read the peak voltage <var>V_{pk}</var> and compute <var>P_{RF}</var> = (<var>V_{pk}</var> / √2)² / 50, where <var>V_{pk}</var> / √2 converts the sine's peak voltage to its RMS (root-mean-square) value, 50 is the dummy load's resistance in ohms, and the whole thing is just the <var>P</var> = <var>V</var>² / <var>R</var> form of the power law.
ch2_3.labStep4: Work out the efficiency: <var>η</var> = <var>P_{RF}</var> / <var>P_{DC}</var> × 100 %. Expect roughly 50–65 % for a Class-C stage and 40–50 % for a linear (Class-AB) one — real circuits fall short of the theoretical best case.
ch2_3.labStep5: Now find the missing watts: <var>P_{heat}</var> = <var>P_{DC}</var> − <var>P_{RF}</var>. Hold your hand near — not on — the heatsink while transmitting. That warmth is exactly the power that did not become radio wave.
ch2_3.labExpected: An efficiency somewhere in the 40–70 % range, and a heatsink that grows noticeably warm. The fraction missing from your efficiency figure is the fraction you can feel as heat.
ch2_3.labConnection: You have just measured both ends of the chapter — <var>P_{DC}</var> going in, <var>P_{RF}</var> coming out — and confirmed with your own hand that the difference is heat. Efficiency stops being an abstract percentage the moment the heatsink warms your palm.
ch2_3.labTrouble1: Output far lower than expected, or no reading at all: the dummy load must be the right <rsc>resistance</rsc> (50 Ω) and rated for the power — an ordinary <res>resistor</res> overheats and reads wrong.
ch2_3.labTrouble2: The scope shows a clipped or fuzzy wave: the probe may be on ×1 where ×10 is needed, or the transmitter is overdriven. Set the probe to ×10 and reduce the drive.
ch2_3.labTrouble3: Efficiency above 100 %, which is impossible: you have a measurement error — most often the peak-voltage reading, or current read on the wrong scale. Recheck <var>V_{pk}</var> and the supply current.
ch2_3.quizTitle: Quiz — DC input, RF output, and PEP
ch2_3.quiz_q1: A radio runs from a 12 V supply and draws 10 A on transmit. What is its DC input power?
ch2_3.quiz_q1_explanation: DC input power is voltage × current: 12 V × 10 A = 120 W. That is what the supply delivers; the RF output that reaches the antenna will be considerably less.
ch2_3.quiz_q2: An amplifier takes 200 W of DC input and delivers 100 W of RF output. What is its efficiency?
ch2_3.quiz_q2_explanation: Efficiency is RF output ÷ DC input = 100 / 200 = 0.5, or 50 %. Half of the supplied power becomes signal.
ch2_3.quiz_q3: In that same amplifier — 200 W in, 100 W out — where do the other 100 W go?
ch2_3.quiz_q3_a: They are lost; energy is destroyed in the transistor
ch2_3.quiz_q3_b: They are stored in the antenna for later
ch2_3.quiz_q3_c: They become heat in the final amplifier
ch2_3.quiz_q3_d: They are reflected back into the power supply
ch2_3.quiz_q3_explanation: Energy is conserved, never destroyed. Every watt that does not leave as RF becomes heat in the final amplifier: <var>P_{heat}</var> = <var>P_{DC}</var> − <var>P_{RF}</var> = 200 − 100 = 100 W. That is what the heatsink must carry away.
ch2_3.quiz_q4: Why must SSB and AM be amplified by a linear amplifier (Class A, AB, or B)?
ch2_3.quiz_q4_a: Because they use far higher frequencies than other modes
ch2_3.quiz_q4_b: Because linear amplifiers are far cheaper to build
ch2_3.quiz_q4_c: Because they simply need more power than other modes
ch2_3.quiz_q4_d: Because their information rides on the amplitude
ch2_3.quiz_q4_explanation: SSB and AM carry the message in how the wave's amplitude swells and shrinks. A nonlinear amplifier (like Class C) would mangle that envelope, so these modes must use a linear class even though it is less efficient.
ch2_3.quiz_q5: Which mode can use an efficient Class-C amplifier without losing its information?
ch2_3.quiz_q5_explanation: FM keeps a constant amplitude — its information is in the frequency, not the envelope. There is no envelope shape for a nonlinear Class-C amplifier to spoil, so FM can use the more efficient class. SSB and AM cannot.
ch2_3.quiz_q6: As you go from Class A to Class B to Class C, what happens to efficiency?
ch2_3.quiz_q6_a: It falls steadily from A to C
ch2_3.quiz_q6_b: It rises from A up to C
ch2_3.quiz_q6_c: It stays roughly the same throughout
ch2_3.quiz_q6_d: It changes in no predictable way
ch2_3.quiz_q6_explanation: Efficiency rises from Class A (≤ 50 %) through AB and B to Class C (the highest), because the device conducts for less of each cycle and so wastes less power as heat. The cost is rising distortion — Class C is nonlinear.
ch2_3.quiz_q7: What does PEP (peak envelope power) measure?
ch2_3.quiz_q7_a: The power averaged over an entire transmission
ch2_3.quiz_q7_b: The power in the RF cycle at the loudest peak
ch2_3.quiz_q7_c: The DC input power drawn from the supply rail
ch2_3.quiz_q7_d: The heat the final amplifier dissipates
ch2_3.quiz_q7_explanation: PEP is the average power over one RF cycle at the crest of the modulation envelope — the most the signal ever is. It is what transmitters are rated at and what the rules limit.
ch2_3.quiz_q8: A 100 W PEP SSB voice signal — roughly what is its average power, and why does that number matter?
ch2_3.quiz_q8_a: 100 W — the average always equals the PEP
ch2_3.quiz_q8_b: Exactly 50 W — the average is always half the PEP
ch2_3.quiz_q8_c: About 20 W, since speech is mostly quiet gaps
ch2_3.quiz_q8_d: 200 W — the average is double the PEP
ch2_3.quiz_q8_explanation: An SSB voice is mostly quiet gaps and low-level sound, so its average power is only about a fifth of the PEP — roughly 20 W here. Average power, not PEP, is what heats the final amplifier, which is why an SSB rig runs cool on voice but hot on a continuous carrier of the same PEP.

ch3_1.heroAriaLabel: Pen-and-ink sketch of a receiver: at the left an antenna catches several overlapping radio waves of different lengths; they funnel through a tuning dial and a small block, and out of the right comes a single clean wave feeding a loudspeaker.
ch3_1.intro1: Right now, in the air around you, hundreds of radio signals are passing through the room at once — broadcast stations, aircraft, satellites, distant amateurs — each one at a different <freq>frequency</freq>, and almost all of them breathtakingly faint. An <ssb>SSB</ssb> voice from across an ocean can reach your antenna as less than a millionth of a volt. Your receiver's job is to reach into that crowd, pick out the one signal you want, lift it a million-fold until it can drive a loudspeaker, and strip the sound back off it.
ch3_1.intro2: Almost every receiver built in the last hundred years does this with one elegant trick: instead of building a superb filter and amplifier at each station's own frequency, it slides every station down onto a single fixed frequency and does the hard work there, once, perfectly. That trick is the superheterodyne, and this chapter builds it up block by block — what each stage does, the one price the trick charges (the image), and how only the very last stage changes when you switch between AM, SSB, CW and FM.
ch3_1.jobsP1: Picture a loud party. Dozens of people are talking at once, yet you can follow the one friend in front of you, lean in to catch their quietest words, and understand what they mean. A receiver faces exactly this room — and does exactly these three things.
ch3_1.jobsP2: First, selectivity: singling out one signal and rejecting all its neighbours, the way you lock onto one voice and tune the rest of the party out. Second, sensitivity: hearing a very weak signal at all, the way you strain to catch a whisper — what limits it is the faint hiss the receiver's own electronics make — its noise floor. Third, detection: recovering the actual message — the voice, the Morse, the data — from the wave that carried it, the way you turn sounds into meaning.
ch3_1.jobsP3: The amplifying job is a feat of sheer size. The signal at the antenna might be one microvolt (1 µV, a millionth of a volt); a loudspeaker needs a few volts. That is a voltage gain of roughly a million — about 120 dB in the language of Chapter 0.4. No single amplifier delivers that much gain at one frequency without breaking into a howl of self-oscillation, so the gain must be spread across several stages — and, as we are about to see, across several frequencies.

jobs.caption: Everything a receiver does, in one line: it picks one signal out of many, amplifies it about a millionfold, and detects the message off it. The voltage climbs from roughly a microvolt at the antenna to a few volts at the speaker.
jobs.ariaLabel: A flow diagram. An antenna at about one microvolt feeds three stages labelled select, amplify and detect; the output is a loudspeaker at about one volt. The whole chain is marked as a gain of about one million, or 120 decibels.
jobs.speaker: speaker

ch3_1.sectionTrf: The straight receiver, and why it struggles
ch3_1.trfP1: The most obvious way to build a receiver is to do each job in order, right at the signal's own frequency: tune a <sel>selective</sel> circuit to the wanted station, amplify what gets through, tune another selective circuit, amplify again, then detect. Because every amplifying stage is tuned to the incoming radio frequency, this is the <trf>tuned radio frequency</trf> (TRF) receiver — also called a «straight» receiver, because the signal travels straight through at one frequency from antenna to detector.
ch3_1.trfP2: It works, and the earliest radios were built this way. But it has three stubborn problems. To change station you must re-tune every tuned circuit at once and keep them perfectly in step — a mechanical nightmare of dials linked on a single shaft. The selectivity drifts as you tune, too: a tuned circuit's bandwidth widens as you tune it higher (its sharpness, the Q factor from Chapter 1.7, stays fixed), so the set is sharp at the low end of a band and mushy at the high end. And stacking that much gain at a single frequency invites the stages to feed back into one another and oscillate. The straight receiver is the honest first attempt; the next idea fixes all three problems at once.

trf.caption: A straight (TRF) receiver: every stage is tuned to the station's own frequency, so all of them must be retuned together each time you change station. Simple, but hard to keep sharp and stable across a band.
trf.ariaLabel: A block diagram in a single row: antenna, then two tuned RF amplifier blocks, then a detector, then an audio amplifier, then a speaker. A bracket under the tuned stages notes that every stage must be retuned together for each station.
trf.speaker: speaker
trf.retune: every stage retunes together for each station

ch3_1.sectionHeterodyne: The heterodyne trick: two frequencies make a third
ch3_1.hetP1: Here is the idea that changed everything. Pluck two guitar strings tuned almost to the same note and you hear a slow throb — «wah… wah… wah» — rising and falling a few times a second. The rate of that throb is the difference between the two pitches: strings 10 Hz apart throb ten times a second. You are not hearing a new note, though — the two sounds simply add together in the air, and what you notice is their difference, showing up as a beat. Combining frequencies so that their difference appears like this is called heterodyning (from the Greek for «other force»).
ch3_1.hetP2: A radio does this deliberately — and more powerfully than two strings can — with a component called the mixer. Crucially, the mixer does not merely add its two inputs the way sounds add in the air; it multiplies them, and that multiplication genuinely creates two brand-new frequencies that were not there before: the sum and the difference. Feed it the incoming station at frequency f_{RF} and a steady tone made inside the receiver by a local oscillator at frequency f_{LO}, and out come a real signal at the sum f_{RF} + f_{LO} and another at the difference f_{RF} − f_{LO}. A filter keeps the difference and throws the rest away. That difference is the intermediate frequency (IF):
ch3_1.hetFormula: <var>f_{IF}</var> = | <var>f_{RF}</var> − <var>f_{LO}</var> |   (the bars mean the size of the gap — we ignore which frequency is larger)
ch3_1.hetP3: The magic is in that little subtraction: the frequency that comes out is set by the gap between the station and the local oscillator, not by the station itself. So to make the difference land on, say, 455 kHz no matter which station we pick, we just keep the local oscillator 455 kHz away from wherever we are tuned. On the 40-metre band (≈ 7 MHz): to hear 7.000 MHz we set the oscillator to 7.455 MHz (difference 455 kHz); to hear 7.100 MHz we move it to 7.555 MHz (difference still 455 kHz). The station changes; the frequency leaving the mixer never does.
ch3_1.hetP4: That one fact is the whole point. Every station, wherever it sits in the band, is slid down to the same fixed intermediate frequency. Now we can build one superb filter and one high-gain amplifier at that single frequency, tune them once, and reuse them for every station for ever. Tuning the radio becomes nothing more than moving the local oscillator.

mixing.caption: A mixer beats the station against the local oscillator and produces both the sum and the difference of their frequencies. A filter keeps the difference — the fixed intermediate frequency — and discards the rest.
mixing.ariaLabel: A diagram: a station signal and a local-oscillator signal both enter a mixer block. Out of the mixer, on a frequency axis, sit two new signals — a low difference frequency and a high sum frequency. A filter passband sits over the difference, marking it as the intermediate frequency.

ch3_1.blocksP1: Put the mixer and its fixed intermediate frequency at the centre, add the stages that feed and follow it, and you have the <superhet>superheterodyne</superhet> — «superhet» for short, invented by Edwin Armstrong in 1918. Nearly every receiver you have ever used, from a car radio to a satellite ground station, is built on this plan. Here is the whole signal path — tap any block to read what it does.
ch3_1.blocksP2: Follow the signal from left to right. On the left it is weak and still at the station's own radio frequency; by the right it is strong audio driving a speaker. The two oscillators below the line are the receiver's own internally generated tones — one to do the frequency-shifting, one to help certain detectors. And underneath everything sits the power supply, feeding direct current to every stage.

superhet.caption: The analog superheterodyne receiver. The front end (antenna through mixer) slides the chosen station down to a fixed intermediate frequency; the IF amplifier does the heavy filtering and gain; the detector recovers the audio. Tap a block to read its job.
superhet.ariaLabel: An interactive block diagram of a superheterodyne receiver. The signal path runs: antenna, RF amplifier, mixer, IF amplifier, detector, AF amplifier, speaker. A local oscillator feeds the mixer and a beat-frequency oscillator feeds the detector, both drawn below the path. A power supply block sits at the bottom feeding every stage. A squelch block gates the audio amplifier. Each block can be selected to show an explanation.
superhet.clickHint: Tap a block to read what it does.
superhet.selectPrompt: Tap any block above to see what that stage does.
superhet.speaker: speaker
superhet.rfDesc: The RF amplifier gives the tiny antenna signal its first gentle boost and — with a tuned filter ahead of it — rejects far-off frequencies. Because it handles the signal while it is still buried in noise, its own quietness sets the receiver's sensitivity. ERC Report 32 calls it the «HF amplifier» (high-frequency); handbooks call it the «RF amplifier» (radio-frequency). Same stage.
superhet.mixerDesc: The <mixer>mixer</mixer> beats the incoming signal against the local oscillator and produces their difference. This is the stage that slides the chosen station down to the fixed intermediate frequency.
superhet.loDesc: The <lo>local oscillator</lo> generates the clean reference tone the mixer beats against — and it is the tuning control. Sweep it with a variable-frequency <osc>oscillator</osc> (a <vfo>VFO</vfo>) to tune across a band, or switch in a fixed <crysosc>crystal oscillator</crysosc> for a fixed channel.
superhet.ifDesc: The intermediate-frequency amplifier is the heart of the receiver. Because every station arrives here at the same fixed frequency, this is where almost all the gain and all the sharp selectivity live — one filter, tuned once, setting the bandwidth for every station.
superhet.detDesc: The <det>detector</det> (or demodulator) recovers the original message from the intermediate-frequency signal. Exactly how it works depends on the mode — AM, SSB, CW or FM — which is the subject of the next section.
superhet.bfoDesc: The <bfo>beat frequency oscillator</bfo> (BFO) is a small extra oscillator used only for <cw>CW</cw> and <ssb>SSB</ssb>. It supplies the carrier those modes leave out, so the detector can turn them back into audible sound. For AM and FM it stays switched off.
superhet.afDesc: The audio-frequency (AF) amplifier boosts the recovered audio enough to drive a loudspeaker or headphones. ERC Report 32 calls it the «LF amplifier» (low-frequency); it is the ordinary audio amplifier at the end of the chain.
superhet.squelchDesc: <squelch>Squelch</squelch> mutes the audio amplifier whenever no signal is present, so you are not left listening to a loud hiss between transmissions. It is what keeps an idle FM channel silent until someone speaks.
superhet.psDesc: The power supply feeds direct current to every stage above. It carries no signal, which is why it is easy to forget on a signal-path diagram — but nothing runs without it.

ch3_1.sectionImage: The price of the trick: the image frequency
ch3_1.imgP1: The heterodyne trick charges one price, and every superhet pays it. To the mixer, only the size of the gap between the station and the local oscillator matters — not which side of the oscillator the station sits on. With the oscillator at 7.455 MHz and an intermediate frequency of 455 kHz, the wanted station at 7.000 MHz sits 455 kHz below the oscillator — but a second frequency 455 kHz above it, at 7.910 MHz, has exactly the same gap and is slid down to the very same intermediate frequency. This unwanted twin is the image frequency.
ch3_1.imgP2: The image always sits twice the intermediate frequency away from the station you want:
ch3_1.imgP3: If a strong signal happens to be transmitting on that image frequency, it lands in your receiver right on top of the station you wanted — and no amount of filtering after the mixer can separate them, because by then they are the same frequency. The cure must come before the mixer: that is the real job of the tuned filter and RF amplifier at the front end — to let the wanted frequency through and shut the image out.
ch3_1.imgP4: This also explains the intermediate frequencies receivers actually use. A higher intermediate frequency pushes the image twice as far away again, where the front-end filter rejects it easily — but a lower intermediate frequency makes the sharp selectivity at the IF easier to build. Designers split the difference, which is why you meet 455 kHz in simple AM sets, 10.7 MHz in FM broadcast receivers, and around 9 MHz in shortwave amateur radios. (Modern software-defined radios sidestep the problem by sampling at a very high frequency — but the image is still there in the mathematics.) Try the trade-off yourself:

mixerCalc.title: Local-oscillator and image calculator
mixerCalc.description: Pick a station and an intermediate frequency, choose which side the local oscillator sits, and see where the oscillator must go — and where the unwanted image lands.
mixerCalc.hint: The local oscillator sits one IF away from the station; the image sits one IF away on the other side of the oscillator — that is, 2 × IF from the station. Raise the IF and watch the image move further away, where the front-end filter can reject it more easily.

imageAxis.caption: Why the image exists. The local oscillator sits one IF away from the wanted station; the image sits one IF beyond the oscillator, so it is 2 × IF from the station — and lands on the same IF after mixing. Only the front-end filter (shaded) can keep it out.
imageAxis.ariaLabel: A frequency axis. The wanted station is marked on the left, the local oscillator one intermediate frequency to its right, and the image one intermediate frequency beyond that — twice the IF from the wanted station. A shaded front-end filter passband covers the wanted station but not the image.

ch3_1.modesP1: Here is the tidy part. Everything from the antenna to the intermediate-frequency amplifier — the whole front end — is the same for every mode. Only the detector at the end changes, depending on the modulation that put the message onto the wave back in Chapter 2.2. Switching your radio from AM to SSB to FM is, at heart, switching detectors.
ch3_1.modesP2: AM. Amplitude modulation carries the sound in the rising and falling envelope of the wave. The detector is just a diode and a capacitor that trace that envelope — exactly the rectifier from Chapter 1.10, and exactly the crystal radio you will build at the end of this chapter. No BFO needed.
ch3_1.modesP3: SSB. Single sideband sends just one sideband and throws the carrier away to save power (Chapter 2.2), so the detector has to put one back. The BFO supplies that missing carrier, and a «product detector» (itself a small mixer) combines the two to rebuild the voice. Turn the BFO off and an SSB voice is an unintelligible quack.
ch3_1.modesP4: CW. Morse is nothing but the carrier switched on and off. With no BFO you would hear silent gaps where the dots and dashes should be. The BFO beats against the incoming carrier — the «wah» of the heterodyne trick again, but on purpose — turning each dot and dash into an audible tone, typically around 600 Hz.
ch3_1.modesP5: FM. Frequency modulation keeps a constant amplitude and hides the message in tiny frequency wiggles, so it needs two extra stages. A limiter first flattens the amplitude, clipping off any noise spikes — this is why FM sounds so clean. Then a discriminator, a frequency detector, converts the frequency wiggles into audio. And because an idle FM channel hisses loudly, FM is where squelch earns its keep.

modeDetectors.caption: The front end is shared; only the detector changes with the mode. AM uses a diode envelope detector; SSB and CW add the BFO; FM swaps in a limiter and discriminator.
modeDetectors.ariaLabel: A diagram. A shared front-end block, ending at the IF amplifier, feeds four alternative detector blocks: AM with a diode envelope detector, SSB with a product detector plus BFO, CW with a BFO producing an audible tone, and FM with a limiter followed by a discriminator.

ch3_1.keyTakeaway1: A receiver does three jobs: select one signal (selectivity), amplify it about a millionfold (sensitivity, limited by the receiver's own noise), and detect the message off it.
ch3_1.keyTakeaway2: A <trf>straight (TRF)</trf> receiver does all three at the signal's own frequency. It works, but every tuned stage must retune together, its selectivity drifts across the band, and high gain at one frequency tends to oscillate.
ch3_1.keyTakeaway3: Heterodyning mixes the station (f_{RF}) with a local oscillator (f_{LO}) to produce a fixed intermediate frequency f_{IF} = f_{RF} − f_{LO}. Tuning just moves the oscillator; the IF never changes.
ch3_1.keyTakeaway4: The <superhet>superheterodyne</superhet> does all the sharp filtering and most of the gain once, at that fixed IF. Its stages: RF (HF) amplifier · oscillator · mixer · IF amplifier · detector · BFO · AF (LF) amplifier · squelch · power supply.
ch3_1.keyTakeaway5: The price is the image: a second frequency f_{image} = f_{RF} + 2 × f_{IF} that maps to the same IF. Only filtering before the mixer can reject it — which is why a higher IF and a good front-end filter help.
ch3_1.keyTakeaway6: The front end is the same for every mode; only the <det>detector</det> changes: a diode <env>envelope</env> detector for <am>AM</am>, a <bfo>BFO</bfo> plus product detector for <ssb>SSB</ssb> and <cw>CW</cw>, and a <lim>limiter</lim> plus <disc>discriminator</disc> (with <squelch>squelch</squelch>) for <fm>FM</fm>.
ch3_1.labGoal: Build the simplest possible receiver — a straight receiver with no battery and no amplifier — and hear a real AM broadcast station with your own hands.
ch3_1.labEquip2: Oscilloscope (optional — to see the detected signal)
ch3_1.labComp1: Ferrite rod with about 100 turns of 0.3 mm enamelled wire, tapped near turn 10 for the antenna
ch3_1.labComp2: Variable capacitor (about 500 pF) — the tuning control
ch3_1.labComp3: Germanium diode (1N34A) or a Schottky diode (BAT43) — the detector
ch3_1.labComp4: 1 nF capacitor, a <hze>high-impedance (crystal) earpiece</hze>, 10–20 m of wire for an antenna, and a good earth connection
ch3_1.labStep1: Wind about 100 turns of wire along the <ferr>ferrite</ferr> rod and connect the winding across the variable capacitor. This coil-and-capacitor pair is the <tunedc>tuned circuit</tunedc> from Chapter 1.7 — it is your <sel>selectivity</sel>, the part that picks one station out of the band.
ch3_1.labStep2: Connect the long antenna wire to the tap near turn 10, counting up from the earthed bottom of the coil; connect a good earth — a cold-water pipe or a ground rod — to that same bottom end. The longer the antenna and the better the earth, the louder the result.
ch3_1.labStep3: The earpiece has two terminals. Connect the germanium diode from the top of the tuned circuit to one of them, and wire the other terminal to the earth rail. Then put the 1 nF capacitor across the earpiece — one lead to each of the same two terminals — so it sits in parallel with the earpiece. The diode is the <det>detector</det>: it traces the <env>envelope</env> of the <am>AM</am> signal just as a rectifier does, while the capacitor smooths away the leftover radio-frequency carrier.
ch3_1.labStep4: Slowly turn the variable capacitor. As you sweep it you move the tuned circuit's <resf>resonant frequency</resf> across the band; one position at a time, a station should appear in the earpiece.

labSchematic.caption: The detector (crystal) radio you build. The antenna taps low on the coil; the coil and variable capacitor form the tuned circuit; the diode detects the AM envelope; the earpiece — with a 1 nF capacitor across it to smooth away the radio-frequency carrier — turns it into sound. The bottom rail is the common earth.

ch3_1.labExpected: In the evening, with a decent antenna and earth, you should hear one or more local AM broadcast stations — faint but clear — powered by nothing but the radio wave itself.
ch3_1.labConnection: You have just built, in miniature, the selectivity and detection stages of every receiver in this chapter: the tuned circuit chooses the station, the diode strips the audio off the carrier. A superhet simply adds the frequency-shifting and the amplification that let it do the same job on a microvolt signal from the other side of the world.
ch3_1.labTrouble1: Nothing at all: almost always the antenna or the earth. Make the antenna longer and higher, and find a better earth — without a real ground a crystal set stays silent.
ch3_1.labTrouble2: Several stations at once: the antenna is over-coupling and swamping the tuned circuit. Move the antenna tap to fewer turns (closer to the earth end) to sharpen the selectivity.
ch3_1.labTrouble3: Connections check out but still nothing: try the germanium or <schottky>Schottky diode</schottky> rather than an ordinary silicon one — silicon's forward voltage is too high for these tiny signals, and you will likely hear nothing through it.
ch3_1.quiz_q1: A receiver picks one station out of a band crowded with others. What is this ability called?
ch3_1.quiz_q1_explanation: Selectivity is the ability to single out one signal and reject its neighbours. Sensitivity is a different job — hearing a very weak signal at all.
ch3_1.quiz_q2: Why does a straight (TRF) receiver become awkward to use across a band?
ch3_1.quiz_q2_a: Every tuned stage must be retuned together
ch3_1.quiz_q2_b: It has no detector at all, so it cannot recover the audio signal
ch3_1.quiz_q2_c: It can only receive narrow-band FM signals
ch3_1.quiz_q2_d: It needs two separate antennas to work at all
ch3_1.quiz_q2_explanation: In a TRF set every stage is tuned to the station's own frequency, so changing station means re-tuning all of them at once and keeping them tracking — and the selectivity drifts across the band as well.
ch3_1.quiz_q3: A mixer combines a 7.000 MHz station with a 7.455 MHz local oscillator. What intermediate frequency comes out?
