ch3_1.quiz_q3_explanation: The intermediate frequency is the difference: 7.455 − 7.000 = 0.455 MHz, which is 455 kHz. (The mixer also makes the sum, 14.455 MHz, but the IF filter discards it.)
ch3_1.quiz_q4: As you tune a superhet from one station to the next, what happens to the intermediate frequency?
ch3_1.quiz_q4_a: It rises and falls in step with the tuned station
ch3_1.quiz_q4_b: It drops to zero in the gaps between stations
ch3_1.quiz_q4_c: It doubles with each station you select
ch3_1.quiz_q4_d: It stays fixed; only the oscillator moves
ch3_1.quiz_q4_explanation: That is the whole point of the superhet: the local oscillator moves to keep its gap from the station constant, so every station arrives at the same fixed intermediate frequency. Tuning is just moving the oscillator.
ch3_1.quiz_q5: Which stage provides almost all of a superhet's gain and sharp selectivity?
ch3_1.quiz_q5_explanation: Because every station is slid down to the same fixed intermediate frequency, one filter and one high-gain amplifier can be built and tuned there once — so the IF amplifier carries most of the gain and sets the selectivity.
ch3_1.quiz_q6: What is the beat frequency oscillator (BFO) for?
ch3_1.quiz_q6_a: Supplying the carrier that CW and SSB leave out
ch3_1.quiz_q6_b: Powering every stage of the receiver from the supply
ch3_1.quiz_q6_c: Muting the audio in the gaps between signals
ch3_1.quiz_q6_explanation: CW and SSB arrive without a usable carrier. The BFO supplies one to beat against, turning a Morse carrier into an audible tone and rebuilding an SSB voice. AM and FM do not need it.
ch3_1.quiz_q7: An idle FM channel would hiss loudly. Which stage keeps it silent until a signal arrives?
ch3_1.quiz_q7_explanation: Squelch mutes the audio amplifier when no signal is present, so the loud background hiss only opens up when someone actually transmits.
ch3_1.quiz_q8: ERC Report 32 lists an «HF amplifier» and an «LF amplifier». In ordinary handbook terms, these are…
ch3_1.quiz_q8_a: The mixer stage and the detector stage
ch3_1.quiz_q8_b: The BFO and the squelch circuit
ch3_1.quiz_q8_d: The RF amplifier and the AF amplifier
ch3_1.quiz_q8_explanation: «HF amplifier» (high-frequency) is the RF amplifier at the front end; «LF amplifier» (low-frequency) is the audio amplifier at the output. Same stages, different names.
ch3_1.quiz_q9: A receiver tuned to 7.000 MHz uses a 455 kHz IF with the local oscillator above the station. Where is its image?
ch3_1.quiz_q9_explanation: The image sits twice the IF from the wanted station: 7.000 + 2 × 0.455 = 7.910 MHz. It is one IF beyond the local oscillator (7.455 MHz), so it maps to the same IF and only the front-end filter can reject it.
ch3_1.quiz_q10: FM hides its message in frequency, not amplitude. Which pair of stages does an FM receiver use to recover the audio?
ch3_1.quiz_q10_b: A BFO feeding a product detector
ch3_1.quiz_q10_explanation: The limiter flattens the amplitude (removing noise and any AM), and the discriminator turns the frequency wiggles into audio. An envelope detector suits AM; a BFO and product detector suit SSB and CW.

ch3_2.heroAriaLabel: Pen-and-ink sketch of a transmitter: on the left a microphone and a Morse key feed a row of blocks that grows taller from left to right; out of the tallest block a single bold radio wave leaves an antenna into the sky.
ch3_2.intro1: In Chapter 3.1 you followed a whisper from the antenna down to a loudspeaker. A transmitter runs that same journey in reverse. It begins with your message — your voice, a <cw>Morse</cw> key, a stream of data — builds a clean radio-frequency wave to carry it, prints the message onto that wave, and pushes it out of the antenna with enough power to be heard on the far side of the planet.
ch3_2.intro2: Three jobs sit at the heart of every transmitter. First it generates a steady, precise carrier — a pure wave at exactly the frequency you intend, and nowhere else. Second it modulates that carrier — folds your message onto it, the mirror image of the detection you met in Chapter 3.1, and the step that differs for CW (Morse), SSB (single-sideband voice) and FM (frequency modulation). Third it amplifies the result to full power without smearing it across the band. This chapter walks the signal block by block — oscillator, buffer, modulator, driver, power amplifier — and ends at the one stage no transmitter may skip: the filter that stops your signal from splattering across everyone else's.
ch3_2.sectionJobs: The three jobs of a transmitter
ch3_2.jobsP1: A receiver, you saw, reaches into a crowded band and lifts one faint whisper out of it. A transmitter has the opposite task, and it meets that task with three jobs of its own. Picture a singer stepping up to the microphone in a stadium. First they find and hold a clear, steady note. Then they shape that note into words. And finally the note has to fill the whole stadium without collapsing into a blur. Generate, modulate, amplify — always in that order.
ch3_2.jobsP2: Generating the note comes first. The transmitter builds a carrier: a pure, unwavering radio wave at exactly the frequency you are licensed to use, and at no other. Everything that follows rides on this wave, so the smallest wobble in it becomes a wobble smeared across your whole signal. Modulating comes second — the message, whether your voice, a Morse key or a stream of data, is folded onto the carrier. This is the exact mirror of the detection a receiver performs, and it is the one job that genuinely changes from mode to mode, which is why most of this chapter lives there.
ch3_2.jobsP3: Amplifying comes last, and it is a feat of sheer size. The carrier leaves the oscillator at roughly a milliwatt (1 mW, a thousandth of a watt); a typical rig pushes it out of the antenna at around 100 W. That is a power gain of about a hundred thousand — close to 50 dB in the language of Chapter 0.4 — and it has to happen without bending the wave out of shape or smearing it onto the bands next door. No single stage manages all of it at once, so the power is built up across several, the same way a receiver spread its gain across several stages.

jobs.caption: Everything a transmitter does, in one line: it generates a clean carrier, folds your message onto it, and amplifies the result from about a milliwatt up to full power — here roughly 100 W at the antenna, a power gain near 50 dB.
jobs.ariaLabel: A flow diagram. A microphone marked 'your message' feeds three boxes labelled generate, modulate and amplify; the output goes to a transmitting antenna at about 100 watts. A bracket under the three boxes marks a power gain of about one hundred thousand times, or 50 decibels.

ch3_2.sectionOsc: It all starts with an oscillator
ch3_2.oscP1: Every signal a transmitter sends begins life in one place: the <osc>oscillator</osc>. Feed it nothing but steady <dc>DC</dc> power and it produces a clean, continuous radio tone — the <carrier>carrier</carrier> — with no input signal at all. It manages this much the way a child on a swing keeps moving: a <tunedc>tuned circuit</tunedc> (the coil-and-<cap>capacitor</cap> <tank>tank</tank> from Chapter 1.7) stores energy and sloshes it back and forth between the coil's magnetic field and the capacitor's electric field, while a <tx>transistor</tx> gives it a small push each cycle to top up what little leaks away. Push in time with the swing and the oscillation never dies.
ch3_2.oscP2: There are two common ways to build that tank, and choosing between them is a straight trade-off between tunable and steady. A variable-frequency oscillator (VFO) uses an ordinary tunable LC tank: turn the dial and the frequency moves, so one VFO can sweep across a whole band. Its weakness is drift — as the parts warm up, the frequency slowly wanders. A crystal oscillator instead uses a thin slice of quartz that vibrates mechanically. Its resonance is far sharper than any LC tank — a quality factor Q of 10 000 to 100 000, against perhaps 200 for a good coil — so it holds its frequency far more tightly. The catch mirrors the VFO's exactly: a crystal is rock-steady but fixed, married to the single frequency it was cut for.
ch3_2.oscP3: How tightly an oscillator holds its frequency is its frequency stability, and it is measured in parts per million (ppm) — a 10 MHz oscillator that drifts by 10 Hz is off by just 1 ppm. It matters because the bands are crowded: a transmitter that drifts crawls onto its neighbours or smears its own note. The biggest enemy is temperature — parts change value as they warm — which is why steadier references either electronically compensate the crystal for temperature, or seal it inside a tiny temperature-controlled oven. Two smaller thieves are worth naming: a change in the load the oscillator drives can pull its frequency (the reason the very next stage exists), and a sagging power supply can shift it too. The scale below spans the whole range, from a bare VFO to that oven-controlled crystal — and the smaller the number, the steadier the oscillator:
ch3_2.oscCaution: A crystal does not force the frequency stamped on it. It is tempting to think that dropping a crystal marked «7.000 MHz» into a circuit guarantees exactly 7.000 MHz. It does not. The crystal strongly favours that frequency, but the circuit around it still has to be right — and a mistreated crystal can refuse to start, or jump to an unexpected overtone (a stray higher resonance, well above its intended frequency). Treat it as a very firm suggestion, not a command.

osc.ladderAria: A vertical ladder of oscillator types ordered by frequency stability. From top (least steady) to bottom (steadiest): a simple VFO at about plus or minus 100 parts per million, a plain crystal at 10 ppm, a temperature-compensated crystal at 1 ppm, and an oven-controlled crystal at 0.01 ppm. Each step down is roughly ten to a hundred times steadier.
osc.ladderCaption: Typical frequency stability, least steady at the top. Each rung down is about ten times steadier — from a bare VFO that drifts as it warms, to a crystal sealed in a temperature-controlled oven holding to parts per billion.
osc.vfoDesc: a simple LC VFO — drifts as it warms up
osc.xoDesc: a plain crystal (XO) — the hobby workhorse
osc.ocxoDesc: an oven-controlled crystal (OCXO) — parts per billion

ch3_2.sectionStages: Protecting and reaching: the buffer and multiplier
ch3_2.stagesP1: The oscillator, you just saw, is delicate: change the load on its output and its frequency shifts. Yet a transmitter exists precisely to load it heavily — eventually a power amplifier will be pulling hard at the far end. The answer is to follow the oscillator immediately with a buffer: an amplifier whose special talent is reverse isolation. It passes the signal forward freely while blocking anything that tries to travel back upstream, so nothing the power stages do can reach in and pull the oscillator. Picture a one-way valve, or an airlock, sealing the fragile oscillator off from the rough power stages ahead.
ch3_2.stagesP2: After the buffer, many transmitters add a frequency multiplier. Crystals and VFOs are easiest to build — and steadiest — at fairly low frequencies, yet you may want to transmit far higher, up on the VHF and UHF bands — the higher-frequency ranges above roughly 30 MHz. A multiplier bridges that gap. It deliberately distorts the carrier to create harmonics — exact whole-number multiples of the input — and a tuned circuit then keeps only the one it wants. A «doubler» puts out twice the input frequency; a «tripler», three times. So a rock-steady 4 MHz crystal, tripled, becomes a rock-steady 12 MHz signal: the stability of the low frequency carried all the way up to the high one. (As a bonus, a multiplier also multiplies an FM signal's frequency swing — a trick we meet in the next section.)

stages.caption: The buffer isolates the oscillator from everything downstream — a one-way valve for the signal. The multiplier then lifts a low, steady frequency to a higher one: here a 4 MHz crystal tripled to 12 MHz, keeping all of the crystal's steadiness.
stages.ariaLabel: A block chain: an oscillator at 4 megahertz feeds a buffer amplifier, which feeds a times-three frequency multiplier, whose output is 12 megahertz on its way to the driver.

ch3_2.sectionModulators: Putting your message on the carrier
ch3_2.modP1: Now the carrier is clean, steady and ready to work with — but it carries no message yet. <mod>Modulation</mod> is the act of folding your message onto it, and it is the exact reverse of the detection a receiver performs in Chapter 3.1. It is also the one stage that genuinely changes from mode to mode. The three modes you met in Chapter 2.2 — <cw>CW</cw>, <ssb>SSB</ssb> and <fm>FM</fm> — are really three different modulators, so let us see how each one is built.
ch3_2.modP2: CW is the simplest of all, because there is no modulator at all. A Morse signal is just the carrier switched fully on for a dot or dash and fully off in the gaps — the key itself does the modulating. The one subtlety is the shape of those on-and-off transitions. Switch the carrier instantly, with a hard square edge, and the abrupt jump sprays energy far up and down the band as key clicks that splatter onto other stations. So a good keyer rounds the edges, ramping the carrier up and down over a few milliseconds — typically about 5 ms — which holds the signal to roughly 150 Hz wide while still sounding crisp.
ch3_2.modP3: SSB is the cleverest. Recall from Chapter 2.2 that an ordinary AM signal wastes most of its power on a carrier that carries no information, and sends the same voice twice over in two identical sidebands. SSB throws away the dead weight. First a balanced modulator — a special mixer — blends the audio with the carrier in such a way that the carrier itself cancels out, leaving only the two sidebands (that cancelling is why it is called «balanced»). Then a sharp filter removes one of those sidebands, leaving just one — upper (USB) or lower (LSB) — about 2.5 kHz wide. No carrier, no second sideband: every watt goes into the one sideband that actually carries your voice. Both removals have a number attached to them: Ukraine's Regulations require the carrier and the unwanted sideband each to be attenuated by at least 40 dB — a ten-thousandth of the power — so «cancelled» and «removed» are measured quantities here, not loose description.
ch3_2.modP4: FM takes a different route again: instead of adding anything to the carrier, it wiggles the carrier's frequency in step with your voice. The stage that does this is a reactance modulator — in effect a voltage-controlled capacitor (a varactor diode) sitting across the oscillator's tuned circuit. The audio varies the capacitor's reactance, gently pushing the oscillator's frequency up and down. Louder audio swings it further, and that swing is the deviation. Because the amplitude never changes, FM is a constant-envelope mode — which is exactly why, in the very next section, it will let us reach for a brutally efficient amplifier.
ch3_2.modCarson: An FM signal's frequency is always on the move, so it technically spreads across infinitely many <sideband>sidebands</sideband> — but almost all of its power fits inside a band given by <carson>Carson's rule</carson>: <var>B</var> ≈ 2 × (<var>f_{d}</var> + <var>f_{m}</var>), where <var>f_{d}</var> is the peak <dev>deviation</dev> and <var>f_{m}</var> the highest audio frequency. For typical narrow-band FM with <var>f_{d}</var> = 5 kHz and <var>f_{m}</var> = 3 kHz, that is 2 × (5 + 3) = 16 kHz — far wider than SSB's 2.5 kHz, which is why FM lives up on the roomy VHF and UHF bands. (You can play with this in the FM explorer back in Chapter 2.2.)

modulators.caption: How each mode is generated. CW just keys the carrier on and off; SSB suppresses the carrier in a balanced modulator and then removes one sideband with a filter; FM nudges the oscillator's own frequency with a reactance modulator.
modulators.ariaLabel: A comparison. The carrier and your message feed three modulators: CW keys the carrier on and off, SSB uses a balanced modulator followed by a sideband filter, and FM uses a reactance modulator acting on the oscillator.

ch3_2.sectionAmplify: Making it loud — without making a mess
ch3_2.ampP1: The signal is finished now — the right frequency, carrying your message — but still feeble, perhaps a milliwatt or two. Turning that into the tens or hundreds of watts an antenna wants is not one amplifier's job but a relay team's. Each transistor can only multiply power so far before it runs out of headroom, and the big final transistor cannot be driven straight from a milliwatt. So the signal climbs a chain of ever-larger stages: a low-power stage called the exciter creates it, one or more driver stages build it up, and the power amplifier (PA) — the final, biggest stage — delivers the full output. The driver's whole job is to hand the PA exactly the push it needs.
ch3_2.ampP2: Which kind of amplifier you may use turns on a single question: does the message live in the signal's amplitude? For SSB and AM it does — the voice is the rising and falling envelope — so the amplifier must be linear, faithfully enlarging the wave's shape without flattening it. Those are the Class A and Class AB amplifiers from Chapter 2.3. For FM and CW the amplitude carries nothing — FM hides its message in frequency, and CW is simply on or off — so the wave can be squashed and clipped without losing anything. That frees you to use a far more efficient Class C amplifier. The catch is the trade-off you already met: the more linear the amplifier, the less efficient it is, and the other way round. You buy faithfulness with wasted heat.
ch3_2.ampP3: How much power comes out is quoted as PEP (peak envelope power) — the power at the crest of the modulation — because a voice signal's power is forever changing. The numbers span a huge range: QRP operators chase contacts with 5 W or less, a typical bench rig runs around 100 W, and the biggest legal stations push a kilowatt or more. The exact ceiling is set by your licence and your country's regulator, not by the radio itself.
ch3_2.ampOnair: In Ukraine the power you may transmit is set band by band and class by class, in the Regulations of the Amateur Radio Service approved by the regulator НКЕК in 2023. Across the shortwave bands from 3.5 to 29.7 MHz the ceiling is 200 W for the highest class A, 100 W for class B and 40 W for class C. Above 30 MHz it falls steeply: 50 W at 50 MHz for class A alone, and 5 W at 144 and 430 MHz for every class. Your callsign and operating document are issued by УДЦР. The same Regulations require you to work at the lowest power that gives the contact the quality it needs, so the figure in your document is a ceiling and not a target.

classMode.caption: The amplifier class you may use depends on whether the message lives in the signal's amplitude. CW and FM keep a constant envelope, so an efficient Class C amplifier is fine; AM and SSB carry the message in the envelope, so the amplifier must stay linear — Class A or AB.
classMode.ariaLabel: Two panels. On the left, a constant-amplitude wave labelled CW and FM that can use an efficient Class C amplifier. On the right, a wave with a rising and falling envelope labelled AM and SSB that must use a linear Class A or AB amplifier.
classMode.verdictEnv: must stay linear — Class A / AB
classMode.reasonEnv: clip it and you mangle the voice

ch3_2.sectionFilter: The one filter you are not allowed to skip
ch3_2.filterP1: There is one last stage between the power amplifier and the antenna, and it is the one no transmitter may go without. Recall that an efficient Class C amplifier works by brutally clipping the wave — and clipping a wave manufactures harmonics: faithful copies of your signal at exactly two, three and four times the frequency you transmit on. Transmit on 7 MHz and your power amplifier also pours energy out at 14, 21 and 28 MHz — and 14 MHz lands squarely on the 20-metre amateur band, where you have no business being. Worse still, once a harmonic has left the antenna nobody can ever filter it back out. It has to be stopped at the source.
ch3_2.filterP2: The stopper is a low-pass filter bolted to the PA's output. Low-pass is exactly right, for a simple reason: your wanted signal is the lowest frequency present — the fundamental — and every harmonic sits above it. A filter that passes everything below a cutoff and blocks everything above lets your signal through and throttles the harmonics. The classic form is the pi-network (in Ukrainian the «П-контур», after the Greek letter π whose shape it resembles): two capacitors to ground bridged by an inductor, as the schematic below shows. The inductor is what does the sorting: sitting in series, right in the signal's path, it lets the low fundamental pass but chokes the higher harmonics ever harder, while the two capacitors shunt to ground on each side and offer those harmonics an easy path to earth. A series inductor flanked by capacitors to ground is exactly what makes a filter low-pass. The network does two jobs at once — it knocks the harmonics down by 30 dB or more, and it matches the PA's output impedance to the antenna's 50 ohms so the power actually flows. The matching is impedance transformation: choosing the right inductor and capacitor values makes the antenna look, from the PA's side, like exactly the load the PA needs for full power — a lossless electrical gearbox between the two.
ch3_2.filterP3: Seen as a spectrum (below), the filter's job is obvious. The PA hands it a tall fundamental and a comb of harmonics; the filter's <pband>passband</pband> (shaded) waves the fundamental through untouched and chops everything above it down to a sliver.
ch3_2.filterCalcIntro: Work out where your own harmonics would fall — and whether any of them land in another band:
ch3_2.filterKey: Every transmitter needs a low-pass filter after its power amplifier. This is not an optional refinement — it is what keeps your harmonics off other amateur bands, off broadcast TV and FM, and inside the law. A transmitter without one is not really a transmitter; it is an interference generator with an antenna.

piSchematic.caption: The output low-pass filter in its classic pi-network (П-контур) form: two capacitors to ground bridged by an inductor, in the classic pi-network shape. It passes the fundamental through to the antenna while shorting the harmonics to ground, and matches the power amplifier to the antenna's 50 ohms.

harmSpectrum.caption: Why the filter is low-pass. The fundamental (your signal) sits inside the filter's passband, shaded, and passes untouched. The harmonics the power amplifier makes — drawn dashed — all fall above the passband, so the filter's response curve crushes them down to the solid stubs that actually reach the antenna.
harmSpectrum.ariaLabel: A spectrum. A tall fundamental spike sits inside a shaded low-pass passband. The second, third and fourth harmonics, drawn as tall dashed spikes above the passband, are cut down to tiny solid stubs by the filter's falling response curve.

harmCalc.title: Where do my harmonics land?
harmCalc.description: Enter your transmit frequency. The power amplifier also throws out harmonics at 2×, 3× and 4× that frequency — see where each one falls, and whether it lands in another amateur band the filter must keep it out of.
harmCalc.hint: The harmonics of a 7 MHz (40 m) signal land right on the 20 m, 15 m and 10 m bands — which is exactly why the low-pass filter is not optional.

ch3_2.sectionChain: The whole transmitter, block by block
ch3_2.chainP1: You have now met every stage on its own. How they fit together depends on the mode, so here are the two common shapes. The first is an SSB transmitter: a fixed oscillator hands the modulator a carrier, your voice rides onto it, and a mixer beats the result against a tunable VFO to slide the whole signal up to the operating frequency. The second is a CW/FM transmitter: it has no separate modulator and no mixer — the key simply switches the oscillator on and off for CW, or a reactance modulator nudges its frequency for FM, and a multiplier then lifts the result to the higher bands. Both share the same back end: driver, power amplifier, filter, antenna. Tap any block in either diagram to see its job.
ch3_2.chainP2: Real transmitters shuffle these blocks around depending on the mode — an FM rig modulates the oscillator directly and may skip the mixer, while an SSB rig builds the signal at one fixed frequency and mixes it up to the band — but every one of these stages is in there somewhere, doing exactly the job you just learned.

txBlocks.clickHint: Tap a block to read what it does.
txBlocks.selectPrompt: Tap any block above to see what that stage does.
txBlocks.oscDesc: The <osc>oscillator</osc> generates the <carrier>carrier</carrier> — a steady reference wave a <crysosc>crystal</crysosc> holds rock-steady. In the SSB transmitter it runs at one fixed frequency; in the CW/FM transmitter the message goes on right here — the key switches the carrier for <cw>CW</cw>, and a reactance modulator nudges the frequency for <fm>FM</fm>.
txBlocks.bufferDesc: The buffer isolates the oscillator from everything after it, so the heavy power stages cannot reach back and pull its frequency. It is a one-way valve for the signal.
txBlocks.multDesc: The frequency multiplier raises a low, steady oscillator frequency by an exact whole number to reach the VHF and UHF bands. It sits on the FM/CW path, not the SSB chain: an SSB signal can't be multiplied without smearing its modulation, so only a clean carrier passes through it.
txBlocks.mixerDesc: The mixer combines the modulated signal with the VFO, producing the sum and difference frequencies and so translating everything up to the exact output frequency.
txBlocks.modDesc: The modulator folds your message onto the carrier at a fixed intermediate frequency. For SSB it is a balanced modulator plus a sideband filter; for FM it nudges the oscillator's frequency. CW needs none — the key does the job.
txBlocks.micDesc: Your message coming in — your voice on a microphone, or a <cw>Morse</cw> key. In the SSB transmitter it drives the modulator; in the CW/FM transmitter it acts straight on the oscillator.
txBlocks.driverDesc: The driver is the middle muscle of the amplifier chain — it builds the signal up just enough to drive the final power amplifier.
txBlocks.paDesc: The <pa>power amplifier</pa> (PA) is the final, biggest stage, delivering the full output power. It is linear (Class A or AB) for SSB and AM, and efficient Class C for CW and FM.
txBlocks.filterDesc: The <filt>low-pass filter</filt> — the pi-network — is mandatory: it strips off the harmonics the power amplifier makes before they can reach the antenna and splatter onto other bands.
txBlocks.vfoDesc: The <vfo>VFO</vfo> — a tunable oscillator — feeds the mixer. Sliding its frequency moves the whole signal to the exact operating frequency, so this is the knob you turn to tune across the band.
txBlocks.ssbCaption: SSB transmitter (up-conversion): the carrier is modulated at a fixed frequency, then a mixer shifts it to the band.
txBlocks.cwfmCaption: CW/FM transmitter (direct): the key or reactance modulator acts at the oscillator, and a multiplier reaches the higher bands — no modulator block, no mixer.
txBlocks.ssbAria: Block diagram of an SSB transmitter: carrier oscillator, buffer, modulator fed by the microphone, mixer fed by a VFO, driver, power amplifier, low-pass filter, antenna.
txBlocks.cwfmAria: Block diagram of a CW/FM transmitter: the microphone or key feeds the oscillator, then buffer, frequency multiplier, driver, power amplifier, low-pass filter, antenna.

ch3_2.charP1: A receiver is judged by what it can hear; a transmitter, by how clean a signal it puts out. Four numbers tell the story, and you have already met every one of them. Its frequency stability — does it hold its frequency or drift (Section 2)? Its occupied bandwidth — how much spectrum its signal takes up, which depends on the mode (Section 4)? Its output power, measured in PEP (Section 5)? And, above all, its spectral purity — how free it is of harmonics and other spurious signals it should not be radiating at all (Section 6). A good transmitter is a quiet, well-behaved neighbour.
ch3_2.charP2: Operators have a compact shorthand for what a transmitter is sending, borrowed from the International Telecommunication Union (ITU): the emission designator. It is three characters. The first says how the carrier is modulated (A for AM, J for SSB, F for FM); the second describes the modulating signal (1 for a signal simply switched on and off (a digital one), 3 for an analogue one); the third names the information carried (A for Morse read by ear, E for telephony — ordinary voice). So CW is A1A, SSB voice is J3E, and FM voice is F3E. You will meet these exact codes in band plans and in the Ukrainian regulations.
ch3_2.charP3: The bandwidth each mode occupies is part of its character too — and the spread is enormous, from a CW signal barely 150 Hz wide, through SSB and AM, up to narrow-band FM at around 16 kHz:
ch3_2.charP4: Finally, spectral purity is not merely good manners — it is the law. The ITU Radio Regulations set the international baseline: a spurious emission outside your channel must sit at least 43 dB below the transmitter's mean (average) power, and no higher than 50 mW in absolute terms — tens of thousands of times weaker than the signal you meant to send. Ukraine's own Regulations, drawn up inside that framework and the one agreed by CEPT (the European telecommunications body), put the figure for the amateur service at 40 dB and 50 mW below 30 MHz, with tighter absolute limits above it. Either way, that is precisely the bar the output low-pass filter from the last section exists to clear. Build the chain right, fit the filter, stay inside your power limit, and you are a transmitter the whole band is glad to hear.
ch3_2.charKey: A transmitter's worth is measured by its cleanliness: a steady frequency, no more bandwidth than the mode needs, the right power for the job, and as few harmonics and spurious signals as the components allow. Everything in this chapter — the buffered oscillator, the right amplifier class, the mandatory output filter — exists to serve those four goals.

emDecoder.caption: The ITU emission designator, decoded. The first character is the carrier modulation (A for AM, J for SSB, F for FM), the second the modulating signal (1 for on/off keyed, 3 for analogue), the third the information (A for Morse by ear, E for voice).
emDecoder.ariaLabel: A decoder table for ITU emission designators. CW is A1A: amplitude modulation, keyed, Morse. SSB is J3E: single sideband, analogue, voice. FM is F3E: frequency modulation, analogue, voice. AM is A3E: amplitude modulation, analogue, voice.
emDecoder.cwMean: Morse — carrier keyed on and off

bwLadder.title: How wide? Occupied bandwidth by mode
bwLadder.aria: A ladder of occupied bandwidth by mode, widest at the top: narrow-band FM about 16 kHz, AM about 6 kHz, SSB about 2.7 kHz, and CW about 150 Hz.
bwLadder.caption: Occupied bandwidth, widest at the top. CW slips through the narrowest gap; SSB needs about a tenth the room of narrow-band FM, which is one reason crowded HF bands favour SSB and CW.

ch3_2.labGoal: See for yourself that a square (clipped) wave is stuffed with <harmonic>harmonics</harmonic> — and watch a low-pass filter strip them away, exactly as a transmitter's output filter does.
ch3_2.labEquip1: Oscilloscope with an FFT (Fast Fourier Transform) / spectrum function
ch3_2.labComp1: A low-pass filter from Chapter 1.8 (an RC or LC low-pass)
ch3_2.labStep1: Set the Arduino to output a 1 kHz <square>square wave</square> on pin 9 (the tone(9, 1000) sketch from Chapter 0.2). A square wave is the harshest, most clipped wave there is — which makes its harmonics easy to see.
ch3_2.labStep2: Probe pin 9 and switch the oscilloscope into FFT (spectrum) mode. Instead of the square wave in time, you now see it in frequency: a tall spike at 1 kHz — the fundamental — and a row of smaller spikes marching up the axis at 3, 5 and 7 kHz. Those are the harmonics. (A square wave carries only the odd ones; a transmitter's clipping makes all of them.)
ch3_2.labStep3: Read off the heights. Each harmonic is smaller than the last, but they reach a surprising distance up the band — proof that a clipped wave is anything but pure.
ch3_2.labStep4: Now wire your Chapter 1.8 low-pass filter between pin 9 and the scope probe, with its cutoff set just above 1 kHz. Watch the FFT.
ch3_2.labStep5: The fundamental at 1 kHz barely moves, but the harmonics collapse — the higher the harmonic, the harder it is crushed. You are watching the exact job a transmitter's output filter does, only at audio instead of radio frequencies.
ch3_2.labExpected: Without the filter: a tall 1 kHz spike plus a comb of odd harmonics (3, 5, 7 kHz…) stepping downward in height. With the filter: the 1 kHz spike is almost untouched while the harmonics drop away into the noise.
ch3_2.labConnection: A transmitter's Class C power amplifier clips its wave just as harshly as this square wave is clipped, and makes the very same harmonics — only up at radio frequencies, where they would land on other bands. The output low-pass filter from Section 6 does exactly what you just did on the bench: keep the fundamental, kill the harmonics. (With a real transmitter you would never probe it directly — you would feed a <dload>dummy load</dload> and tap a tiny, attenuated sample into a spectrum analyser. Full transmitter power destroys instruments.)
ch3_2.labTrouble1: No FFT mode on your scope: a cheap USB spectrum analyser, or a NanoVNA in spectrum mode, works just as well; failing that, trust the theory — the harmonics are there.
ch3_2.labTrouble2: Harmonics don't drop: check the filter's cutoff sits above 1 kHz (so the fundamental passes) but below 3 kHz (so the first harmonic is attenuated). An RC filter rolls off gently; an LC filter is sharper.
ch3_2.labTrouble3: The whole trace is noisy: shorten the probe's ground lead and make sure every breadboard connection is firm.
ch3_2.quiz_q1: Every signal a transmitter sends out begins life in which stage?
ch3_2.quiz_q1_explanation: The oscillator generates the carrier — the pure wave everything else is built on. The stages after it shape, amplify and radiate that wave, but none of them create it.
ch3_2.quiz_q2: Compared with a crystal oscillator, a VFO (variable-frequency oscillator) is…
ch3_2.quiz_q2_a: more stable, but locked to one fixed frequency
ch3_2.quiz_q2_c: unable to generate a carrier at all
ch3_2.quiz_q2_d: less stable, but tunable across a band
ch3_2.quiz_q2_explanation: That is the central trade-off: a crystal is rock-steady but fixed, while a VFO can be tuned across a band but drifts more. The crystal is the more stable of the two — so option (a) has it backwards.
ch3_2.quiz_q3: Which of these holds its frequency most tightly?
ch3_2.quiz_q3_a: a simple LC VFO you tune by hand
ch3_2.quiz_q3_d: a bare LC tuned circuit, no crystal
ch3_2.quiz_q3_explanation: Sealing the crystal inside a temperature-controlled oven (OCXO) reaches parts-per-billion stability — far steadier than a plain crystal, and steadier still than a drifting VFO.
ch3_2.quiz_q4: What is the buffer's main job, sitting right after the oscillator?
ch3_2.quiz_q4_a: to isolate the oscillator from its load
ch3_2.quiz_q4_b: to multiply the carrier frequency upward
ch3_2.quiz_q4_c: to fold the message onto the radio carrier
ch3_2.quiz_q4_d: to filter the harmonics out of the output
ch3_2.quiz_q4_explanation: The buffer's reverse isolation acts as a one-way valve: it passes the signal forward but stops changes downstream from reaching back and pulling the oscillator's frequency.
ch3_2.quiz_q5: A frequency multiplier is used to…
ch3_2.quiz_q5_a: amplify the signal right up to full power
ch3_2.quiz_q5_b: raise a low oscillator to a higher band
ch3_2.quiz_q5_c: strip away one of the two sidebands
ch3_2.quiz_q5_d: switch the carrier rapidly on and off
ch3_2.quiz_q5_explanation: Crystals and VFOs are steadiest at low frequencies. A multiplier lifts that steady low frequency up to the VHF or UHF band by an exact whole number, carrying its stability with it.
ch3_2.quiz_q6: In an SSB transmitter, what does the balanced modulator do?
ch3_2.quiz_q6_a: amplify the whole signal to full power
ch3_2.quiz_q6_b: key the carrier fully on and off
ch3_2.quiz_q6_explanation: The balanced modulator cancels the carrier — that is why it is «balanced» — leaving just the two sidebands. A sharp filter then removes one of them, giving single sideband.
ch3_2.quiz_q7_explanation: SSB throws away the carrier (it carries no information) and one redundant sideband, so every watt goes into the single sideband that actually carries the voice.
ch3_2.quiz_q8: Why can FM and CW use an efficient Class C amplifier, while SSB cannot?
ch3_2.quiz_q8_a: FM and CW are always higher in frequency
ch3_2.quiz_q8_b: FM and CW have a constant envelope
ch3_2.quiz_q8_c: SSB simply needs much more power
ch3_2.quiz_q8_d: Class C only works up on the VHF bands
ch3_2.quiz_q8_explanation: Class C clips the wave, mangling its amplitude. FM and CW carry no information in the amplitude (constant envelope), so that is harmless; SSB carries the voice in the envelope, so it needs a linear amplifier.
ch3_2.quiz_q9: Why must every transmitter have a low-pass filter after its power amplifier?
ch3_2.quiz_q9_a: to boost the transmitter's output power
ch3_2.quiz_q9_b: to tune the antenna into resonance
ch3_2.quiz_q9_explanation: A power amplifier — especially an efficient Class C one — generates harmonics at two, three and four times the frequency. The low-pass filter strips them off before they reach the antenna and splatter onto other bands.
ch3_2.quiz_q10: Which ITU emission designator means single-sideband voice?
ch3_2.quiz_q10_explanation: Here J stands for single sideband, 3 for an analogue signal, and E for telephony — voice — so single-sideband voice is J3E. For contrast, A1A is CW (Morse), F3E is FM voice, and A3E is AM voice.

ch3_3.heroAriaLabel: Pen-and-ink sketch of an antenna system: a centre-fed half-wave dipole — its two halves converging into the feedline at the centre — launches concentric radio waves into the sky, while a coaxial feedline runs down to a small transceiver.
ch3_3.intro1: In Chapter 3.1 your radio learned to hear, and in Chapter 3.2 it learned to talk. But every word it speaks and every whisper it catches has to cross the boundary between the wires of your station and the open sky — and that crossing is the job of the <ant>antenna</ant>. It is the one part of your station that actually touches the radio wave. A brilliant transmitter feeding a poor antenna will always lose to a modest rig feeding a good one.
ch3_3.intro2: An antenna never works alone. Power has to travel from the rig out to it along a feedline, and the antenna has to accept that power rather than bounce it back. This chapter follows the whole system, in order: what an antenna really does, how its length sets its resonance, the common shapes you will meet, what antenna gain does and does not mean, the feedlines that carry the power, the SWR that tells you how well it all fits together, and the baluns and tuners that smooth the joins.
ch3_3.transducerP1: An antenna is a translator between two worlds. Inside your coax, energy travels as a current sloshing back and forth along a wire — guided, penned in, going where the metal tells it. Out in the sky it travels as a free radio wave, loose and spreading at the speed of light. The antenna is the device that turns one into the other, in both directions. A loudspeaker does the same trick between an electrical signal and sound in the air; an antenna does it between an electrical signal and an electromagnetic wave in space.
ch3_3.transducerP2: So how does a wire actually launch a wave? The key is that the dipole endlessly reverses its polarity. The oscillating current sloshes charge from end to end: for half a cycle the top is + and the bottom −, setting up an electric field that arcs between them; half a cycle later the current reverses, the ends swap to − and +, and the field flips with them. That flipping is what radiates: a changing electric field gives rise to a magnetic field, and a changing magnetic field to an electric field, so once the dipole stirs up a changing field the two regenerate each other and the disturbance rolls outward on its own. And because a field can only keep up at the speed of light, by the time the dipole reverses, the field far from the wire is too late to be pulled back — it closes into a loop, breaks free, and travels off as a radio wave. The panel below shows it, slowed right down.
ch3_3.transducerP2b: The wave is driven by an uneven pattern of current and voltage along the wire. On a half-wave <dipole>dipole</dipole> the current is largest in the middle and falls to almost nothing at the two ends, while the voltage does the exact opposite — largest at the ends, smallest in the middle. That fixed pattern of highs and lows is itself a <sw>standing wave</sw>, the same phenomenon you will meet on the feedline later in this chapter. And because physics does not care which way the energy flows, the very same antenna transmits and receives identically — a good transmitting antenna is an equally good receiving one.
ch3_3.transducerP3: From the feedline's point of view, the feed point of the antenna simply looks like a resistor that swallows power. But the power is not turned into heat the way a real resistor would — it leaves as radio waves. We give that useful, power-launching effect its own name: <radres>radiation resistance</radres> (call it <var>R</var>). For a half-wave dipole in the clear it works out to about <var>R</var> ≈ 73 Ω. (A little real resistance always sneaks in too — warm wire, lossy ground — and that part genuinely is wasted as heat, which is why an efficient antenna keeps its radiation resistance well above its loss resistance.)
ch3_3.transducerKey: The antenna is the highest-leverage part of your station. Watts are expensive and gain on the antenna is cheap; a better antenna helps every contact you ever make, on transmit and on receive alike, because the two are the same thing. Spend your effort here before you spend it chasing power.

dipoleIV.caption: Current and voltage along a half-wave dipole. The current (solid) is greatest at the centre feed point and falls to zero at the ends; the voltage (dashed) does the opposite. Feeding at the centre, where the current is high and the voltage low, is what gives the dipole its convenient ~73 Ω feed impedance.
dipoleIV.ariaLabel: A horizontal dipole drawn as two wires meeting at a central feed point. A solid curve shows the current peaking at the centre and falling to zero at both ends. A dashed curve shows the voltage doing the reverse: zero at the centre, maximum at both ends.

radiation.title: How a dipole radiates
radiation.description: See it in slow motion. The alternating current sloshing up and down the dipole piles charge onto the ends — the ± dots — and drags an electric field along with it; on every half-cycle a loop of that field pinches off and sails outward at the speed of light. The loops drawn here are the electric field; the magnetic field circles the wire at right angles — straight out of the screen — and the two together are the radio wave. Charge and current take turns: the dots are biggest the instant the current reverses and is momentarily zero, then shrink as the current floods back. One wavelength of the radiated wave matches one full period of the current: λ = c · T.
radiation.ariaLabel: Animated cross-section of a radiating dipole: the alternating current oscillates along the dipole while closed loops of electric field detach and travel outward at the speed of light. A trace below plots the current over time.

ch3_3.resonanceP1: Why half a wavelength? Look back at the current pattern from the section before: along the wire the current must fall to zero at each open end — there is nowhere for charge to flow past the tip — yet it runs largest in the middle, exactly where you feed it. The shortest wave that fits a zero at both ends with a single peak in the centre is precisely one half-wave; picture half a hump of a sine laid along the wire. It is the same reason a plucked guitar string sounds its fundamental — its lowest, fullest note — with exactly one half-wave spanning its two fixed ends. Cut the wire to that length and its natural rhythm falls into step with the current driving it: the charge swings to its peak at the ends just as the current drops to zero and reverses to sweep it back the other way, so every push lands in time and the oscillation builds — the wire is at resonance. This half-wave wire, fed in the middle, is the dipole: the reference against which every other antenna is measured.
ch3_3.resonanceP2: The length follows straight from the wave. A full wavelength in metres is λ = 300 / f, with f the frequency in megahertz, so a half-wave is half of that, 150 / f. In practice a real dipole has to be cut about 5 % shorter than this — the wire's blunt ends store a little charge (capacitance to the surroundings), which makes the antenna behave as if it were slightly longer than it is, so you trim it back. That gives the working rule for the total length of a half-wave dipole:
ch3_3.resonanceFormula: <var>L</var> ≈ 143 / <var>f</var>   (<var>L</var> in metres, <var>f</var> in MHz)  —  about 71.5 / <var>f</var> per leg
ch3_3.resonanceP3: For the 40-metre band at f = 7.1 MHz, that is 143 / 7.1 ≈ 20.1 m of wire in total, roughly 10.1 m for each half. (Hams from countries that work in feet know the same rule as 468 / f; it is the identical number, just in feet instead of metres.) Cut it, hang it, and it resonates on 40 m. The calculator below does the arithmetic for any band — try it:
ch3_3.resonanceP4: At resonance the dipole's feed point is purely resistive at that ~73 Ω, which is a happy accident: it is close enough to the 50 Ω of standard coax that a plain dipole feeds it well, with only a mild mismatch (an <swr>SWR</swr> of about 1.5 to 1, as the section on SWR below will make precise). Stray off the resonant frequency, though, and the feed point grows a <react>reactance</react> — it starts to look part-capacitor or part-inductor — and the match worsens. That is exactly why an 80-metre dipole will not behave on 40 metres without help.
ch3_3.resonanceKey: The half-wave dipole is the yardstick antenna. Its gain is defined as zero dBd — every other antenna's gain is quoted relative to it — and its ~73 Ω feed point is a near-match for 50 Ω coax. Learn the dipole and every other antenna is a variation on it.

dipoleCalc.title: Half-wave dipole length calculator
dipoleCalc.description: Enter a frequency, or pick a band, and read off how long to cut the wire. The total length uses the working rule <var>L</var> ≈ 143 / <var>f</var> — the free-space half-wave trimmed by 5 % for real-world end effect.
dipoleCalc.note: These are starting lengths. Hang the antenna, measure the SWR, and trim a few centimetres at a time to move resonance where you want it — surroundings always shift it a little.

ch3_3.typesP1: Once you understand the dipole, the rest of the antenna zoo falls into place — they are all the same physics dressed for different jobs: fitting a small garden, covering every direction at once, packing down for a hike, or reaching one distant station. Three are worth knowing well.
ch3_3.typesP2: The quarter-wave vertical is, quite literally, half a dipole standing up. A single rod a quarter-wave tall (L ≈ 71 / f in metres) does the work of one dipole leg; the missing lower half is supplied by its mirror image in a conducting ground plane — a set of wires called radials laid on or under the ground (a vertical without radials is mostly a heater for the soil). It is a monopole: it radiates equally in all horizontal directions — wonderful for working everyone, useless for ignoring a noisy direction — and its wave is vertically polarised. Its feed impedance is lower than a dipole's, around 36 Ω in the ideal case, and nearer 50 Ω over real ground.
ch3_3.typesP3: The end-fed half-wave (EFHW) is a dipole fed at one end instead of the middle — and you saw why that is awkward: the end is the high-voltage, low-current point, so its feed impedance is enormous, a few thousand ohms. A small transformer (a 49:1 unun) steps that down to 50 Ω. In return you get an antenna that needs only one support and a single feed at the far end, works on several bands at once, and rolls up into a pocket — which is why it is the darling of portable and QRP (low-power) operators.
ch3_3.typesP4: The Yagi is how you aim. Alongside the one driven element that is actually fed, it carries a few parasitic elements — a slightly longer reflector behind and one or more slightly shorter directors in front — that are connected to nothing at all. The driven element's field washes over them, they re-radiate it, and with their spacing and length chosen just so, all those re-radiated waves add up forwards and cancel backwards. The result is a beam: a three-element Yagi concentrates about four times the power of a dipole in the direction it points — a gain of roughly 6 dB — at the price of its size and the need to rotate it. You meet it again in the next section, where we put a number on that focusing.
ch3_3.typesTip: Which antenna? A dipole is the honest all-rounder for a fixed station with room for a wire. A vertical buys you all-round coverage and a low takeoff angle for distant stations where space is tight. An end-fed half-wave is the one you take on holiday. A Yagi is for when you know which way the action is and want to shout in that direction.

antennaGallery.caption: Three common antennas, all built from the same half-wave idea: the dipole fed at its centre, the quarter-wave vertical standing on a ground plane of radials, and the Yagi that adds parasitic elements to form a beam.
antennaGallery.ariaLabel: Three antennas side by side. Left: a horizontal half-wave dipole fed at its centre. Middle: a vertical quarter-wave rod with radial wires spreading from its base. Right: a Yagi with a reflector, a fed driven element, and two directors mounted along a boom, with an arrow showing the forward beam direction.

ch3_3.sectionGain: Pattern and gain: focusing, not amplifying
ch3_3.gainP1: Here is the single most misunderstood idea in antennas, so meet it with the right picture first. Take a bare light bulb and a torch with the same bulb inside. The torch is not brighter because it has a bigger battery — it has the same bulb, drawing the same power — it is brighter ahead because a mirror gathers the light that would have sprayed sideways and pours it forward. Point it at a wall and that spot is dazzling; stand behind it and you are in the dark. An antenna with gain does exactly this with radio energy. It makes no new power. It simply takes power that a dipole would have wasted in directions you do not care about and redirects it where you do.
ch3_3.gainP2: The map of where an antenna sends its energy is its radiation pattern. A dipole's is a figure-of-eight: strong broadside (out from the flat of the wire), with deep nulls off the two ends where it barely radiates at all. A vertical's pattern, seen from above, is a full circle — the same in every direction. A Yagi's is a single fat lobe pointing forward with only a stub poking backwards; the difference between the forward and backward strength is its front-to-back ratio, and the angular width of that forward lobe is its beamwidth.
ch3_3.gainP3: To put a number on gain you need something to compare against, and there are two references in common use. The first is the <iso>isotropic</iso> radiator — an imaginary point that radiates equally in every direction, the bare bulb of the radio world; gain against it is written <dbi>dBi</dbi>. The second is our friend the dipole; gain against it is <dbd>dBd</dbd>. A dipole already beats an isotropic source by 2.15 dB in its best direction, so the two scales differ by exactly that:
ch3_3.gainFormula: <dbi>dBi</dbi> = <dbd>dBd</dbd> + 2.15   →   a dipole is 0 dBd = 2.15 dBi; a 6 dBd Yagi is 8.15 dBi
ch3_3.gainP4: Finally, how strong is your signal once it leaves the antenna? That is captured by a figure for effective radiated power. Start from your transmitter's output, subtract whatever the feedline loses, add the antenna's gain, and you have the power your station behaves as if it were radiating. Referenced to a dipole it is called ERP (effective radiated power); referenced to an isotropic source it is EIRP — the extra I stands for isotropic — so it is always 2.15 dB larger. It matters because licence and band-plan limits are often written in these terms, not in raw transmitter watts.
ch3_3.gainErpFormula: <erp>ERP</erp> = <var>P</var> × 10^((<var>G</var> − <var>L</var>) / 10)  —  with <var>P</var> the transmitter power, <var>G</var> the antenna gain in dBd and <var>L</var> the feedline loss in dB
ch3_3.gainP5: A worked case: feed a +6 dBd Yagi from a 100 W transmitter through a feedline that loses 1 dB, and the system gain is +5 dB. So the ERP is 100 × 10^(5/10) ≈ 316 W — your station throws as much signal in the favoured direction as a dipole fed with 316 W would. As an EIRP that same signal is 2.15 dB more, about 518 W. Try your own numbers below — enter the gain as dBd, the dipole-referenced figure:
ch3_3.gainKey: Antenna gain is redistribution, not amplification. A high-gain antenna invents no power; it concentrates the power it is given into a narrower cone, trading coverage in unwanted directions for strength in the wanted one. "6 dB of gain" always means "6 dB stronger here, at the cost of weaker somewhere else."

gainPatterns.caption: The same power, shaped three ways. An isotropic source radiates a uniform sphere (a circle here). A dipole squeezes that into a broadside figure-of-eight with nulls off the ends. A Yagi concentrates it into a single forward lobe — that concentration is what we measure as gain.
gainPatterns.ariaLabel: Three radiation patterns drawn as polar plots. Left: an isotropic source, a plain circle, 0 dBi. Middle: a dipole, a figure-of-eight with two lobes broadside and nulls off the ends, 2.15 dBi. Right: a Yagi, one large forward lobe and a small rear lobe, about 8 dBi, with an arrow marking the beam direction.

erpCalc.title: ERP and EIRP calculator
erpCalc.description: Enter the transmitter power, the feedline loss and the antenna gain. The system gain is the antenna gain minus the line loss; ERP applies it to your power, and EIRP is the same figure referenced to an isotropic source (2.15 dB higher).
erpCalc.note: Gain entered in dBd. A plain dipole is 0 dBd; a typical 3-element Yagi is about 6 dBd.

ch3_3.sectionLines: Getting the power there: transmission lines
ch3_3.linesP1: Between the rig and the antenna runs the <feeder>feedline</feeder>, and its job sounds simple: carry the power from one end to the other. It must do so without leaking energy into the air along the way (a feedline is not supposed to radiate) and without wasting too much of it as heat. Think of it as a pipe for radio power — and like any pipe, the fitting at each end has to be right or the flow backs up.
ch3_3.linesP2: Feedlines come in two families. Coaxial cable ("coax") buries a central wire inside a tubular metal shield, with insulation between; the fields stay sealed inside the tube, so coax does not radiate and does not care if it runs along a gutter or through a wall. Almost all amateur coax is 50 Ω; the 75 Ω kind is the stuff of TV aerials. Balanced or parallel lines instead run two conductors side by side — twin-lead at 300 Ω, ladder line (window line) near 450 Ω, open-wire feeders around 600 Ω. They lose far less power than coax but must be kept clear of metal and damp, since their fields live in the open air between the conductors.
ch3_3.linesP2b: First, a word on what actually travels down a feedline, since this is where intuition often slips. At mains frequency a cable is far shorter than the wavelength (kilometres long), so the current is essentially the same all along it — the familiar picture of 'current in a wire'. At radio frequencies the wavelength shrinks to metres, often shorter than the cable itself, and that picture breaks down: a disturbance launched at one end takes real time to reach the other, so voltage and current vary along the line and travel as a wave. It is the same electromagnetic wave that will later leave the antenna — only here it is still guided, held in the field between the two conductors, instead of radiating free in space. 'Current in the wire' and 'a wave along the line' are two descriptions of one thing.
ch3_3.linesP3: Each line has a <ci>characteristic impedance</ci>, written <var>Z_{0}</var> — and it is less abstract than it sounds. Two conductors with insulation between them are, electrically, two things at once: a capacitor (the gap between them holds charge) and an inductor (every length of wire resists a change in its current). Spread evenly along the cable, that is a small capacitance and a small inductance per metre — so the line really does behave like a long chain of tiny coils in series along the wire and tiny capacitors across the gap. Feed a wave in and the chain sets the pace: each coil limits how fast the next capacitor can charge, so the wave travels at a fixed speed and, at every step, meets the same ratio of voltage to current. That ratio is <var>Z_{0}</var>, fixed by the conductors' thickness and spacing and not by the line's length. It works out to √(<var>L</var>/<var>C</var>) from the inductance and capacitance per metre, as the figure below shows. Fat conductors close together give a low <var>Z_{0}</var> (50 Ω coax), thin ones far apart a high <var>Z_{0}</var> (450 Ω ladder line).
ch3_3.linesP3b: Why does that ratio matter? Picture the chain running on forever: a wave fed into an endless line travels outward and never returns, so to the source it is indistinguishable from a single Z_{0} resistor quietly absorbing the power. A real line, though, ends in a load — your antenna — and the goal is to make that ending invisible to the wave. If the load equals Z_{0}, the wave reaches the end and finds the very same voltage-to-current ratio it has met all along: the load is indistinguishable from more line, so the wave pours straight into it and is absorbed completely. That is what a matched, or properly terminated, line means — the far-end load equals Z_{0}. If the load is anything else, the wave arrives carrying a ratio the load cannot satisfy, and the only way to balance voltage and current at that junction is to send part of the wave back toward the source — a reflection (at an open or a shorted end, all of it bounces back). That reflected power is exactly what you work to avoid, and it is why a 50 Ω line wants a 50 Ω antenna.

lcLadder.caption: Any line carries the inductance of its own conductors (<var>L</var>) and the capacitance between them (<var>C</var>), spread along its length; their ratio fixes the characteristic impedance <var>Z_{0}</var> = √(<var>L</var>/<var>C</var>). The chain is effectively endless — the wave always sees more line ahead.

ch3_3.linesP4: Waves also travel slower inside a line than in free space, because the insulation drags on the field. The fraction of full speed they manage is the velocity factor: about 0.66 for ordinary solid-plastic coax, 0.80 for foam-filled coax, and over 0.90 for airy ladder line. This is not a curiosity — it shortens any length you cut to a fraction of a wavelength. A quarter-wave in free space at 7.1 MHz is 300 / 7.1 / 4 ≈ 10.6 m, but the same electrical quarter-wave inside 0.66 coax is only 0.66 × 10.6 ≈ 7.0 m. Cut a matching stub by the free-space length and it will be far too long.
ch3_3.linesP5: Finally, no line is free: every metre turns a little of your power into heat, and the loss grows worse as the frequency climbs. A long run of thin RG-58 that barely sips your signal on 80 m can swallow half of it on the 2-metre band. The rules that fall out of this are simple — keep feedlines as short as practical, use fatter or better cable for long runs, and treat loss as the silent tax it is, especially up at <vhf>VHF</vhf> and <uhf>UHF</uhf> — the bands above roughly 30 MHz.

Right: balanced twin-lead, two conductors held apart by insulation, with the field shown in the gap between them, marked 300 to 600 ohms.
