ch3_3.sectionSwr: Matching: SWR and what it really means
ch3_3.swrP1: What happens when the antenna does not accept all the power the line brings it? The leftover bounces back. Just as a wave runs back up a hose when you block the nozzle, or your shout echoes off a far wall, the reflected power travels back down the feedline and meets the power still coming forward. Where the two line up they reinforce; where they oppose they cancel — and the result is a fixed pattern of high and low voltage standing along the cable: a <sw>standing wave</sw>.
ch3_3.swrP2: How pronounced that pattern is — the ratio of the high points to the low points — is the standing wave ratio (SWR). A perfectly matched line, where the load equals Z_{0}, reflects nothing: the voltage is even all along it and the SWR is 1 to 1. The worse the mismatch, the more it reflects and the lumpier the wave, so the higher the SWR. What fraction of the wave bounces back is the reflection coefficient Γ. Writing Z for the antenna's feed impedance and Z_{0} for the line's, it is Γ = (Z − Z_{0}) / (Z + Z_{0}), and the two are tied together by SWR = (1 + |Γ|) / (1 − |Γ|). For a plain resistive load you do not even need that: the SWR is just the larger of Z / Z_{0} or Z_{0} / Z. So our 73 Ω dipole on 50 Ω coax sits at 73 / 50 ≈ 1.5 to 1, while a 25 Ω load would give 50 / 25 = 2 to 1. Hams often quote the same reflection as return loss: how far below the forward wave the reflected one sits, in decibels — a 1.5-to-1 SWR is about 14 dB. A better match reflects less, so a bigger return loss means a better match, the opposite way to SWR.
ch3_3.swrP3: It is worth knowing how little a "bad" SWR actually throws away, because the numbers are gentler than the folklore. The fraction of power reflected is |<var>Γ</var>|², and at <hf>HF</hf> (the high-frequency shortwave bands, roughly 3–30 MHz) most of even that reflected power is not lost — it bounces off the rig and heads back to the antenna again. The table tells the story:

swrTable.caption: What each SWR really costs. The reflected power is not all lost — at HF most of it is re-reflected toward the antenna — so even 2:1 is a mild affair.
swrTable.r4Verdict: workable on HF with good line

ch3_3.swrP4: Try it for yourself — set the load impedance and watch both the standing wave on the line and the numbers it produces:
ch3_3.swrP5: Three myths are worth puncturing here, because chasing them wastes more antennas than it saves. First, a low SWR does not mean a good antenna: a dummy load shows a flawless 1:1 and radiates not a single watt — SWR measures the match, not how well you get out. Second, high SWR does not by itself cause interference or make the feedline radiate; that is the job of common-mode current, a separate problem you meet in the next section. Third, feedline loss flatters the SWR you measure: read through a long, lossy cable, the reflection is attenuated on its round trip, so the meter in the shack shows a kinder figure than the antenna really has. Be suspicious of a wonderfully flat SWR at the end of a long thin coax.
ch3_3.swrKey: Aim for a good match, not a perfect one. Below about 1.5:1 is excellent and a plain dipole gets there on its own; up to 2:1 is comfortable, and modern rigs begin to ease back their power only beyond it. On HF with decent cable you still work the world well above 2:1 — so do not spend an afternoon shaving 1.5 down to 1.3 when you could be making contacts.

swrExplorer.title: Standing wave explorer
swrExplorer.description: Slide the antenna's feed impedance away from the 50 Ω the line wants. Watch the voltage along the cable swell into a standing wave, and read the SWR, reflection, reflected power and return loss it produces.
swrExplorer.matched: Matched — no reflection, a flat line.
swrExplorer.mild: A mild mismatch — nothing to worry about.
swrExplorer.high: A heavy mismatch — most rigs would fold back power.
swrExplorer.ariaLabel: An interactive standing-wave display. A slider sets the antenna feed impedance on a 50 ohm line; the voltage envelope along the line is drawn, and the SWR, reflection coefficient, reflected power and return loss are shown.

ch3_3.matchingP1: Two small devices live where the feedline meets the antenna and the rig, and both exist to make mismatched things get along. The first solves a problem hiding inside every coax-fed dipole. A dipole is balanced — its two legs are mirror images — while coax is unbalanced, an inner conductor and an outer shield that are not equals. Bolt one straight to the other and the outside surface of the shield quietly becomes a third wire: some of the antenna current flows back down the outside of the coax instead of staying on the antenna. This common-mode current radiates where you do not want it (warping the pattern and filling in the deep nulls a clean pattern should have), follows the cable back into the shack as RF — radio-frequency energy — loose in the shack (the classic "my microphone bites me when I transmit"), and confuses your SWR meter.
ch3_3.matchingP2: The cure is a balun — balanced-to-unbalanced. The everyday kind is a choke (current) balun: a few turns of the coax wound through a ferrite ring, which puts a high impedance in the way of any current trying to flow on the outside of the shield, while the wanted signal sealed inside passes by untouched. (A low wire dipole works happily without one; it matters most for a directional antenna like a Yagi, where shield current would wreck the very pattern you built it for.) Its cousin the unun — unbalanced-to-unbalanced — does the impedance-changing job between two unbalanced points: the 49:1 unun feeding an end-fed half-wave is the example you have already met.
ch3_3.matchingP3: The second device is the antenna tuner (ATU, or antenna matching unit), and it is the most misunderstood box in the shack — so be very clear about what it does. It sits at the rig end of the feedline and transforms whatever impedance it sees there into the 50 Ω your transmitter wants, so the power amplifier delivers full power instead of folding back. That is all it does, and it is genuinely useful. But notice what it does not do:

matchingList.notTune: It does not "tune the antenna." The antenna out there is exactly as resonant — or not — as it was before; the tuner never touches it.
matchingList.notSwr: It does not lower the SWR on the feedline between itself and the antenna. That mismatch, and the loss it adds, are still there; the tuner only flattens the short stretch back to the rig.
matchingList.notLoss: It cannot recover power already lost as heat in the line. Once a watt is gone in the coax, no tuner brings it back.

ch3_3.matchingP4: In short, an ATU keeps your transmitter happy; it does not improve your antenna. If you can, the best place to correct a bad match is out at the antenna itself, not back in the shack — but a tuner at the rig is what lets one antenna serve several bands.
ch3_3.matchingKey: An ATU matches the rig to the line, not the antenna to the sky. It transforms the shack-end impedance to the 50 Ω the transmitter needs — nothing more. It does not tune the antenna, it does not lower the SWR out on the feedline, and it cannot undo feedline loss.

systemBlock.caption: The whole antenna system, and where the SWR really lives. The tuner flattens the match only on the short link back to the transmitter (1:1); the true SWR set by the antenna is still present on the feedline beyond it. A choke balun at the antenna keeps current off the outside of the coax.
systemBlock.ariaLabel: A block chain from left to right: transceiver, antenna tuner, SWR meter, then a long feedline, a choke balun, and a dipole antenna. A bracket over the link from transmitter to tuner is marked SWR 1 to 1; a bracket over the feedline beyond the tuner is marked true antenna SWR.

ch3_3.sectionSystem: The antenna system as a whole
ch3_3.systemP1: Step back and the picture is one system in three parts, each able to spoil the others. A resonant antenna, cut to length and hung in the clear, turns your power into waves. A feedline of the right impedance, kept short and decent, carries the power to it with little loss. And a little matching — a balun where balance demands it, an ATU when the rig needs coaxing — smooths the joins. Get all three right and the modest 100 W from Chapter 3.2 reaches the sky almost intact.
ch3_3.systemP2: The real-world traps are all failures of one of those three. An 80-metre dipole pressed into service on 40 metres is no longer a half-wave — its feed impedance goes wild and the SWR with it, so it needs an ATU (or feeding with ladder line). A long run of thin RG-58 up at 2 m can lose half your power to heat before it ever reaches the antenna. A quarter-wave vertical with no radials warms the lawn instead of working DX (distant stations). And more often than any of these, the cure is simply height and a clear space — where the antenna sits usually matters more than which antenna it is.
ch3_3.systemP3: Which is why the antenna system is where your effort pays back best. Because transmit and receive are the same physics, every decibel you win on the antenna helps you twice — heard better and hearing better — on every contact, for as long as the antenna stands. Watts cost money and run out at the licence limit; antenna gain is, as the saying goes, the cheapest dB you will ever buy.

chooseTable.caption: Choosing an antenna — the trade-offs at a glance.

ch3_3.systemKey: The antenna system — antenna, feedline and matching — is the best investment in your station. It works for you on every transmit and every receive, it never runs out like power does, and a good one forgives a modest radio. Build the antenna first; chase watts last.
ch3_3.labGoal: Cut a dipole for the 2-metre band, then use a <vna>vector network analyser (VNA)</vna> to find the exact frequency where it resonates and watch its <swr>SWR</swr> dip — the same picture an SWR meter shows you, with the full story added.
ch3_3.labEquip1: Vector network analyser (a NanoVNA is perfect)
ch3_3.labComp1: About 1.1 m of thin wire (the two dipole legs)
ch3_3.labComp2: A small centre piece — two terminals, or a choc-block connector
ch3_3.labComp3: A short length of 50 Ω coax with the right connector for your VNA
ch3_3.labStep1: Pick 145 MHz, in the middle of the 2-metre band. The dipole is tiny here: total length L ≈ 143 / 145 ≈ 0.99 m, so cut two legs of about 50 cm each.
ch3_3.labStep2: Fix the two legs to the centre piece in a straight line, and connect the coax — shield to one leg, centre to the other. Connect the far end of the coax to the VNA's port 1.
ch3_3.labStep3: Calibrate the VNA (open, short, load) at the end of the coax, so the cable itself is taken out of the measurement, then sweep from 130 to 160 MHz.
ch3_3.labStep4: Look at the SWR (or return-loss) trace. You will see a sharp dip — the frequency where the antenna best accepts power. Is it near 145 MHz?
ch3_3.labStep5: If the dip sits too low in frequency, the antenna is too long — trim a centimetre off each leg and sweep again. Too high, and it is too short; you will have to start with slightly longer legs. A centimetre per side moves it a surprising amount.
ch3_3.labStep6: At the dip, read the impedance the VNA reports. A dipole in the clear lands near 73 Ω resistive; yours will be pulled around by its height and whatever is nearby — which is the real lesson.
ch3_3.labExpected: A clear SWR dip somewhere in the 130–160 MHz sweep, settling close to 145 MHz once trimmed, with the impedance at the dip somewhere in the region of 50–75 Ω.
ch3_3.labConnection: The dip is resonance — the spot where the feed point is purely resistive and the antenna swallows power instead of reflecting it. Your SWR meter only ever shows you this one number at one frequency; the VNA shows the whole curve, so you can see resonance and watch it move as you trim. This is exactly the standing-wave story from the SWR section above, made visible.
ch3_3.labTrouble1: No dip anywhere: check the coax connections at the centre piece (shield to one leg, centre to the other) and that the legs are not touching.
ch3_3.labTrouble2: Dip at the wrong frequency: that is normal — it is what the trimming step is for. Surroundings shift it; measure in the spot where the antenna will actually live.
ch3_3.labTrouble3: Jumpy, restless trace: re-do the calibration, and keep your hands and metal objects away from the antenna while you sweep.
ch3_3.quiz_q1: What is an antenna's fundamental job?
ch3_3.quiz_q1_a: to amplify the transmitter's power before it ever leaves the station
ch3_3.quiz_q1_b: to convert between a guided current and a free radio wave
ch3_3.quiz_q1_c: to filter the harmonics out of the signal
ch3_3.quiz_q1_d: to store energy like a battery
ch3_3.quiz_q1_explanation: An antenna is a transducer between two worlds: the current guided along the feedline and the radio wave travelling free in space. It adds no power — and because the physics is reciprocal, it works identically on transmit and receive.
ch3_3.quiz_q2: A half-wave dipole, resonant and in the clear, has a feed-point impedance of about…
ch3_3.quiz_q2_explanation: A resonant half-wave dipole presents about 73 Ω of (mostly radiation) resistance at its centre feed point — close enough to 50 Ω coax to feed it directly at an SWR around 1.5:1.
ch3_3.quiz_q3: Why is a real dipole cut about 5 % shorter than a free-space half wavelength?
ch3_3.quiz_q3_a: because end effect makes it act electrically longer than it is
ch3_3.quiz_q3_c: to raise its feed-point impedance up to the 50 Ω that coaxial cable expects
ch3_3.quiz_q3_d: so it works on every band at once
ch3_3.quiz_q3_explanation: Charge stored at the wire's blunt ends (capacitance to the surroundings) makes the antenna behave as if it were slightly longer than its physical length, so it is trimmed by about 5 % to resonate on frequency — the working rule <var>L</var> ≈ 143 / <var>f</var>.
ch3_3.quiz_q4: A quarter-wave vertical needs radials (or a ground plane) because…
ch3_3.quiz_q4_a: they protect the whole antenna from nearby lightning strikes
ch3_3.quiz_q4_c: they supply the missing other half of the antenna
ch3_3.quiz_q4_explanation: A vertical is half a dipole standing up; the ground plane of radials provides its mirror image — the missing lower half. Without that conducting plane the antenna is inefficient, dumping power into the lossy soil.
ch3_3.quiz_q5: When we say a Yagi has "gain," we mean it…
ch3_3.quiz_q5_a: it somehow creates extra transmit power out of the feedline's energy
ch3_3.quiz_q5_b: lowers the SWR of the system
ch3_3.quiz_q5_c: concentrates the available power into a preferred direction
ch3_3.quiz_q5_explanation: Gain is focusing, not amplifying — like a torch reflector. The antenna makes no new power; it redirects power that a dipole would have wasted in other directions into the one you point at, at the cost of coverage elsewhere.
ch3_3.quiz_q6: If an antenna's gain is 6 dBd, what is it in dBi?
ch3_3.quiz_q6_explanation: A dipole beats an isotropic source by 2.15 dB, so dBi = dBd + 2.15. A 6 dBd antenna is therefore 8.15 dBi. dBi is always the larger number because the isotropic reference is the weaker one.
ch3_3.quiz_q7: The characteristic impedance of the coax used for almost all amateur work is…
ch3_3.quiz_q7_explanation: Amateur radio is built around 50 Ω coax. 75 Ω is the television standard, while 300 Ω twin-lead and 450–600 Ω balanced lines are the parallel-line family used with tuners.
ch3_3.quiz_q8: A dummy load measures a perfect 1:1 SWR. What does this tell you about how well it radiates?
ch3_3.quiz_q8_b: nothing — SWR measures the match, not radiation
ch3_3.quiz_q8_c: it must be resonant and efficient on every amateur band
ch3_3.quiz_q8_explanation: A dummy load is a perfect 50 Ω match, so its SWR is a flawless 1:1 — yet it radiates nothing, turning all the power into heat. SWR tells you how well the load matches the line, never how well it gets out.
ch3_3.quiz_q9: Why is a choke (current) balun used where coax feeds a dipole?
ch3_3.quiz_q9_a: to stop current flowing on the outside of the coax shield
ch3_3.quiz_q9_b: to step the voltage up for the antenna
ch3_3.quiz_q9_c: to tune the antenna to resonance
ch3_3.quiz_q9_d: to filter out the stray harmonics that the transmitter's final stage produces
ch3_3.quiz_q9_explanation: A dipole is balanced and coax is not, so without a balun, common-mode current flows back down the outside of the shield — radiating where it shouldn't, causing RF in the shack and upsetting the SWR meter. A choke balun puts a high impedance in the way of that current.
ch3_3.quiz_q10: What does an antenna tuner (ATU) actually do?
ch3_3.quiz_q10_a: it physically retunes the actual antenna out at the mast, putting it back into resonance
ch3_3.quiz_q10_b: it lowers the SWR on the whole feedline
ch3_3.quiz_q10_c: it transforms the shack-end impedance to the 50 Ω the rig wants
ch3_3.quiz_q10_d: it recovers power lost as heat in the coax
ch3_3.quiz_q10_explanation: An ATU transforms whatever impedance appears at the rig end of the line into 50 Ω, so the transmitter delivers full power. It does not tune the antenna, does not lower the SWR on the feedline beyond it, and cannot recover power already lost in the line.

ch3_4.heroAriaLabel: A single signal feeds three instruments: an oscilloscope showing a waveform, an analog meter with a needle, and a digital multimeter showing a number.
ch3_4.intro1: You have built receivers, transmitters and antennas. Now comes the question every one of those projects eventually asks: is it actually doing what I think it is? Measurement is how you find out. Each instrument on the bench is a different window onto the same physical reality — a voltage here, a current there, a wave on a wire — and learning to read several windows and cross-check them is the habit that separates guessing from knowing.
ch3_4.intro2: This chapter walks the bench end to end: the <mm>multimeter</mm> for steady volts, amps and ohms; the analog needle that still earns its place; the <swr>SWR meter</swr> that watches power flow to your antenna; the <wm>wavemeter</wm> that sniffs out a frequency; and the <dl>dummy load</dl> that lets you test a transmitter safely. Every reading ties back to a number you can calculate — so each instrument comes with the formula behind it.
ch3_4.mmP1: The multimeter (often DMM, for digital multimeter) is the first tool you reach for. One box measures three things: voltage (the push), current (the flow), and resistance (the opposition). A rotary switch or auto-ranging picks which, and an internal analog-to-digital converter turns the measured quantity into the number on the display.
ch3_4.mmP2: How you connect it depends on what you are measuring, and the rule never changes: measure voltage in parallel, measure current in series. To read a voltage you touch the two probes across the part — like standing on the bank and watching the river without disturbing it. To read a current you must break the circuit open and let all the flow pass through the meter — like wading in and standing in the river itself.
ch3_4.mmDanger: Putting an ammeter across a voltage — wiring it like a voltmeter, with the probes still in the current jacks while you touch a battery — is the classic beginner mistake. An ideal ammeter is nearly a short circuit, so it dumps a huge current and blows its internal fuse (or worse). Switch back to the voltage jacks before measuring voltage.
ch3_4.mmP3: Resistance works differently: there is no current to read on an unpowered part, so the meter makes its own. Its internal battery pushes a small known current through the component and measures the voltage that results — Ohm’s law, run backwards, gives the resistance. (This is why you measure resistance only on a part that is switched off and out of circuit.)
ch3_4.mmP4: One number on the datasheet decides how honest your voltage readings are: the meter’s input impedance, typically 10 MΩ. The moment you connect it, the meter becomes the lower leg of a voltage divider, with the circuit’s own resistance as the upper leg. If the circuit’s resistance is small compared with 10 MΩ the meter sips a negligible current and reads true; if the circuit is itself in the megohms, the meter loads it down and reads low. Ideal voltmeter: infinite resistance. Ideal ammeter: zero. Exact opposites.
ch3_4.mmTrueRms: On AC, cheap meters are average-responding: they rectify the waveform and scale the result assuming a perfect sine. Feed them anything else — a clipped wave, a digital signal — and they read wrong. A true-RMS meter computes the real heating value and is correct for any shape. Also remember: more digits on the display is resolution, not accuracy; the analog front-end sets the true error (often 0.5–1 % on DC, more on AC).
ch3_4.mmKey: Voltage across (parallel), current through (series), resistance only on a dead part. A 10 MΩ input loads most circuits negligibly — but not high-impedance ones.
ch3_4.sectionAnalog: The analog needle and why it survives
ch3_4.anP1: Before the digital display there was the moving-coil (or d’Arsonval) movement, and it still ships in millions of meters. A coil hangs on jewelled pivots inside a permanent magnet; current through the coil makes it twist against a hairspring, swinging a needle across a scale. The deflection is proportional to the current, so the basic scale is beautifully linear. A typical movement reaches full scale on a tiny current — I_{fs} of about 50 µA.
ch3_4.analogMeterCaptionLead: That single movement reads many ranges by adding one resistor at a time:
ch3_4.anP2: To measure large currents, a small R_{sh} (a shunt) is wired in parallel with the movement. Most of the current takes the bypass lane through the shunt; only the movement’s full-scale 50 µA ever flows through the delicate coil. To measure voltage, a large R_{m} (a multiplier) goes in series: it drops almost all the voltage so that full scale again corresponds to that same tiny coil current. A 50 µA movement plus a 20 kΩ multiplier reads 1 V full scale (50 µA × 20 kΩ = 1 V).
ch3_4.anP3: That fixed appetite gives the movement’s figure of merit: its ohms-per-volt sensitivity, the reciprocal of the full-scale current. A 50 µA movement is 1 ÷ 50 µA = 20 000 Ω/V. On the 1 V range its input resistance is only 20 kΩ; on the 10 V range, 200 kΩ. Compared with a DMM’s steady 10 MΩ, an analog meter loads the circuit far more — and it loads less on higher ranges, where the series resistor is bigger.
ch3_4.anP4: The ohms scale is the odd one out. Shorted probes pass the most current, so 0 Ω sits at full deflection (the right end) and ∞ sits at no deflection (the left) — the scale runs backwards. And because deflection follows 1 ÷ R, the high-resistance numbers crowd together at the left end, where reading is least precise. A last hazard is parallax: the needle reads differently depending on your eye angle, which is why good meters add a mirror strip — line the needle up with its reflection to read straight-on.
ch3_4.anKey: A needle is worse than a DMM at a precise number but better at a trend: peaking or nulling an adjustment, its physical inertia smooths a wobble into a clear direction a flickering digit cannot. That is why a moving-coil meter still earns bench space.
ch3_4.sectionSwr: The SWR meter: power out, power back
ch3_4.swrP1: Feed a transmitter into an antenna and two waves live on the line at once: the forward wave heading out, and — if the antenna is not a perfect match — a reflected wave bouncing back, like an echo off a wall. A directional wattmeter uses a directional coupler to sample each wave separately, and derives the SWR (standing-wave ratio) from the two.
ch3_4.crossNeedleLead: The friendliest version is the cross-needle meter you will meet on most benches:
ch3_4.swrP2: The size of the echo is captured by the reflection coefficient Γ — the fraction of the wave’s amplitude that comes back. An SWR meter senses only its size, written |Γ| — the bars mean magnitude, the amount ignoring sign — and that size ties directly to SWR:
ch3_4.swrP3: Square |Γ| and you get the fraction of power that bounces back. The numbers are gentler than they feel: even a 2:1 SWR sends only 11 % of the power back, so 89 % still reaches the antenna. The table makes the pattern concrete:
ch3_4.swrP4: Turn an SWR into actual watts of lost and delivered power:
ch3_4.swrP5: Most rules of thumb draw the line at 2:1. It is not that the lost watts matter much at 2:1 — it is that the reflected power and the resulting voltage peaks stress a solid-state transmitter’s output stage, so the rig folds its power back to protect itself.
ch3_4.swrKey: An SWR meter shows the magnitude of the mismatch and nothing else — a 25 Ω load and a 100 Ω load both read 2:1. To learn the actual resistance and reactance behind the number you need a VNA (vector network analyser). The SWR meter is a thermometer; the VNA is a blood test.
ch3_4.sectionWavemeter: The absorption wavemeter: finding a frequency
ch3_4.wmP1: Sometimes you just need to know roughly where a signal is. An absorption wavemeter is the simplest answer: a coil and a variable capacitor forming a tuned circuit, with a diode detector and a meter to show a reading. Hold its coil near the transmitter so the two couple loosely, then turn the capacitor. When the tuned circuit resonates at the transmitter’s frequency it absorbs the most energy and the meter peaks — and you read the frequency off the capacitor’s calibrated dial. Like a wine glass that hums loudest at one pitch, the circuit answers only when the frequencies match.
ch3_4.wmP2: It is a passive eavesdropper — no wires into the signal, just a whiff of RF picked up nearby — which is also why it is only approximate. The <reson>resonance</reson> is broad (low <var>Q</var>), so the peak is soft and the dial reading rough. Its modern replacement is the <fc>frequency counter</fc>, which shows the frequency directly to many digits. The wavemeter survives as a teaching tool and a quick “is it roughly on this band?” check.
ch3_4.wmKey: Tune for a peak, read the dial: a wavemeter gives you the ballpark frequency with no connection to the transmitter. For a precise figure, reach for a frequency counter.
ch3_4.sectionDummy: The dummy load and measuring RF power
ch3_4.dlP1:
To test a transmitter at full power without putting a signal on the air, you feed it a
dummy load
: nothing more than a high-power 50 Ω resistor with a coaxial connector. It is a non-radiating stand-in for a perfectly matched antenna — a treadmill for your transmitter, which runs at full effort and full power without going anywhere. The rig cannot tell the difference between a perfect 50 Ω antenna and a 50 Ω load.
ch3_4.dlP2: The catch is that it must stay 50 Ω across the whole band. An ordinary wirewound resistor secretly has inductance too, so at radio frequencies it stops looking like a clean 50 Ω and the transmitter sees a mismatch — defeating the point. Proper loads use special low-inductance resistors; the classic amateur trick is to drown a resistor in a tin of mineral oil (the famous “cantenna”) to soak up the heat.
ch3_4.benchLead: A typical test bench wires the transmitter through a power meter into the dummy load, with a scope probe on the load:
ch3_4.dlDanger: Testing into a dummy load is also good manners and good law: your test signals stay off the air, so you interfere with no one and transmit nothing unidentified while you tune and measure.
ch3_4.rfP1: With the transmitter into a known 50 Ω, power is just a voltage measurement. RF (radio-frequency) power is always based on the <rms>RMS</rms> value, and for a sine wave <var>V_{rms}</var> = <var>V_{peak}</var> ÷ √2, so:
ch3_4.rfP1b: That last form is one of the handiest shortcuts in ham radio: in a 50 Ω world, watts equal peak-volts squared over 100. Work out 100 V peak across the dummy load? That is 100 W, instantly. (A scope reads peak-to-peak, so divide <var>V_{pp}</var> by 2 first to get <var>V_{peak}</var>.)
ch3_4.scopeLead: Read the peak-to-peak voltage straight off the trace:
ch3_4.rfP2: One subtlety: a voice signal’s power is not steady. <pep>PEP</pep> (peak <env>envelope</env> power) is the average power during the single RF cycle at the crest of the <mod>modulation</mod> — the sprinter’s burst — while the average power that actually heats the dummy load is much lower, the marathon pace. For a steady carrier (<cw>CW</cw> or <fm>FM</fm>) the two are equal; for <ssb>SSB</ssb> speech, PEP is far higher, which is why measuring it needs a fast-responding meter.
ch3_4.rfP3: Finally, power is often quoted in <dbm>dBm</dbm> — decibels relative to 1 mW, where 0 dBm = 1 mW, +30 dBm = 1 W, and every +10 dB is ten times the power. Convert between watts and dBm here:
ch3_4.rfKey: On 50 Ω, <var>P</var> = <var>V_{peak}</var>² ÷ 100. Measure the steady (average) power for CW and FM; measure PEP for SSB. dBm is just a power ruler with its zero at 1 mW.
ch3_4.sysP1: No single instrument tells the whole story. The multimeter sees steady volts and amps but is blind to a 14 MHz wave; the SWR meter sees the mismatch but not the <imp>impedance</imp> behind it; the scope shows the waveform but reads power only after a calculation; the VNA shows impedance across a whole sweep but says nothing about your supply voltage. Put them side by side on the same station and they must agree — and when they do not, the disagreement is itself the most useful measurement you will make.
ch3_4.sysKey: Cross-checking instruments is a professional habit: every window shows the same reality from a different angle, and two readings that should agree but do not are pointing straight at a problem.

ch3_4.labGoal: Practise every measurement type as one connected sequence, the way you would when setting up a real station — each step a different instrument, all describing the same transmitter.
ch3_4.labEquip1: A transceiver or transmitter, a 13.8 V supply, and a 50 Ω dummy load
ch3_4.labEquip2: Multimeter, SWR/power meter, oscilloscope (and a VNA if you have one)
ch3_4.labComp1: Coax jumpers with the right connectors
ch3_4.labComp2: Your dipole from Chapter 3.3 (for the on-antenna step)
ch3_4.labComp3: A notebook — write every reading down so you can cross-check them
ch3_4.labStep1: Multimeter (voltage): measure the supply at the rig’s power terminals. It should read 13.8 V, give or take half a volt.
ch3_4.labStep2: Multimeter (current): with the meter in series on the supply lead, key the transmitter into the dummy load and read the current. Multiply volts × amps for the DC input power.
ch3_4.labStep3: Dummy load + power meter: read the RF output power. Divide it by the DC input power for a rough efficiency figure.
ch3_4.labStep4: SWR meter: swap the dummy load for your dipole and read the SWR. A well-cut antenna should come in below 2:1.
ch3_4.labStep5: VNA (if available): sweep the same dipole and confirm the SWR. The meter and the VNA should agree at the operating frequency.
ch3_4.labStep6: Oscilloscope: probe the line into the dummy load, read V_{pp}, and compute the power with P = V_{peak}² ÷ 100. Compare it with the power meter.
ch3_4.labExpected: Five instruments, one transmitter — and every cross-check should line up: input power above output power, output power matching the scope calculation, SWR meter agreeing with the VNA.
ch3_4.labConnection: This is the chapter’s thesis made physical: each instrument is a window onto the same reality, and learning to make them agree is what station work actually is.
ch3_4.labTrouble1: Scope power far off the meter? Check you used <var>V_{peak}</var> (half of <var>V_{pp}</var>), not <var>V_{pp}</var> itself, in <var>V_{peak}</var>² ÷ 100.
ch3_4.labTrouble2: Supply voltage sagging on key-down? The supply or its wiring cannot deliver the transmit current — measure the current and check the supply’s rating.
ch3_4.labTrouble3: SWR meter and VNA disagree? Make sure the VNA calibration includes the same coax jumper, and that both read at the exact same frequency.
ch3_4.quiz_q1: How do you connect a meter to measure current?
ch3_4.quiz_q1_a: across the two ends of the component, in parallel, just as you would to read a voltage
ch3_4.quiz_q1_b: in series, by breaking the circuit so all the current flows through it
ch3_4.quiz_q1_c: with one probe only, to the positive terminal
ch3_4.quiz_q1_d: it does not matter, the meter sorts it out
ch3_4.quiz_q1_explanation: An ammeter must carry the current it measures, so the circuit is opened and the meter inserted in series. Voltage, by contrast, is measured in parallel — across the part.
ch3_4.quiz_q2: Why does a digital multimeter have a 10 MΩ input impedance on its voltage ranges?
ch3_4.quiz_q2_a: so it draws almost no current and does not load the circuit it measures
ch3_4.quiz_q2_b: to make the display update faster
ch3_4.quiz_q2_c: to protect the meter's delicate internal circuitry from dangerously high voltages on the upper measurement ranges
ch3_4.quiz_q2_explanation: The meter forms a voltage divider with the circuit’s own resistance. A high input impedance (10 MΩ) draws negligible current, so the reading stays true — except on very high-impedance circuits.
ch3_4.quiz_q3: On an analog ohmmeter, where does 0 Ω sit on the scale?
ch3_4.quiz_q3_a: at the far left end of the scale, exactly where the needle comes to rest when no current at all is flowing
ch3_4.quiz_q3_b: at the right end, at full deflection
ch3_4.quiz_q3_explanation: Shorted probes (0 Ω) pass the most current, giving full deflection — at the right end. ∞ sits at the left with no deflection, so the ohms scale runs backwards and crowds at the high-resistance end.
ch3_4.quiz_q4: A 50 µA movement has what ohms-per-volt sensitivity?
ch3_4.quiz_q4_explanation: Ohms-per-volt is the reciprocal of the full-scale current: 1 ÷ 50 µA = 20 000 Ω/V. The smaller the full-scale current, the higher (better) the figure.
ch3_4.quiz_q5: At an SWR of 2:1, roughly how much of the forward power is reflected?
ch3_4.quiz_q5_explanation: With <var>Γ</var> = (2 − 1) ÷ (2 + 1) = 0.33, the reflected fraction is <var>Γ</var>² ≈ 0.11, or about 11 %. So 89 % of the power still reaches the antenna at 2:1.
ch3_4.quiz_q6: What can an SWR meter NOT tell you?
ch3_4.quiz_q6_b: whether the impedance match is gradually getting better or worse while you adjust the antenna or the tuner
ch3_4.quiz_q6_d: the actual resistance and reactance of the load
ch3_4.quiz_q6_explanation: SWR depends only on the magnitude of the mismatch, so a 25 Ω and a 100 Ω load both read 2:1. To get the resistance and reactance behind the number you need a VNA.
ch3_4.quiz_q7: How does an absorption wavemeter indicate the transmitter’s frequency?
ch3_4.quiz_q7_c: tune the circuit for a peak at resonance, then read the dial
ch3_4.quiz_q7_d: it compares the incoming signal against the 50 Hz mains frequency from the wall socket and counts the beat note between the two
ch3_4.quiz_q7_explanation: A wavemeter is a passive tuned circuit loosely coupled to the transmitter. Tune the capacitor until resonance makes the meter peak, then read the frequency off the calibrated dial — approximate, because the resonance is broad.
ch3_4.quiz_q8: Why must a dummy load stay close to 50 Ω across the band, not just at DC?
ch3_4.quiz_q8_a: so it does not overheat and burn out while it dissipates the transmitter's full output power as heat over a long test
ch3_4.quiz_q8_b: so the transmitter sees a clean match and behaves as it would into a real antenna
ch3_4.quiz_q8_c: to make the SWR meter read higher
ch3_4.quiz_q8_d: so it radiates a clean signal
ch3_4.quiz_q8_explanation: A wirewound resistor has inductance, so at RF it no longer looks like 50 Ω and the transmitter sees a mismatch. A good dummy load uses low-inductance resistors to stay resistive across the band.
ch3_4.quiz_q9: You read 100 V peak across a 50 Ω dummy load. What is the power?
ch3_4.quiz_q9_explanation: On 50 Ω, <var>P</var> = <var>V_{peak}</var>² ÷ 100 = 100² ÷ 100 = 100 W. Equivalently, <var>V_{rms}</var> = 100 ÷ √2 ≈ 70.7 V and <var>P</var> = 70.7² ÷ 50 = 100 W.
ch3_4.quiz_q10: For a steady CW carrier, how does PEP compare with the average power?
ch3_4.quiz_q10_explanation: PEP is the average power over the RF cycle at the modulation crest. For an unmodulated, steady carrier (CW or FM) the envelope is flat, so PEP equals the average power. For SSB speech, PEP is far higher than the average.

ch4_1.heroAriaLabel: A frequency spectrum bar from LF to UHF. Above the low bands a wave hugs the curved earth (ground wave); above HF a wave bounces off the ionosphere (sky wave); above VHF and UHF a straight line-of-sight arrow — the frequency decides how the signal travels.
ch4_1.intro1: You key up a hundred watts into a wire strung across your garden, and a few seconds later a station eight thousand kilometres away comes back to you. Nothing physical connects the two of you — no cable, no relay, just air and the near-vacuum above it. So how does the signal actually get there? That question is the whole of this chapter, and its answer is one of the quiet miracles of radio: the sky itself does the work.
ch4_1.intro2: A radio wave can reach the far station by three different routes — hugging the ground, flying in a straight line to the horizon, or bouncing off an invisible mirror 300 km up. We will follow each route in turn, then meet the <iono>ionosphere</iono> that makes worldwide contacts possible, the <fad>fading</fad> that makes signals breathe in and out, the weather in the lowest air that opens the <vhf>VHF</vhf> bands, and the <sun>sunspot</sun> cycle that quietly runs the entire show. By the end you will be able to look at a band, a time of day and today’s space weather, and make a fair guess at who you can talk to.
ch4_1.modesP1: Your antenna throws its wave out in every direction at once. Only a sliver of that energy ever reaches the far station — and depending on the frequency, it gets there by one of three routes. Think of getting a message to a friend across a wide valley: you could shout so the sound rolls along the ground, throw a note in a flat straight line, or lob it up so it bounces off an invisible ceiling high overhead and drops back down to them. Radio has exactly those three choices.
ch4_1.modesP2: The ground wave clings to the earth’s surface, following its curve for tens or hundreds of kilometres before it fades. It works best at low frequencies — the medium-wave AM broadcast band lives on ground wave by day. The higher the frequency, the faster the ground wave dies away, so above a few megahertz it is good for only a short local range.
ch4_1.modesP3: The <sp>space wave</sp> is the line-of-sight route: the wave travels in a nearly straight line, just like light, and reaches only a little past the visible horizon because the atmosphere bends it very slightly downward. This is the world of <vhf>VHF</vhf> and <uhf>UHF</uhf> — your 2-metre handheld, repeaters, and most local FM. If nothing is in the way, you are connected; put a hill between the antennas and you usually are not.
ch4_1.horizonLead: Because the space wave stops at the horizon, its reach is set almost entirely by how high the two antennas are. A little geometry turns antenna height into distance:
ch4_1.horizonP1: The 4.12 already includes the gentle atmospheric bending, so this radio horizon sits about 15 % beyond the purely visual one. Two antennas 10 m up reach roughly 4.12 × (3.16 + 3.16) ≈ 26 km apart; put one on a 300 m tower and a handheld user can work the repeater from far further away. Raising an antenna does more for VHF range than almost anything else — height is everything up here.
ch4_1.modesP4: The third route is the one that reaches around the planet. Aim the wave upward and, at the right frequency, it does not escape into space — it is bent back toward the ground by a layer of charged gas high overhead and comes down again hundreds or thousands of kilometres away. This is the sky wave, and it is why HF operators with modest antennas talk to the other side of the world. To understand it we have to go up to the mirror itself.
ch4_1.modesKey: Ground wave follows the earth (low bands, local); space wave goes line-of-sight to the horizon (VHF/UHF); sky wave bounces off the ionosphere (HF, worldwide). Frequency decides which one you get.
ch4_1.sectionIonosphere: The ionosphere: a mirror in the sky
ch4_1.ionoP1: Sixty to a thousand kilometres up, the air is so thin that it is barely there at all — but what little remains is bathed in raw ultraviolet and X-rays from the sun. That radiation is energetic enough to knock electrons off the gas atoms, leaving a soup of free electrons and charged ions. This is the <iono>ionosphere</iono>, and those free electrons are what a radio wave reacts to. By day the sun keeps making them; by night, with the sun gone, the electrons slowly recombine and the ionosphere thins out. Picture a set of partly-silvered mirrors hung in the sky whose reflectivity brightens and dims with the sun.
ch4_1.ionoLead: The ionisation is not uniform — it stacks into distinct layers, each at its own height and with its own habits:
ch4_1.ionoP2: Lowest is the D layer (about 60–90 km). It is a poor mirror but a greedy sponge: it absorbs energy from lower-frequency HF waves passing through it, and it exists only in daylight. Above it the E layer (around 110 km) reflects weakly and is home to the odd summer surprise of sporadic-E. Higher still are the F layers — F1 (about 200 km) and F2 (250–400 km). The F2 layer is the workhorse of long-distance HF: it is the highest, most strongly ionised layer, and it is the one that bends your sky wave back to earth.
ch4_1.ionoP3: At night the picture simplifies. The D layer vanishes (so its absorption lifts), F1 and F2 merge into a single F layer, and the E layer weakens. That is exactly why the low bands change character after dark — 80 m and 40 m are noisy and short-range by day, when the D layer is eating them, then open up for long-distance work at night once that sponge is gone.
ch4_1.ionoP4: One more idea makes the rest of the chapter click. The wave is not really reflected like light off glass — it is refracted, bent gradually as it climbs into ever-denser ionisation, the way a straw looks bent in a glass of water. Bend it far enough and it curves back down; don’t, and it sails on into space. Higher frequencies bend less, so there is always some frequency high enough to punch straight through. The highest frequency the layer can still send straight back when you fire it vertically upward is called the critical frequency — remember it, because it sets everything that follows.
ch4_1.ionoKey: The sun ionises the upper air into layers: D (day-only, absorbs low HF), E (weak), and the all-important F2 that bends HF sky waves back to earth. The wave is bent (refracted), not mirror-reflected — and higher frequencies bend less.
ch4_1.sectionSkip: Skip: how HF reaches around the world
ch4_1.skipP1: Fire a sky wave up at a shallow angle and the ionosphere bends it back to earth a long way off — the ground distance to where it lands is the <skd>skip distance</skd>. Right underneath the path, the far edge of the ground wave has already faded but the sky wave has not yet come down, so there is a ring of ground that hears nothing at all: the <skz>skip zone</skz>, or dead zone. It is the exact reason you can clearly hear a station 2000 km away while someone 200 km down the road hears only silence. Skip a stone across a pond and it touches down some distance out; the water in between is never touched.
ch4_1.skipP2: One bounce off the F2 layer can span up to about 4000 km — the geometry runs out beyond that because the take-off angle would have to dip below the horizon. To go further, the wave simply does it again: it reflects off the ground back up to the ionosphere and down once more, hop after hop, chaining halfway around the planet. Each hop loses a little energy to the ground and the D layer, so a ten-thousand-kilometre signal is faint — but it gets there.
ch4_1.skipP3: Whether a band works at all comes down to a window of frequencies. Aim a wave too high in frequency and it bends too little, punches through the F2 layer and is gone to space — the top of the window is the <muf>MUF</muf> (maximum usable frequency) for that path. Aim too low and the D layer simply absorbs it before it ever gets up there — the bottom is the <luf>LUF</luf> (lowest usable frequency). Between LUF and MUF the band is open; outside them it is dead. The MUF climbs by day and with an active sun, and falls at night — which is why the same 8000 km path might be wide open on 20 m at noon and only on 40 m at midnight.
ch4_1.mufLead: Drag the take-off angle to see the skip distance stretch, and set the critical frequency to watch the MUF window slide across the bands:
ch4_1.skipTip: The operator’s rule of thumb: work the highest band that is open. Just below the MUF the wave takes the shallowest path, suffers the least absorption, and needs the fewest hops — so signals are strongest and the least power gets the job done.
ch4_1.skipKey: A single ionospheric hop reaches up to ~4000 km; multiple hops reach worldwide. A band is usable only between the LUF (below it, absorbed) and the MUF (above it, lost to space) — and that window moves with the time of day and the sun.
ch4_1.fadingP1: Tune in a distant HF station and its strength almost never holds steady — it swells and sinks over seconds or minutes. Operators call this <fad>fading</fad>, or by its Morse abbreviation <qsb>QSB</qsb>. The ionosphere is not a fixed mirror; it is a living, drifting, rippling thing, and the signal usually reaches you by more than one path at once — say a two-hop route and a three-hop route of slightly different length. When the two arrivals fall into step they reinforce; when they drift out of step they partly cancel. That is <mp>multipath</mp> fading, and it is just two sets of ripples crossing on a pond, alternately piling up and flattening out.
ch4_1.fadingP2: There are gentler cousins too. The ionosphere can slowly twist the wave’s polarisation so it no longer matches your antenna (polarisation fading), and the whole path can dim and brighten as D-layer absorption rises and falls (absorption fading). Receivers fight back with automatic gain control, which turns the volume up as the signal sinks, and serious stations use two spaced antennas (diversity) so that when one path fades the other often has not.
ch4_1.fadingKey: Fading (QSB) is the signal rising and falling because it arrives by several ever-changing paths that drift in and out of step. It is normal on HF sky-wave paths — not a fault in your radio.
ch4_1.tropoP1: Everything so far has been about the ionosphere, high above. But the lowest slice of atmosphere — the <trop>troposphere</trop>, the bottom dozen kilometres where all our weather happens — has its own tricks, and they are the ones that matter on <vhf>VHF</vhf> and <uhf>UHF</uhf>. Normally these bands just travel line-of-sight straight through the troposphere and stop at the horizon. Certain weather bends that rule.
ch4_1.tropoP2: Usually the air cools steadily with height. But under a stable high-pressure system, or over a cool sea on a warm evening, you get a temperature inversion: a lid of warm air sitting on top of cooler air. Radio waves bend toward the denser (cooler) air, and a strong inversion can trap VHF/UHF signals in a duct between the warm lid and the ground or sea, guiding them far past the normal horizon — hundreds, occasionally over a thousand, kilometres. A quiet 2-metre band can suddenly fill with distant stations for a day or two; this is a tropo opening, and it follows the weather map, not the sun.
ch4_1.tropoTip: Watch for a large, stable high-pressure system — especially the calm, damp evenings of late summer and autumn. That is prime tropo season on 2 m and 70 cm; a look at the weather chart is a genuine propagation forecast up here.
ch4_1.tropoKey: In the troposphere, a temperature inversion (warm air over cool, often under high pressure or over the sea) can duct VHF/UHF signals far beyond the horizon. VHF/UHF propagation follows the weather; HF sky wave follows the sun.
ch4_1.sunP1: Since it is the sun’s radiation that builds the ionosphere, the sun’s mood sets the MUF — and the sun is not constant. Its activity waxes and wanes over an eleven-year cycle, tracked for centuries by counting the dark sunspots on its face. More sunspots mean more ultraviolet, which means a more strongly ionised F2 layer, which means a higher MUF — and that throws open the high bands. At the peak of a good cycle, 10 m can carry a signal clear around the world on a few watts and a bit of wire; at the bottom of the cycle it can lie silent for months.
ch4_1.sunP2: Two numbers tell you where the bands stand: the solar flux index (SFI) and the K index. You will see them on any space-weather app, or on the DX cluster — the online feed where hams post the stations they hear. The SFI measures the sun’s radio output at 10.7 cm and tracks its ionising power day to day — roughly 65 at a quiet minimum, climbing past 200 at an active maximum. The A and K indices measure the opposite thing: geomagnetic disturbance from solar flares and the solar wind. A high K (say 5 and up) means a geomagnetic storm — auroras, and HF paths near the poles going muddy or dead. So you want the SFI high and the K low.
ch4_1.sunP3: Where are we right now? Solar Cycle 25 peaked in 2024–2025, and ran a little stronger than the forecasters expected. As of 2026 the sun is easing down from that maximum but is still lively, with the next quiet minimum expected around 2030. In plain terms: the high bands have been in excellent shape lately, so this is a fine few years to spend time on 10 and 15 metres before the cycle winds down again.
ch4_1.conditionsLead: Pick a band, a time of day and a state of the sun, and see what you could expect to work:
ch4_1.sunNote: These indices are forecasts of a chaotic system, not guarantees. A big solar flare can wipe out HF for hours (a radio blackout) even while the SFI reads high — the sun giveth and the sun taketh away.
ch4_1.sunKey: The ~11-year sunspot cycle sets HF conditions: more sunspots → higher F2 ionisation → higher MUF → the high bands (10/15 m) open worldwide. Track it with the solar flux index (want it high) and the A/K indices (want them low). Cycle 25 peaked in 2024–2025 and is now slowly declining.
ch4_1.sectionRanges: HF, VHF and UHF: what each is for
ch4_1.rangesP1: Put it all together and the frequency you choose decides the kind of propagation you get — which is really a choice about who you can reach. <hf>HF</hf> (3–30 MHz) is the sky-wave band: bounce off the ionosphere for regional or worldwide contacts, ruled by the sun and the clock. <vhf>VHF</vhf> (30–300 MHz) is mostly line-of-sight and local, with tropo and sporadic-E openings for occasional reach. <uhf>UHF</uhf> (300 MHz–3 GHz) is line-of-sight too, with even shorter everyday range but small antennas, wide channels, and the gateway to satellites and microwave.
ch4_1.rangesLead: Each amateur band has its own personality, and knowing it is half of operating. One thing to settle first, though: a band does not have the same edges everywhere in the world. The International Telecommunication Union (<itu>ITU</itu>) — the United Nations agency that divides up the radio spectrum by international treaty — splits the world into three regions. Region 1 covers Europe, Africa, the Middle East and northern Asia, and Ukraine sits in it; Region 2 covers the Americas; Region 3 covers the rest of Asia and the Pacific. The physics travels with the band and is the same wherever you are. Where a band stops does not — that is set by treaty, and each region hands the same slice of spectrum to a different mix of services. So the tour below lists Regions 1 and 2 side by side:
ch4_1.rangesP2: Notice the pattern down the table: the lower you go in frequency, the more the band leans on ground wave and night-time sky wave and the more local-to-regional it feels by day; the higher you go through HF, the more it depends on the sun for worldwide reach; and once you cross into VHF/UHF you leave the ionosphere behind and live by line-of-sight, repeaters and the weather. Matching the band to the distance you want, the time of day and today’s conditions is the everyday craft of the operator.
ch4_1.rangesRegionOnair: Four of the seven bands above stop in a different place depending on which ITU region you are in, and that difference reaches you on the air. Tune to 7.250 MHz one evening and you may well hear a station in the United States — the <cs>callsign</cs> prefix tells you where it is — holding a relaxed conversation. That station is well inside its own rules: in Region 2 the 40-metre band runs to 7.300 MHz, while Region 1 hands that same slice of spectrum to shortwave broadcasters. The Region 1 amateur allocation stops at 7.200 MHz, so you can listen and log what you hear, but you may not answer there — and your own national licence and class may allow less still. The same thing happens at the high-frequency end of 80 metres and of 2 metres, where Region 2 again runs higher; on 70 centimetres the Region 2 band is wider at both ends. Contacts between stations in different regions happen in the overlap — the stretch of band both are allowed to use.
ch4_1.rangesKey: Low HF: local by day, DX by night. High HF: worldwide when the sun cooperates. VHF/UHF: line-of-sight, repeaters, and weather-driven openings. The band you pick is really a choice of how far — and how — you want to reach. And while the physics is the same worldwide, the band edges are not — they depend on your ITU region, and your licence may narrow them further.

conditions.title: Band conditions — what’s open?
conditions.description: A rough guide, not a live forecast. Pick a band, the time of day and the state of the sun; the panel gives the kind of contact you could expect and why.
conditions.hereNote: You are here — 2026: Cycle 25 is easing down from its 2024–2025 peak, so “high sun” is still a realistic setting for now.
conditions.rDxHigh: Strong sun lifts the MUF above this band — long multi-hop paths open up.
conditions.rDayAbsorbed: By day the D layer absorbs this low band, so it stays short-range.
conditions.rNightOpen: At night the D layer is gone and the low band comes alive for long distances.
conditions.rNeedSun: This high band needs an active sun to raise the MUF; with a quiet sun it stays closed.
conditions.rReliable: The middle HF bands carry sky wave in most conditions.
conditions.rLineOfSight: VHF/UHF is line-of-sight — range depends on antenna height and tropo, not the sun.

horizonCalc.title: Radio horizon calculator
horizonCalc.description: How far can two line-of-sight (VHF/UHF) stations reach? Enter each antenna height and read the radio horizon — the distance already includes the atmosphere’s gentle bending.
horizonCalc.note: The radio-horizon constant (4.12) is about 15 % larger than the visual-horizon constant (3.57) because the lower atmosphere bends VHF/UHF waves slightly downward, so they follow the earth’s curve a little past the line of sight.

mufSkip.title: MUF & skip explorer
mufSkip.description: Two ideas in one: how the take-off angle sets the skip distance, and how the critical frequency sets the MUF window across the bands.
mufSkip.skipCapNote: capped near 4000 km — beyond that you need a second hop
mufSkip.note: Lower take-off angles reach farther per hop but need a clear, low horizon. The MUF is the critical frequency multiplied by a factor that grows as the path gets longer (the angle gets lower) — so the longest paths can use the highest bands.

threeModes.caption: The three routes a radio wave can take from transmitter to receiver: ground wave along the surface, space wave to the horizon, and sky wave off the ionosphere.
threeModes.aria: A curved earth with a transmitter on the left. A ground wave hugs the surface, a space wave travels straight to a nearby receiver at the horizon, and a sky wave goes up to the ionosphere and bends back down to a distant receiver.

ionoLayers.caption: The ionospheric layers by day and by night. By day all four layers are present; at night the D layer vanishes and F1 and F2 merge into a single F layer.
ionoLayers.aria: Two stacked cross-sections of the atmosphere. The daytime side shows D, E, F1 and F2 layers at rising altitudes; the night side shows the D layer gone and F1 and F2 merged into one F layer.

skipGeom.caption: Skip geometry: the sky wave leaves at an angle, refracts off the ionosphere and lands a skip distance away. Between the ground wave and that landing point lies the silent skip zone; further hops reach further still.
skipGeom.aria: A transmitter sends a ray up at an angle to the ionosphere, which bends it back to earth at the skip distance. The ground between the short ground-wave range and the landing point is marked as the skip zone. A second hop carries the signal further to a distant receiver.

fading.caption: Multipath fading: the same signal arrives by two paths of slightly different length. As they drift in and out of step the combined strength swells and sinks — the fading (QSB) an operator hears.
fading.aria: Two wavy paths of slightly different length arrive at a receiver and combine. The resulting signal-strength trace over time rises and falls, marked where the paths add up in step and cancel out of step.

tropoDuct.caption: Tropospheric ducting: a temperature inversion puts warm air over cool air, and VHF/UHF signals bend into the duct and travel far past the normal line-of-sight horizon.
tropoDuct.aria: A layer of warm air sits over cooler air near the sea. A VHF signal from the left is trapped in the duct between the warm lid and the surface, bouncing along it to reach a receiver far beyond the normal horizon on the right.

sunspot.caption: Sunspot number over the last three solar cycles. More sunspots mean a higher MUF and better high-band propagation. Cycle 25 peaked in 2024–2025 and is now slowly declining.
sunspot.aria: A curve of yearly sunspot number rising and falling over three roughly eleven-year cycles labelled 23, 24 and 25. A marker on the declining side of Cycle 25 shows the year 2026.

ch4_1.labGoal: Turn the sky into your laboratory: log real signals over a week and watch the propagation rules in this chapter play out on the bands — no bench instruments, just your receiver and a notebook.
ch4_1.labEquip1: Any HF receiver or transceiver with an antenna (even a short wire)
ch4_1.labEquip2: Optionally a phone or laptop for a solar-flux widget and an online DX map
ch4_1.labComp1: <lb>A logbook</lb> or spreadsheet: time, band, callsign, rough distance
ch4_1.labComp2: The day’s solar flux and K index (from a space-weather site)
ch4_1.labComp3: Patience across different times of day and, ideally, a week or two
ch4_1.labStep1: Evening, 40 m (7 MHz): tune across the band and note the farthest stations you can hear. Log the time, frequency, callsign and approximate distance.
ch4_1.labStep2: Midday, 40 m: try the same band again. Notice how the very distant signals have thinned out — the daytime D layer is absorbing them.
ch4_1.labStep3: Midday, 20 m (14 MHz): now the higher band should be busy with long-distance signals while the sun is up. Log a few and their distances.
ch4_1.labStep4: 10 m (28 MHz): with today’s active sun, check the highest band. When it is open you will hear stations thousands of kilometres away on very little power.
ch4_1.labStep5: Note the sun: record the solar flux index and K index for each session. Over several days, see whether higher flux lines up with better high-band conditions.
ch4_1.labExpected: A pattern emerges: 40 and 80 m are best at night and short-range by day; 20 m is the daytime workhorse; 10 and 15 m come alive when the sun is active. Higher solar flux should track with better high-band openings; a high K index should track with poorer HF, especially toward the poles.
ch4_1.labConnection: This is not a circuit you can measure with a meter — it is the real ionosphere doing exactly what the diagrams in this chapter describe. Propagation theory stops being abstract the first time you hear a station on the far side of the world on 10 m with a few watts and a piece of wire.
ch4_1.labTrouble1: Hearing almost nothing on 10 m? That is data, not failure — the band is often closed when the sun is quiet or after dark. Drop down to 20 or 40 m and it should come to life.
ch4_1.labTrouble2: All signals weak and watery with rapid fading? Check the K index — a geomagnetic storm may be in progress, which disturbs the ionosphere and degrades HF.
ch4_1.labTrouble3: Only local stations on every band? Suspect the antenna (too low, disconnected, or badly matched) before you blame propagation — a dead antenna looks a lot like a dead band.
ch4_1.quiz_q1: Which propagation mode lets an HF station be heard on the far side of the world?
ch4_1.quiz_q1_a: the sky wave, refracted back to earth by the ionosphere
ch4_1.quiz_q1_b: the ground wave, following the earth’s surface all the way around the globe
ch4_1.quiz_q1_c: the space wave, in a straight line to the horizon
ch4_1.quiz_q1_d: the tropospheric duct, trapped in the weather layer
ch4_1.quiz_q1_explanation: Long-distance HF works by sky wave: the wave is refracted back to earth by the ionosphere, hop after hop. Ground wave fades within tens or hundreds of km, and the space wave stops at the horizon.
ch4_1.quiz_q2: Which ionospheric layer is mainly responsible for bending HF sky waves back to earth for long-distance work?
ch4_1.quiz_q2_explanation: The F2 layer is the highest and most strongly ionised, and it is the one that returns HF sky waves from long distances. The D layer mostly absorbs; the E layer reflects only weakly.
ch4_1.quiz_q3: Why do the 80 m and 40 m bands work better for long distances at night?
ch4_1.quiz_q3_a: the F2 layer disappears at night, so signals travel straight up
ch4_1.quiz_q3_b: there is less man-made noise at night, and lower noise always means longer range on any band
ch4_1.quiz_q3_c: antennas work better in cool night air
ch4_1.quiz_q3_d: the D layer, which absorbs these low bands, disappears at night
ch4_1.quiz_q3_explanation: The D layer exists only in daylight and absorbs the lower HF bands. After dark it vanishes, the absorption lifts, and the low bands open up for long-distance sky-wave contacts.
ch4_1.quiz_q4: What is the skip zone (dead zone)?
ch4_1.quiz_q4_a: the area right next to the antenna where the transmitted signal is far too strong to copy
ch4_1.quiz_q4_b: the ring of ground beyond the ground wave but nearer than where the sky wave lands, where nothing is heard
ch4_1.quiz_q4_c: a fixed band of frequencies that can never be used for sky-wave contacts, no matter the conditions
ch4_1.quiz_q4_d: the region directly beneath the reflecting layer where sky waves pass overhead and cannot bend back to ground
ch4_1.quiz_q4_explanation: Between the edge of the ground-wave range and the point where the first sky-wave hop returns to earth, neither wave reaches — so that ring of ground hears nothing. This is why a station 2000 km away can be louder than one 200 km away.
ch4_1.quiz_q5: You raise your operating frequency above the MUF for a path. What happens to the sky wave?
ch4_1.quiz_q5_a: it is absorbed by the D layer before it can reach the reflecting F region
ch4_1.quiz_q5_b: it speeds up in the thinner air and reaches the far station noticeably sooner
ch4_1.quiz_q5_c: it splits into two separate rays that reach the receiver a fraction of a second apart
ch4_1.quiz_q5_d: it bends too little, passes through the ionosphere and is lost to space
ch4_1.quiz_q5_explanation: The MUF (maximum usable frequency) is the top of the window. Above it the wave bends too little to be returned, so it passes through the F2 layer and escapes. Below the LUF, by contrast, the wave is absorbed.
ch4_1.quiz_q6: A distant HF signal slowly rises and falls in strength. What is the usual cause?
ch4_1.quiz_q6_a: the transmitter’s power is being turned up and down at the far end
ch4_1.quiz_q6_b: your receiver is faulty and its gain is drifting up and down on its own
ch4_1.quiz_q6_c: multipath fading — the signal arrives by paths of slightly different length that drift in and out of step
ch4_1.quiz_q6_d: the earth’s rotation gradually Doppler-shifts the carrier in and out of your receiver’s tuning band over the course of a few seconds
ch4_1.quiz_q6_explanation: Fading (QSB) is normal on sky-wave paths. The signal usually arrives by more than one path through a moving ionosphere; as the paths drift in and out of step they alternately reinforce and cancel.
ch4_1.quiz_q7: What weather condition most often produces long-distance VHF/UHF tropospheric ducting?
ch4_1.quiz_q7_a: a temperature inversion — a lid of warm air over cooler air, often under high pressure
ch4_1.quiz_q7_b: heavy rain and thunderstorms, whose large water droplets scatter the signal far beyond the horizon
ch4_1.quiz_q7_c: a strong, steady wind that physically carries the radio waves along near the ground
ch4_1.quiz_q7_d: freezing fog, whose ice crystals guide the signal along the cold surface for hundreds of kilometres
ch4_1.quiz_q7_explanation: A temperature inversion (warm air above cool, typical of stable high pressure or a warm evening over the sea) can trap VHF/UHF signals in a duct and carry them far past the horizon. Tropo follows the weather map, not the sun.
ch4_1.quiz_q8: How does the sunspot cycle affect the high HF bands like 10 m?
ch4_1.quiz_q8_a: more sunspots flood the ionosphere with so much extra noise and static crash that all of the high HF bands close down completely
ch4_1.quiz_q8_b: more sunspots mean more ionisation, a higher MUF, and the high bands opening for worldwide DX
ch4_1.quiz_q8_c: sunspots change only the higher VHF and UHF bands and leave every one of the HF bands entirely unaffected by the cycle
ch4_1.quiz_q8_d: the eleven-year sunspot cycle has no measurable effect on HF propagation from one season or year to the next
ch4_1.quiz_q8_explanation: Sunspots track the sun’s ultraviolet output, which ionises the F2 layer. More sunspots → higher MUF → the high bands (10/15 m) open for long-distance work. Near solar minimum they can stay closed for months.
ch4_1.quiz_q9: On a space-weather page you see a high solar flux index (SFI) and a high K index. What does that combination mean for HF?
ch4_1.quiz_q9_a: ideal conditions — when both numbers are high at the same time the HF bands are always at their very best
ch4_1.quiz_q9_b: the bands are completely dead, because a high K index always cancels out any benefit from a high solar flux index and shuts the whole ionosphere down
ch4_1.quiz_q9_c: good ionisation from the high SFI, but a geomagnetic storm (high K) is disturbing the ionosphere and degrading HF, especially near the poles
ch4_1.quiz_q9_d: only short local contacts on VHF are possible, since HF never works while the solar flux is this high
ch4_1.quiz_q9_explanation: You want the SFI high (strong ionisation, higher MUF) but the K index low. A high K signals a geomagnetic storm that unsettles the ionosphere and hurts HF paths, particularly polar ones — so high SFI with high K is a mixed bag.
ch4_1.quiz_q10: Roughly how far can a single ionospheric hop carry an HF signal?
ch4_1.quiz_q10_explanation: One hop off the F2 layer spans up to roughly 4000 km; the geometry runs out beyond that. Longer paths are covered by multiple hops, the wave bouncing between the ionosphere and the ground several times.

ch4_2.heroAriaLabel: A transmitter on the left radiates interference outward across a gap to a neighbour's television, whose picture is broken up by a herring-bone interference pattern.
ch4_2.intro1: Your transmitter does one job brilliantly: it pours radio-frequency energy into the air. The trouble is that the air is shared. That same energy can creep into a neighbour's television, buzz through their hi-fi, or swamp their radio — and their gadgets, in turn, can spray noise across the bands you are trying to hear. Learning to be a good neighbour on a crowded spectrum is the whole subject of <emc>electromagnetic compatibility</emc>, and the everyday disturbances it deals with are called <rfi>radio-frequency interference</rfi>.
ch4_2.intro2: This chapter tackles interference from both sides. When your signal upsets a neighbour's equipment you are the culprit — the classic cases are television interference and broadcast interference to their radio, plus buzzing in audio equipment. When someone else's electrical noise ruins your reception, you are the victim. Either way the cure follows one simple map — and by the end you will be able to create interference on the bench and then make it disappear.
ch4_2.whatP1: It is tempting to picture interference as your signal being too strong or too dirty. Sometimes it is — but the useful mental model is a chain of three links. Every case of interference needs a source of radio energy, a path that carries it, and a victim that reacts to it. Miss any one of the three and there is no problem at all: your 100-watt signal is harmless until it finds a path into a set that cannot ignore it.
ch4_2.whatP2: That three-part picture is the single most valuable tool in the chapter, because it hands you three separate places to attack. You can quieten the source, block the path, or toughen up the victim — and you only have to succeed at one of them. The diagram below is the map that every remedy in this chapter hangs on.
ch4_2.whatP3: One subtlety is worth stating early. A set that receives your energy is not automatically faulty, and your transmitter is not automatically dirty. Interference exists only when the victim's function is actually disturbed. A well-designed receiver next door can sit in your field and never notice; a poorly-designed one can be upset by a signal that breaks no rules at all.
ch4_2.whatKey: Every interference problem is a source, a path, and a victim. Break any one link and the interference stops — so you always have three ways to win.
ch4_2.sourceP1: Start at the source. A transmitter is meant to put out one clean signal, but every real one also produces faint extra signals it never intended — its <spur>spurious emissions</spur>. The most common of these are <harm>harmonics</harm>: exact multiples of your operating frequency. Transmit on 7 MHz and the power amplifier also radiates a little on 14, 21 and 28 MHz. Think of a plucked guitar string — alongside the note you meant to play, it quietly sounds the octaves above it.
ch4_2.sourceP2: Harmonics are not the only strays. Over-driving the final amplifier smears the signal sideways into splatter; a badly-built stage can burst into <par>parasitic oscillation</par> on some unrelated frequency; and digital gear and switch-mode power supplies leak broadband noise (hash) even when nothing is being transmitted. Each is a source that a filter or a repair must silence at its origin.
ch4_2.sourceP3: Why worry about a harmonic a thousand times weaker than your signal? Because of where it lands. A harmonic of a short-wave signal can drop straight onto the FM broadcast band, the aircraft band, or a television channel — services whose receivers are so sensitive that even a weak, distant harmonic can upset them. Try a few transmit frequencies below and watch which of your neighbours' bands light up:
ch4_2.sourceKey: Harmonics and other spurious emissions are the transmitter's own fault, so the cure belongs at the transmitter: a clean output filter. This is exactly why every transmitter has a low-pass filter after its final amplifier.
ch4_2.sectionPaths: How It Gets Across: Coupling Paths
ch4_2.pathsP1: A source with no way to reach a victim is harmless, so the path is where most real problems are won or lost. Interference travels by four everyday routes: in through the victim's own antenna, along the mains wiring, along audio or connecting leads, or by radiating directly into a circuit board. The sneaky ones are the cables: a length of speaker wire or a power lead is an accidental antenna, and radio energy rides along the outside of it as common-mode current.
ch4_2.pathsP2: The antenna route hides the single most common cause of interference from a nearby transmitter: <ovl>front-end overload</ovl>, also called fundamental overload. Here nothing is wrong with your signal at all — it is simply so strong, and so close, that the victim's input stage cannot reject it. The tell-tale sign is that turning your power down makes the interference vanish abruptly. Because the fault is in the victim's design, the cure has to go there too, not at your station.
ch4_2.pathsTip: When people say your signal is getting into their speakers, it is almost never your signal quality — it is common-mode current picked up on the speaker cable acting as an antenna. That is good news: you cure the cable, not the transmitter.
ch4_2.pathsKey: Interference reaches a victim by four paths — antenna, mains, leads, and direct radiation. Find the path and you can break it, whatever the source.
ch4_2.sectionFilters: The Right Filter in the Right Place
ch4_2.filtersP1: A <filt>filter</filt> passes the frequencies you want and blocks the ones you do not — and the whole art of curing interference with filters is choosing the right type and putting it in the right place. You already met the four shapes back in the filters chapter; here they are again as a reminder of what each one does to a signal.
ch4_2.filtersP2: Now place them. A low-pass filter at your transmitter passes your wanted band and throws away the harmonics above it — the cure at the source. A high-pass filter at a neighbour's television passes the high television frequencies but blocks your lower short-wave signal from reaching the set — the cure at the victim. And a mains filter on a power lead strips radio energy off the wire before it can be carried indoors.
ch4_2.filtersP3: When a single strong station is the whole problem — one broadcast transmitter, one channel — a <notch>notch</notch>, or band-stop, filter is the surgical tool: it removes just that narrow slice of the spectrum and leaves everything else alone. The schematic below is a notch built from a <tc>tuned circuit</tc>, exactly like the ones you plotted on the analyser.
ch4_2.filtersCaution: Old handbooks tell you to cure speaker buzz by soldering a small capacitor across the amplifier's speaker terminals. Do not. A modern solid-state amplifier driving that capacitive load can break into a destructive, full-power oscillation. Use a ferrite choke and twisted-pair speaker cable instead — the subject of the next section.
ch4_2.filtersKey: Match the filter to the job: low-pass at your transmitter, high-pass at the victim, a notch for one offending station, a mains filter on the power lead.
ch4_2.sectionFerrites: Ferrites: an RF Choke on a Cable
ch4_2.ferritesP1: If any single gadget could be called the interference cure-all, it is the humble <fer>ferrite</fer> core clamped around a cable — a <cmc>common-mode choke</cmc>. Picture a frequency-selective speed bump: to the direct current and audio your equipment cares about it is invisible, but to radio-frequency energy it presents a large <imp>impedance</imp>. The clever part is that it blocks the unwanted common-mode radio energy on a cable while leaving the wanted signal inside the cable completely untouched.
ch4_2.ferritesP2: How does it tell the wanted signal and the interference apart? The wanted signal is differential — it goes out on one wire and back on the other, so its magnetic fields cancel inside the core and the ferrite does nothing to it. The interference is common-mode — the same current on every wire at once — so its fields add up, the core presents a high impedance, and it is choked off. The trick only works because the whole cable — every conductor together — passes through the same core: on coax that is the centre conductor and the shield. Send just one conductor through on its own and the ferrite would choke the wanted signal and the interference alike; it is the shared core that lets the differential fields cancel while the common-mode fields add up. One pass through the core is a single turn; wind the cable through more turns and the impedance grows as the square of the turns, because inductance rises with the square of the turns. Drag the slider and watch a modest clamp become a serious radio stop:
ch4_2.ferritesCoaxNote: How one shield does two jobs at once. If the shield is a single conductor, how can it carry the signal's return current and the interference at the same time? At radio frequencies they never share the metal. The skin effect squeezes each current into a thin layer at a surface, and which surface it takes is decided by where its return partner lies: the signal's return current hugs the inside, facing the centre conductor it pairs with, while the interference — whose return path lies outside the cable altogether — rides the outside. The two faces of the shield therefore act as separate conductors. The centre conductor and the inner face carry equal and opposite currents, so their fields cancel in the core and the ferrite ignores them; the current on the outer face has nothing to cancel it, so the ferrite chokes it. It is the same physics as a choke balun.
ch4_2.ferritesP3: A rule of thumb: you want at least about a thousand ohms of common-mode impedance to make a real difference, and a few thousand is better. The core material matters too — for a choke, mix 31 is the best all-round performer across the short-wave bands: below 5 MHz it beats mix 43 by several decibels, between 5 and 20 MHz mix 43 is about 1 dB ahead, and from 20 to 30 MHz the two are equivalent. So one mix 31 core covers every short-wave band, and the number of turns matters far more than that lone decibel. Mix 43 suppresses from about 20 MHz to 250 MHz, so its range reaches well above the short-wave bands. (Mix 43 is also the classic core for broadband short-wave transformers, which is a different job: there you want the core to couple the windings, not to dissipate energy.) This is why there is a ferrite bead moulded onto almost every cable that leaves a computer, a monitor, or a phone charger.
ch4_2.ferritesKey: A ferrite choke blocks common-mode radio energy on a cable and ignores the differential signal inside it. More turns help fast — the impedance rises with the square of the number of turns.
ch4_2.toolkitP1: Filters and ferrites handle most cases, but a few more tools round out the kit. <shield>Shielding</shield> — a conductive enclosure — stops radiation getting in or out; it is why sensitive circuits live in metal boxes, and why a seam left un-joined can leak like an open window. It works well against the direct-radiation and cable-pickup paths above, though low-frequency magnetic fields slip through all but thick, special materials.
ch4_2.toolkitP2: Then there is the earth — and here beginners are often misled. An RF earth is not a magic sink that swallows unwanted signals. Its value is as a shared reference that keeps every box in your station at the same voltage, which is done by bonding them together with short, heavy straps. A long wire to a ground rod is worse than useless for radio: at these frequencies it is simply an antenna, and it will happily radiate your harmonics around the house.
ch4_2.toolkitP3: The cheapest cures need no parts at all. Separation works because the signal falls off fast with distance — double the gap between the two antennas and its power drops to a quarter, so the trouble often just fades.
