Minimum necessary power is the same idea from the other end: run only the power the contact (the conversation) needs and you make fewer problems for everyone. And be wary of an end-fed antenna brought straight into the station — it dumps radio energy onto your equipment and earth wiring, and is a frequent, self-inflicted source of interference. Use the tool that matches the problem:
ch4_2.toolkitNote: Two habits prevent a lot of grief: bond your gear together with short straps for a solid RF earth, and avoid feeding an end-fed wire straight into the operating position without a proper counterpoise (a counter-weight wire the antenna can push against) and a choke on the feed line.
ch4_2.toolkitKey: Shielding, bonding, distance, and modest power are the rest of the kit. A short bonded earth helps; a long ground wire is just another antenna.
ch4_2.socialP1: Faced with a real complaint, resist the urge to throw parts at it. A few questions place the problem on the map almost every time. Does it happen only when you transmit? On one band or all of them? On one of the neighbour's devices, or every one? Each answer points at the source, the path, or the victim — and tells you which tool to reach for.
ch4_2.socialP2: The last tool is not on any bench. The single most effective thing you can do about interference is stay on good terms with your neighbours. Confirm politely that it really is your station, offer to help even when the fault is in their equipment, and bring in your national amateur-radio society if a case gets stuck. A clean signal and a friendly conversation settle the great majority of complaints — long before a filter is needed.
ch4_2.socialKey: Diagnose before you fix: only-when-transmitting, one-band-or-all, one-device-or-all. Then remember that goodwill with your neighbours cures more interference than any ferrite.

triad.title: Source → path → victim
triad.caption: Every interference problem has all three. Remove or break any single link — quieten the source, block the path, or toughen the victim — and the interference stops.
triad.ariaLabel: Block diagram: a source box, a path box and a victim box joined by arrows, each arrow marked with scissors to show the link can be cut.

harmReach.title: Where do your harmonics land?
harmReach.description: A transmitter also radiates weak harmonics at 2×, 3×, 4×… the operating frequency. Enter a frequency and see which broadcast or safety service each harmonic falls on.
harmReach.hint: Harmonics that land in the FM broadcast band (87.5–108 MHz), the aircraft band, or a television channel are why a clean transmitter output filter is not optional. The classic case: a 6 m signal at 50 MHz whose 2nd harmonic sits on 100 MHz, right in the middle of the FM dial.

coupling.title: The four coupling paths
coupling.description: Interference has to travel from your station to the neighbour's gear. Pick a route to light it up and see how the energy gets in — and the cure that breaks that particular link.
coupling.ariaLabel: A scene with your station on the left and a neighbour's television and audio box on the right, joined by four numbered interference paths.

antenna.name: Antenna input
antenna.how: The energy is picked up by the victim's own aerial and feedline and runs straight into its receiver — the route of front-end overload.
antenna.cure: A high-pass filter or attenuator at the set's antenna input, plus more distance between the two aerials.

direct.name: Direct into the case
direct.how: The field radiates straight through a plastic or poorly-shielded case onto the circuit board inside, with no cable needed.
direct.cure: Shield the equipment in a metal enclosure, or simply move it further from your antenna.

leads.name: Cables & leads
leads.how: Speaker, audio and connecting leads act as accidental antennas; radio energy rides along the outside as common-mode current and is carried inside.
leads.cure: A ferrite common-mode choke on the offending lead, and twisted-pair rather than parallel cable.

mains.name: Mains / power
mains.how: Radio energy is conducted along the mains wiring and delivered to the device through its power lead.
mains.cure: A mains RF filter at the affected equipment, and a ferrite choke on the power cord.

filterPlace.title: The right filter in the right place
filterPlace.caption: A low-pass filter at your transmitter blocks harmonics on the way out; a high-pass (or notch) at the neighbour's set blocks your signal on the way in; a mains filter strips radio energy off the power lead.
filterPlace.ariaLabel: A signal chain from a transmitter to a television: a low-pass filter sits at the transmitter, a high-pass filter at the television, and a mains filter on the power branch.

ferriteChoke.title: Why a ferrite blocks the noise but not the signal
ferriteChoke.caption: The wanted differential signal (out on one wire, back on the other) makes fields that cancel in the core, so it passes. The common-mode interference (the same current on every wire) makes fields that add, so the core chokes it off.
ferriteChoke.ariaLabel: Two rows showing a cable passing through a ferrite core: differential currents pass, common-mode currents are blocked.

ferriteCalc.title: How turns multiply the choking impedance
ferriteCalc.description: Threading a cable through a ferrite core once is a single turn. Wind it through more turns and the choking impedance climbs fast — as the square of the number of turns.
ferriteCalc.multiplier: ≈ {{sq}}× the impedance of a single pass (<var>N</var>² with <var>N</var> = {{count}} turns)
ferriteCalc.effective: Yes — a few thousand ohms is a solid RF choke.
ferriteCalc.weak: Not yet — add more turns to clear a thousand ohms or so.
ferriteCalc.note: These are representative figures for a mix 31 clamp core across the short-wave bands. In practice the <var>N</var>² rule holds up to about five to eight turns, beyond which the core's own stray capacitance takes over.

remedy.title: Match the cure to the problem
remedy.description: There is no universal anti-interference box. Pick a symptom and the tools that help light up — the best one flagged — because the right cure depends on where the energy is.
remedy.hint: Notice how the same few tools cover very different problems — and how less power and more distance help almost everywhere, for free.

prob.commonMode: Interference riding on cables and leads
prob.directPickup: Radio energy getting directly into a device

cure.harmonics: Filter at the source: a low-pass filter on your transmitter output. Running less power helps too.
cure.overload: Cure at the victim: a high-pass or notch filter at its antenna input, plus more distance and less power.
cure.commonMode: Break the path: a ferrite common-mode choke on the cable, backed up by good bonding.
cure.directPickup: Toughen the victim: shield it in a metal enclosure, and move it away from your antenna.
cure.mains: Block the path: a mains RF filter at the equipment and a ferrite choke on the power lead.

diagnose.title: Three questions to find the culprit
diagnose.caption: Each answer places the problem on the source → path → victim map and points at the tool to reach for.
diagnose.q1: Does it happen only when you transmit?
diagnose.q1no: It is external noise or their own faulty equipment — your signal may be perfectly clean.
diagnose.q2: Does it happen on one band only?
diagnose.q2yes: A harmonic or spurious emission. Cure the source: filter your transmitter output.
diagnose.q3: Is only one of their devices or cables affected?
diagnose.q3yes: That cable is the path. Break it with a ferrite choke, or filter the lead.
diagnose.q3no: Fundamental overload of the set. Harden the victim: a high-pass filter, more distance, less power.

ch4_2.labGoal: Deliberately create radio interference on an audio device, then silence it with ferrite cores — the exact move a professional EMC engineer makes.
ch4_2.labEquip1: Arduino (any Uno or Nano) running a fast-PWM sketch as a rough radio-noise source
ch4_2.labEquip2: A small powered speaker, or a cheap AM radio
ch4_2.labEquip3: Two or three clamp-on ferrite cores (type 31 material) sized for the speaker cable
ch4_2.labComp1: USB lead or power bank for the Arduino
ch4_2.labComp2: The speaker's own audio cable (the longer, the better an antenna it makes)
ch4_2.labComp3: A 20–30 cm jumper wire on the PWM pin to act as a small radiator
ch4_2.labStep1: Load a sketch that toggles a pin with fast PWM (tens to hundreds of kilohertz) and attach the jumper wire to that pin as a little antenna. Place the Arduino within 30 cm of the powered speaker.
ch4_2.labStep2: Power everything up and listen. You should hear a buzz or whine in the speaker that changes as you change the PWM frequency — you have just built a tiny interference source and coupled it into the audio.
ch4_2.labStep3: Clip one ferrite core around the speaker cable near the speaker. Does the buzz drop? Note by how much.
ch4_2.labStep4: Add a second core, then a third, spaced along the cable. With two or three cores the interference should fall dramatically.
ch4_2.labStep5: Now pass the cable through a single core and wind it through two or three turns instead of using several cores. A few turns through one core beats one pass through several — the impedance climbs with the square of the turns.
ch4_2.labExpected: The buzz is loudest with no ferrite, drops noticeably with each core you add, and is strongly attenuated once you have three cores — or two to three turns through one.
ch4_2.labConnection: You just filtered a cable, not a circuit. The ferrite choked the common-mode current the speaker lead was picking up as an antenna — the same fix that lives inside every computer cable, and the reason the turns-squared rule matters in practice.
ch4_2.labTrouble1: No buzz at all? Shorten the gap between the Arduino and the speaker, lengthen the antenna wire, or try a higher PWM frequency.
ch4_2.labTrouble2: Buzz will not change with the ferrites? Make sure the core is around the cable, not just near it, and place the first core close to the speaker end.
ch4_2.labTrouble3: Powered speaker too quiet to hear? A basic battery AM radio tuned to a quiet spot low on the dial is an even more sensitive detector.
ch4_2.quiz_q1: Every case of radio-frequency interference involves three things. Which set names them?
ch4_2.quiz_q1_explanation: Every interference problem needs a source of energy, a path that carries it, and a victim that reacts. Break any one of the three links and the interference stops.
ch4_2.quiz_q2: A harmonic of a transmitted signal is best described as:
ch4_2.quiz_q2_a: an exact multiple of the operating frequency
ch4_2.quiz_q2_b: always stronger than the wanted transmitted signal
ch4_2.quiz_q2_c: a signal that sits just below the operating frequency
ch4_2.quiz_q2_d: a stray tone caused only by a faulty antenna
ch4_2.quiz_q2_explanation: Harmonics sit at 2×, 3×, 4×… the operating frequency; transmit on 7 MHz and faint signals also appear on 14, 21 and 28 MHz.
ch4_2.quiz_q3: A neighbour's TV is disturbed only while you transmit, and turning your power down makes it stop abruptly. This is most likely:
ch4_2.quiz_q3_a: a harmonic radiated by your transmitter
ch4_2.quiz_q3_c: a faulty coaxial cable connector nearby
ch4_2.quiz_q3_d: fundamental overload of their television set
ch4_2.quiz_q3_explanation: A strong, clean fundamental that the victim's front end cannot reject is fundamental overload; the abrupt cure with less power is its signature, and the fix belongs at their set.
ch4_2.quiz_q4: Interference picked up on the outside of a speaker or power cable travels as:
ch4_2.quiz_q4_a: a differential-mode signal on the pair
ch4_2.quiz_q4_c: a harmonic of the wanted signal
ch4_2.quiz_q4_d: an intermodulation product of two signals
ch4_2.quiz_q4_explanation: The wanted signal is differential (out and back on the two wires); interference rides the cable's outside together as common-mode current — the thing a ferrite choke blocks.
ch4_2.quiz_q5: Where does a low-pass filter belong to stop a transmitter's harmonics reaching the antenna?
ch4_2.quiz_q5_explanation: Harmonics are the transmitter's own fault, so a low-pass filter at its output passes the wanted band and blocks the higher harmonics — the cure at the source.
ch4_2.quiz_q6: A ferrite common-mode choke leaves the wanted signal in a cable untouched because that signal is:
ch4_2.quiz_q6_a: too weak to influence the ferrite core
ch4_2.quiz_q6_b: blocked from the core by the cable shield
ch4_2.quiz_q6_c: always at a lower frequency than the interference
ch4_2.quiz_q6_d: differential, so its fields cancel in the core
ch4_2.quiz_q6_explanation: Equal-and-opposite differential currents make fields that cancel inside the core, so the choke ignores them; only the common-mode interference sees the impedance.
ch4_2.quiz_q7: You wind a cable three times through a ferrite core instead of one pass. Roughly how much more choking impedance do you get?
ch4_2.quiz_q7_c: about the same as one pass
ch4_2.quiz_q7_explanation: Impedance rises with the square of the turns, so three turns give about three-squared, or nine times, the impedance of a single pass.
ch4_2.quiz_q8: Which statement about an RF earth is correct?
ch4_2.quiz_q8_a: The longer the ground wire, the better it works as an RF earth
ch4_2.quiz_q8_b: Earthing on its own reliably cures interference
ch4_2.quiz_q8_c: A long earth wire can act as an antenna at radio frequencies
ch4_2.quiz_q8_d: An RF earth simply swallows unwanted signals away
ch4_2.quiz_q8_explanation: Ground is a shared reference, not a sink; at radio frequencies a long earth wire is simply an antenna and can radiate harmonics, so bonding with short straps is what actually helps.
ch4_2.quiz_q9: A neighbour reports interference on just one of several devices, only when you transmit. The path is most likely:
ch4_2.quiz_q9_a: a harmonic straight from your transmitter
ch4_2.quiz_q9_b: overload common to all their devices
ch4_2.quiz_q9_c: unusual radio propagation conditions that day
ch4_2.quiz_q9_explanation: One device affected points at that device's cable as the path; a ferrite choke on the lead breaks it without touching your transmitter.
ch4_2.quiz_q10: Beyond filters and ferrites, which is the most effective everyday measure against interference complaints?
ch4_2.quiz_q10_a: staying on good terms with your neighbours
ch4_2.quiz_q10_b: always running the maximum legal power you can
ch4_2.quiz_q10_c: fitting the longest possible earth wire you can
ch4_2.quiz_q10_d: moving your operation up onto higher harmonics
ch4_2.quiz_q10_explanation: A clean signal plus goodwill settles most complaints; cooperation lets you diagnose and fix a problem that might well be in the neighbour's own equipment.

ch4_3.bleederCaption: A high-tension supply, cut down to the part that matters. C1 is the reservoir capacitor — it holds the charge. R1, the bleeder, sits permanently across it and bleeds that charge away once the supply is switched off.
ch4_3.shockScaleAria: Scale of electric current through the human body, from 0.1 to 1000 milliamps, showing what each level does and where a 230-volt mains contact through dry hands lands on it.
ch4_3.shockZoneFelt: Felt — you can still let go
ch4_3.shockScaleCaption: What a current flowing through you actually does. The axis is logarithmic, so the whole span from 0.1 to 1000 mA fits; the marks are the thresholds that matter, not evenly-spaced steps. The red band is not a worst case: it is what 230 V drives through an ordinary person with dry hands — one hand on a live conductor, the other on something earthed. Thresholds are from IEC 60479-1, the European standard.

bodyCalc.title: What that voltage would push through you
bodyCalc.description: Set a voltage and pick how resistant a body you want to be. The widget looks up the total hand-to-hand impedance of dry skin from IEC 60479-1 and works out I = V / Z. Watch what happens to Z as you raise the voltage: it falls.
bodyCalc.p95: The most resistant 5 % — the best case
bodyCalc.note: Impedance is not a property of you alone — it falls as the voltage rises, because the skin stops insulating and starts conducting. So the current does not just double when the voltage doubles; it climbs faster. Try it: at 230 V there is no setting of this widget, not even the best case, that stays out of the range where a heart can lose its rhythm. Figures are for dry skin and a large contact area — wet hands are worse, and this widget does not model them.

ch4_3.mainsColourAria: Two panels comparing mains conductor colours. In Europe and Ukraine: brown line, blue neutral, yellow-green protective earth. In the United States: black hot, white neutral, green ground.
ch4_3.mainsColourCaption: The same three jobs, two colour schemes. The one thing both agree on: the earth/ground conductor has its own reserved colour and is never used for anything else.

capCalc.title: What is still in the capacitor
capCalc.description: The energy stored in a capacitor is <var>E</var> = ½<var>C</var><var>V</var>². Because the voltage is squared, doubling it quadruples the energy — which is why a valve supply is far more dangerous than a 12 V rail, not just a little worse.
capCalc.verdictOver: {{times}}× over the {{threshold}} J limit for this voltage — treat it as live
capCalc.verdictUnder: under the {{threshold}} J limit for this voltage
capCalc.note: The verdict is a work-control threshold from NFPA 70E Article 360, not a prediction that this will kill you. This capacitor holds {{charge}} mC — IEC 60479-2 puts a 50 % chance of fibrillation at about 5 mC. The last box shows the final trap: a discharged electrolytic recharges itself, so a supply you have «made safe» can still bite.

rfCalc.title: What you are really transmitting
rfCalc.description: Exposure limits are averaged over minutes, not measured at the peak. So what counts is not the number on the meter — it is that number multiplied by how much of the time your carrier is actually on — which depends both on the mode and on how much of the time you are transmitting rather than listening.
rfCalc.modeFm: FM, RTTY, FT8 — anything with a constant carrier
rfCalc.txLabel: Share of the time you transmit
rfCalc.ruleWithin: Within the range where 2.4 m of clearance has been shown to be enough
rfCalc.ruleOver: Past 100 W averaged — the rule of thumb no longer covers you; assess properly
rfCalc.note: Try it: leave the power alone and switch from SSB to FM. The averaged figure jumps by five, from the same radio, with the same reading on the same meter. The mode matters more than the amplifier.

ch4_3.mpeAria: Graph of the ICNIRP general-public electric field limit against frequency from 1 to 3000 megahertz, showing the limit falling to a flat 27.7 volts per metre across 30 to 400 megahertz — the whole-body resonance region — and rising again either side.
ch4_3.mpeTroughSub: 30–400 MHz — the limit is at its strictest here
ch4_3.mpeCaption: The limit is not one number — it is a curve that dips to a flat 27.7 V/m from 30 to 400 MHz, where the 4 m and 2 m bands sit. Curve: ICNIRP 2020 reference levels, general public — which, in your own shack, is you.
ch4_3.gprAria: Two panels. On the left, a mast on its own earth rod at 750 kilovolts and a rig on a separate mains rod at zero, with the coax bridging the difference. On the right, both bonded to one rod, so the whole station rises together and no difference appears across the equipment.
ch4_3.gprBondedVerdict: Everything rises together — nothing across it
ch4_3.gprCaption: The same strike, two layouts. Left: separate earths, so the whole difference falls across your coax, through the radio. Right: everything bonded to one point, so the station lifts together and no difference appears across the equipment.
ch4_3.checklistDescription: Nothing here is new — every line is one of this chapter's arguments, compressed. Tick them off as you walk round the station; the page remembers where you got to.
ch4_3.checkPower1: Unplugged at the wall — a front-panel switch is not isolation. Anything hardwired is off at the breaker, and nobody can switch it back on without me noticing.
ch4_3.checkPower2: Tested every conductor before touching it. Colour is a hint, not evidence.
ch4_3.checkPower3: Every fuse is the right rating and the right letter (its speed). None has been replaced with a bigger one to stop it blowing.
ch4_3.checkCharge1: Every capacitor discharged individually and metered — a bank reading zero across it proves nothing.
ch4_3.checkCharge2: Discharged capacitors left shorted, because they charge themselves back up.
ch4_3.checkRf1: Nobody is within a couple of metres of anything that radiates.
ch4_3.checkRf2: If I'm running a constant carrier — FM, or any digital mode — I've remembered it's five times the exposure of the same power on SSB.
ch4_3.checklistGroupStorm: When a storm is coming, or the station is idle
ch4_3.checkStorm1: Feedline disconnected and moved outside — not coiled on the desk, where it will simply arc across to something.
ch4_3.checkStorm2: Mast, feedline shield and every chassis bonded to one point, so they rise together instead of against each other.
ch4_3.checkHabit1: One hand in my pocket whenever I'm probing something live.
ch4_3.checkHabit2: Somebody else in the building knows how to cut the power, and knows how to resuscitate someone.
ch4_3.checkHabit3: There's a fire extinguisher I can actually reach, rated for an electrical fire.
ch4_3.intro1: This chapter is about staying safe while you work. A mistake elsewhere in the course usually costs you only time or a part — a mistuned antenna, a burnt <tr>transistor</tr> — and you simply try again. The hazards here are different: they threaten you, not your equipment, and a few of them can kill you.
ch4_3.intro2: The reassuring part is that radio is not what hurts people. A handheld transceiver is a remarkably safe object. What hurts people is the mains supply the radio is plugged into, the charge still sitting in a power supply after it is switched off, the fields nobody can see, and lightning. Four kinds of energy, and one idea that keeps you clear of all of them: never be in their path.
ch4_3.intro3: So instead of a list of rules to memorise, this chapter gives you the reason behind each one. Every rule below answers the same question: where will this energy flow, and am I in its path? Once you see that, the rules are no longer arbitrary — you can work out even the ones nobody told you.
ch4_3.shockP1: Voltage does not hurt you. Current does. Voltage is only the push; the damage is done by the current that push drives through you. And to flow through you at all, that current has to enter your body at one point and leave at another — you become part of the circuit. The route it takes between those two points is what decides the damage.
ch4_3.shockP2: Your body is a <res2>resistor</res2>, so Ohm's law from Chapter 1.2 applies to it exactly as it applies to a component: <var>I</var> = <var>V</var> / <var>R</var>. Look up the resistance of dry skin and you will find a comfortable number: the resistance through your body, from one hand to the other, comes to something like 100 kΩ. Divide 230 V by it and you get 2.3 mA — a shock you would feel but survive. Every part of that calculation is arithmetically correct, and the conclusion is lethally wrong.
ch4_3.shockP3: It is wrong because skin insulates only up to a point. IEC 60479-1, the European standard on the effects of current on the human body, is clear: at higher voltages the skin's impedance falls sharply, and once the skin breaks down it is almost gone. Mains voltage is well past that point: it breaks through the skin, and the current then flows through the wet tissue underneath — essentially salt water, which conducts it easily.
ch4_3.shockP4: The standard measures what is actually left. At 220 V — the touch voltage nearest European mains that the standard tabulates — hand to hand, with dry skin, total body impedance is about 1 000 Ω for the least resistant 5 % of people, 1 350 Ω for a typical person, and 2 125 Ω for the most resistant (the 95th percentile). Those figures turn 230 V into 230 mA, 170 mA and 108 mA. So even the best case — dry hands, the most resistant person — is over a hundred milliamps.
ch4_3.shockKey1: The 100 kΩ figure is real, and at mains voltage it is irrelevant. This is why «I've touched it before and I was fine» is not evidence of anything except luck.
ch4_3.shockP5: Now put those currents on a scale of what current does. The thresholds below are from IEC 60479-1; read them in order.
ch4_3.shockP6: About 0.5 mA is where you first feel anything. From there up to about 5 mA it hurts, but you are still in charge of your own hand. The next threshold up — somewhere between 5 and 10 mA — is called let-go. Past it, the current drives your flexor muscles harder than you can fight them, and your hand closes on the conductor and will not open. People imagine being thrown clear. Far more often they are held on, conscious, until something else breaks the circuit. The exact figure moves — the standard revised it from 10 mA down to 5 mA, and it is lower for women and lower again for children — which is why the scale above draws it as a band rather than a line.
ch4_3.shockP7: Around 40 mA, if the current lasts more than a second or two, the heart can go into ventricular fibrillation: instead of beating, the muscle quivers, and quivering does not move blood. This is what electrocution actually is. And 40 mA is only the threshold: the driest, most resistant person still draws 108 mA from a 230 V socket — almost three times as much. There is no safety margin at all. Even the safest case is already well past the current that can stop a heart.
ch4_3.shockP8: The other half of the story is the path. Current only endangers the heart if it goes through the region the heart is in, so what matters is where it enters and where it leaves. Hand to hand crosses the chest. Hand to foot on the same side largely does not. This is where the oldest habit on the bench comes from: when probing something live, keep one hand in your pocket. It sounds like superstition. It is a deliberate refusal to offer the current a route across your own chest.
ch4_3.shockP9: Two footnotes that matter. Alternating current at mains frequency is more dangerous than direct current at the same voltage — 50 Hz sits near the worst frequency for provoking fibrillation, and it reverses far too fast to let a clamped muscle release between cycles. And the phrase «high voltage» is a trap: the codes reserve it for higher voltages — above 600 V in American practice, above 1 000 V under IEC — which quietly implies that below that is the safe part. It isn't. There are recorded fatalities at 24 V, under sufficiently unlucky conditions.
ch4_3.shockDanger: Never work on live mains. Switch off at the breaker, verify with a meter that the thing you are about to touch is actually dead, and make sure nobody can switch it back on while your hands are inside it.
ch4_3.sectionMains: The mains: colours, earth and fuses
ch4_3.mainsP1: Ask what the earth wire does, and the usual answer is that it lets electricity escape harmlessly into the ground. That is not what it is for — and its real job is the whole reason a fault blows the fuse instead of waiting for you.
ch4_3.mainsP2: The earth wire is not an escape route. It is a trigger. Its job is to be a fat, low-resistance path from the metal case of your equipment back to the supply, so that if a live wire ever touches that case, the resulting fault current is enormous — hundreds of amps, instantly. That is the point. A current that large blows the fuse in milliseconds and disconnects the fault before anyone touches it. Without the earth wire the case simply sits at 230 V, looking exactly as it always does, with nothing to show that anything is wrong. The fuse never notices, because from the fuse's point of view nothing is drawing current — until someone completes the circuit by touching the case. Then the current flows through them, and it is nowhere near enough to blow anything.
ch4_3.mainsKey1: The earth wire protects you by making a fault current large enough to blow the fuse quickly. Without it, a live wire touching the metal case draws almost no current — so the fuse never blows, and the case stays live until someone touches it.
ch4_3.mainsP3: Which brings us to which wire is which — and the answer depends on where you are. In Europe and Ukraine the harmonised code (ДСТУ EN 60445) is brown for line, blue for neutral, and green-yellow stripes for protective earth. In the United States the NEC (National Electrical Code) is black for the hot line, white for neutral, and green — or bare copper — for ground. Learn the code for your own region. But whichever it is, do not rely on colour alone, because in an older building the wiring may follow no modern code at all.
ch4_3.mainsP5: That older wiring is the real trap. Soviet-era flats — and plenty of old houses elsewhere — were wired before the modern code, and what is behind the plaster is often two wires and no protective earth at all. Frequently both cores are the same colour: white, grey, or black. Where there is colour, it may not be the colour you expect — a blue wire can be a live phase. If you meet old wiring and assume «blue is neutral, blue is safe», nothing will warn you — you find out by being shocked.
ch4_3.mainsP6: So: colour is a hint, never evidence. Test every conductor before you touch it, in every building, every time — with a two-pole voltage tester, or a multimeter on <ac>AC</ac> volts referenced to a known earth. The instrument that settles it costs less than the radio.
ch4_3.mainsP7: A fuse is a deliberate weak point: a thin wire chosen to melt before anything more expensive does. Two things describe it — a rating and a speed — and both are quoted differently depending on the standard the fuse was built to. Most English-language ham advice was written around American fuses, while the ones you buy in Ukraine and Europe follow a different standard — so the advice and the hardware often do not agree.
ch4_3.mainsP8: The rating is the number printed on the fuse — but how much of that number you may actually draw depends on the standard. An IEC 60127 fuse — the kind sold in Ukraine and across Europe — may be run continuously at its full marked current, so you choose one whose number is the equipment's running current, rounded up to the nearest standard value. An American UL fuse is rated colder: it is meant to run continuously at only about 75 % of its marked number — a UL fuse marked 5 A is intended for a steady load of about 3.7 A. So on a UL fuse you go a size up, to roughly 125–150 % of the running current, and for a UL fuse that is exactly right. The rule is sound; it simply describes UL fuses. Take an IEC fuse and size it by the same rule and you end up 25–50 % too large — and because an IEC fuse already runs at its full number, one that big no longer blows soon enough to protect the equipment.
ch4_3.mainsP9: The second is the letter in front of the number, and it matters as much as the number does. F (from the German flink, nimble) is quick-acting; T (träge, sluggish) is time-lag, what English-language sources call slow-blow. The difference is dramatic at real fault currents: at ten times its rating, an F fuse clears in 20–40 ms, while a T fuse will tolerate up to 300 ms — about ten times longer.
ch4_3.mainsP10: That tolerance is not sloppiness; it is the entire reason T exists. A mains transformer draws a magnetising inrush of ten to twelve times its running current for the first few cycles after switch-on, and the reservoir capacitor behind it is empty at that moment, so it looks like a dead short. An F fuse sees that and does exactly what it was designed to do: it blows, every single time you turn the radio on. A T fuse rides the inrush out and still clears a genuine fault long before anything catches fire.
ch4_3.mainsCaution1: Both types react slowly to a mild overload — neither is required to blow at 1.5 times its rating within an hour. A fuse is not there to protect against working your equipment a bit hard. It is there to stop a short circuit becoming a fire.
ch4_3.mainsP11: And the rule that has no exceptions: never fit a bigger fuse to stop it blowing. A fuse that blows is not the problem, it is the symptom — something behind it is drawing current it should not. Uprate it and the fault does not go away; the fusing job moves to the next weakest thing, usually your wiring — which is not built to act as a fuse and can overheat and catch fire instead of simply blowing. The same goes, even more so, for the foil, the coin and the nail across the holder. Match the rating, the letter, the voltage and the breaking capacity, and fix what actually blew it.
ch4_3.mainsP12: One more device deserves naming, because it is easy to expect more of it than it delivers. A residual-current device — ПЗВ in Ukraine, RCD elsewhere — compares the current flowing out along the line with the current coming back along the neutral. In a healthy circuit they are equal. If some current is going missing, it is going somewhere it shouldn't — through the earth, or through a person — and the device disconnects. For protecting people the trip threshold is 30 mA, and it acts within 300 ms at that current, or within 40 ms at five times it.
ch4_3.mainsP13: Note what that means: an RCD does not prevent the shock. It ends it. It is a survivability device, and a very good one. But it has a blind spot that lands exactly where this chapter started. If you take hold of the line in one hand and the neutral in the other, your current goes out on the line and returns on the neutral — perfectly balanced. Nothing is missing. To the RCD you are indistinguishable from a kettle, and it will not trip. That is the classic one-hand-on-each-terminal bench electrocution, and it is precisely the case an RCD cannot see. Which is why the pocket rule is not made redundant by modern wiring.
ch4_3.mainsCaution2: In Ukraine there is a further catch: ПУЕ 1.7.81 forbids fitting an RCD to a TN-C installation — and Soviet-era two-wire wiring, with its combined earth-and-neutral conductor, is normally exactly that. Buying a ПЗВ and bolting it onto old wiring does not make an old flat safe; the installation has to be converted first. ПУЕ is explicit in any case that an RCD is an additional measure and can never be the only one.
ch4_3.hvP1: A capacitor is a spring that stays loaded. Chapter 1.5 introduced it as a store of charge, which is exactly the problem: switching the mains off stops the supply refilling it. It does nothing whatsoever to empty it.
ch4_3.hvP2: The <pa>power amplifier</pa> of Chapter 3.2, and any valve equipment at all, runs on a <ht>high-tension supply</ht> — hundreds to thousands of volts, smoothed by large electrolytic capacitors. Pull the plug and those capacitors hold what they held a second earlier. The lamp goes out, the fan stops, the meter drops to zero, and the reservoir stays exactly as dangerous as it was. It can stay that way for minutes.
ch4_3.hvP3: How dangerous is a matter of arithmetic. A capacitor stores E = ½CV², so a 100 µF reservoir charged to 400 V is holding 8 J. Because the voltage is squared, the energy climbs steeply: the same capacitance at 4 kV — an ordinary valve amplifier — holds 800 J. Ten times the voltage, a hundred times the energy.
ch4_3.hvP4: Now, what does 8 J mean? You will read that «about a joule can stop a heart». That figure is real, but it is quoted out of context: it comes from cardiology, where roughly a joule is used to deliberately start fibrillation while testing an implanted defibrillator — delivered through an electrode sitting inside the heart, timed into the one-tenth of the cardiac cycle when the heart is vulnerable. Through skin, fat and muscle, only about 4 % of a current across the chest reaches cardiac tissue at all. A joule in a capacitor on your bench is not that joule, and fibrillation is not measured in joules anyway: the standards define it as a current, and for a capacitor discharge as a charge.
ch4_3.hvP5: So the useful threshold is not a claim about your heart, it is a rule about how to work. NFPA 70E puts the line at 0.25 J once you are working at 400 V or more — and 8 J is thirty-two times that. What it is warning about, at these energies, is the burn and the startle: the involuntary jerk that puts your hand into the high-tension rail, or your body off the stool, or the screwdriver across the terminals. Most bench injuries at a few joules are not the shock itself, but the involuntary reaction to it — the jerk, the fall, the dropped tool in the instant afterwards.
ch4_3.hvP6: A well-designed supply fits a bleeder resistor permanently across the reservoir, sized to pull the rail down to a safe level within about thirty seconds of switch-off. It costs a few cents, and it is the difference between a supply that discharges its own capacitors and one that leaves them charged until you do it by hand.
ch4_3.hvP7: Never trust it. Bleeders fail open, and a failed bleeder looks exactly like a working one — there is no indicator, no click, nothing. Verify with a meter, every time, on the assumption that the bleeder is not there: DC volts range, probes on the reservoir capacitor's own terminals, and you want to see zero — not «nearly zero», and not a number that is still falling.
ch4_3.hvP8: Then discharge it yourself, with a shorting stick: an insulated rod with an earthed lead on the end. For anything holding more than a few joules use a discharge stick — the same thing with a high-wattage, low-value resistor in series — which limits the discharge to roughly 5–10 A. A dead short across a large capacitor damages the capacitor through its own internal thermal and magnetic stress. And never use a screwdriver: it brings your hand far too close to the thing you are shorting, and it ruins the blade.
ch4_3.hvP9: Two ways this bites people who did everything right. The first is that a discharged capacitor charges itself back up. The effect is called dielectric absorption, or soakage: charge trapped in the dielectric seeps back out after you remove the short, and a big aluminium electrolytic will recover 10–15 % of where it started — within minutes, with the plug on the floor. On a 400 V supply that is 40–60 V — a startling but harmless spark. On a 4 kV valve supply the same 10–15 % is several hundred volts, arriving by itself, in a rig you have already «made safe». This is why the rule is to keep every discharged capacitor shorted the whole time you are working on the equipment. And if you take one out, twist its two leads together with wire before you set it down — on its own, out of circuit, it will charge itself back up, and there is no longer a clip holding it safe.
ch4_3.hvP10: The second is a meter reading that fools you. Put two 400 µF capacitors in series but wired in opposition — their like terminals joined, and that junction earthed — with each charged to 300 V. A meter across the two outer terminals reads zero, because between those two points the voltages cancel — yet each capacitor is still holding 18 J. The correct habit is to discharge every capacitor individually, and clip a shorting jumper onto each one before moving to the next.
ch4_3.hvKey1: A meter reading zero across a bank does not mean the bank is empty. Discharge each capacitor by itself, and leave it shorted while your hands are in there.
ch4_3.rfP1: This is the hazard you cannot feel. You can measure mains with a meter, and a charged capacitor at least sits behind a cover; an RF field gives you neither warning. The best way to picture it is the microwave oven in your kitchen.
ch4_3.rfP2: A microwave oven heats food by shaking its water molecules with a radio-frequency field. That is the whole mechanism, and it is the same mechanism at your antenna — just enormously weaker and enormously more spread out. Radio waves are non-ionising: unlike X-rays, they carry nowhere near enough energy per photon to break a chemical bond, so they cannot break the chemical bonds inside living cells the way ionising radiation does. What they do is heat tissue. That is not nothing, and it is also not radiation in the sense the word usually frightens people with.
ch4_3.rfP3: The quantity that actually matters is therefore a heating rate: the specific absorption rate, or SAR, in watts absorbed per kilogram of tissue. The exposure limits are written in SAR, and for the general public ICNIRP sets 0.08 W/kg averaged over the whole body, and 2 W/kg averaged over any 10 g of the head or torso.
ch4_3.rfP4: There is an obvious practical problem: you cannot measure the watts per kilogram inside your own head. So the guidelines restate the limits as reference levels — field strengths in the air, which you can measure or model, chosen so that staying under them guarantees staying under the SAR limit. That is the number you will actually look up.
ch4_3.rfP5: And that reference level is not a single figure. It sags in the middle of the spectrum, and that dip is worth understanding, because it depends on the size of your body compared with the wavelength.
ch4_3.rfP6: A human body is an antenna. Like any antenna it couples to a field most efficiently at <reson>resonance</reson>, when its size is comparable to half a wavelength — which for a person puts the peak in VHF. Dosimetry measures it near 70 MHz for a standing adult, and about 35 MHz for one standing on conductive ground, because the ground mirrors the body and the two together resonate like something twice as tall. The arithmetic will not land on 70 MHz exactly — half a wavelength there is 2.1 m, well above average human height — because a real body resonates lower than a thin wire of the same height: it is vastly thicker than that wire, lossy, and mostly water. Right through the VHF range, then, a given field produces far more heating in you than the same field would at 80 m or at 70 cm. The limit has to come down to compensate, and it does: from 30 to 400 MHz it flattens out at its strictest value, 27.7 V/m. The 4 m and 2 m bands sit at the bottom of that trough.
ch4_3.rfNote1: <res>Whole-body resonance</res> is why the limits are tightest in VHF, and it shows that the antenna theory of Chapter 3.3 applies to your body too, not just to metal. A half-wave dipole resonates because of its length; at VHF, a standing adult does the same.
ch4_3.rfP7: The other half of RF safety is arithmetic, and it works in your favour: exposure limits are averaged over minutes, not sampled at the peak. So what counts is not the number on the meter — the peak envelope power, or PEP — it is that number reduced twice: once by the duty cycle of the mode, and once by how much of the time you are actually transmitting.
ch4_3.rfP8: Ordinary <ssb>SSB</ssb> speech only reaches peak power on the loudest syllables — its duty cycle is about 20 %. <cw>CW</cw> runs about 40 %; SSB with heavy processing about 50 %. So 100 W of SSB, in a conversation where you talk half the time, averages 100 × 0.2 × 0.5 = 10 W. Ten watts is a very different exposure question from a hundred.
ch4_3.rfP9: Now switch that same radio to FM. A constant carrier runs at full power the whole time you are transmitting — duty cycle 100 %. The averaged figure jumps from 10 W to 50 W — five times the exposure, same amplifier, same reading on the same meter. Every digital mode does the same thing, FT8 included. The mode you choose affects your exposure more than the amplifier itself.
ch4_3.rfP10: For practical purposes the RSGB's rule of thumb is the one to carry: at time-averaged powers up to 100 W, keeping people about 2.4 m away from anything that radiates has been shown by measurement to be enough. Distance is by far the cheapest control you have — the field falls off fast, and moving the antenna up and away is worth more than any amount of worrying.
ch4_3.rfP11: One honest limitation. Below 30 MHz you cannot turn any of this into a tidy «stand this far back» number. The formula that converts power into a safe distance assumes you are far enough from the antenna for the wave to have settled into its <nf>far-field form</nf> — and on 20 m, that distance is bigger than the answer the formula gives. The equation returns a number from a region where it does not apply. This is not a technicality: it is why ICNIRP defines no power-density limit below 30 MHz, and requires the electric and magnetic fields to be checked separately there. On HF, use the 2.4 m rule and keep the antenna away from people.
ch4_3.lightP1: You cannot stop lightning and you cannot armour a house against it. Everything that follows is one idea: offer it a path that is better than the one through your equipment — and through you.
ch4_3.lightP2: The numbers set the scale. A typical stroke peaks around 30 kA, rising to that peak in a few microseconds and decaying over about fifty microseconds. The extremes reach hundreds of kiloamps. The rise time is the part that matters: a pulse that sharp behaves exactly like a great many sine waves added together, and the faster the current rises, the higher the frequencies among them. For a lightning pulse they run from a few kilohertz to over 10 MHz — which is to say, a lightning strike is a radio-frequency event, and everything you learned in Chapter 4.2 about how RF gets into things applies to it.
ch4_3.lightNote1: The median peak current is genuinely disputed. The classic ~30 kA comes from decades of direct measurement on instrumented towers and underlies the IEC design standards; modern lightning detection networks report a median nearer 10 kA. The discrepancy is unresolved and openly acknowledged by the researchers involved. Design for 30 kA.
ch4_3.lightP3: Here is the first surprise. The average current in a stroke is only a few hundred amps, so the conductor needed to carry it without melting is startlingly thin. Lightning conductors are not heavy for current capacity at all. They are heavy to reduce inductance — because at the frequencies in that pulse, what sets the voltage along a wire is not its resistance at all. It is the inductance, multiplied by how fast the current is changing. A single metre of ordinary round wire is about a microhenry, and against a current rising at tens of kiloamps per microsecond, that one metre develops tens of kilovolts across it. So «it's only a short earth wire» is no reassurance — even one metre can develop tens of kilovolts across it.
ch4_3.lightP4: The second surprise is that the direct hit is not what usually destroys stations. The international standard on lightning protection recognises four ways damage arrives: a strike to the structure, a strike near it, a strike to the lines connected to it, and a strike near those lines. Three of the four involve nothing hitting you at all. A discharge a few hundred metres away induces a surge into every long conductor you own — antenna, mains, network, rotator cable — simultaneously.
ch4_3.lightP5: The third surprise is the most important one in practice. Your instinct is to get a good earth: drive a longer rod, get the resistance down, give the strike somewhere to go. Run the arithmetic on what is called ground potential rise. Thirty kiloamps into a typical 25 Ω rod puts that rod at 750 000 volts relative to true earth. Drive a magnificent 5 Ω rod and you have 150 kV. Achieve a heroic 1 Ω — far below what any practical ground rod reaches — and it is still 30 kV. There is no earth resistance low enough to hold the ground anywhere near zero.
ch4_3.lightP6: If the ground is going to rise regardless, the thing to prevent is not the rise — it is a difference. Picture the failure: your mast has its own rod, and your rig is earthed through the mains, whose rod is ten metres away. The strike lifts the mast's rod to 750 kV. The mains rod, far outside the patch of soil the current is flooding, stays near true earth. Three-quarters of a megavolt now exists between two points in your shack, and the only thing bridging them is the coax — through your radio.
ch4_3.lightP7: The fix is bonding, and the word is chosen carefully. Not «earth everything» — bond everything: connect the mast, the feedline shield, and every chassis to one single point, so that when the ground rises, the entire station rises with it. Nothing has been carried away. The rod is still at 750 kV. But there is no longer any difference across the equipment, and difference is what does the damage.
ch4_3.lightKey1: You cannot make a lightning strike small. You can make sure your whole station is at the same voltage while it happens. Bond everything to one point; damage comes from the difference, not the rise.
ch4_3.lightP8: At that single point you put an arrestor in the feedline. A gas discharge tube is the usual choice — broadband, and it passes DC, which you need if the coax also feeds a masthead preamplifier or a remote switch. It fires in around a hundred nanoseconds and lets through a few hundred volts before it does. For a single-band station a quarter-wave stub is dramatically better. It is a piece of line shorted to ground at its far end and cut to a quarter of the wavelength at your operating frequency. It is a dead short to ground at DC; at radio frequencies what decides its behaviour is its length measured in wavelengths. At your operating frequency that length is a quarter wave, and a quarter-wave line inverts whatever sits at its far end, so the short appears at the near end as an open circuit and your signal sees nothing there. A lightning surge carries its energy far below that frequency, where the same line is nowhere near a quarter wavelength and behaves as what it physically is: a wire to ground. So the surge drains away through it, with no turn-on delay because the stub is always connected, and it lets through about forty times less than the gas discharge tube does. It only works on one band, and that is the whole trade.
ch4_3.lightP9: But the most effective protection an amateur has is not a component. It is disconnecting the feedline when the station is idle or a storm is coming. Nothing else gives you actual galvanic isolation; arrestors limit damage, they do not remove the risk.
ch4_3.lightDanger1: Disconnecting is only half of it: put the disconnected end outside. A coax still attached to an antenna is still attached to a large elevated conductor, and a nearby strike can drive that floating connector to tens or hundreds of kilovolts. Air breaks down at roughly 3 kV per millimetre, so a connector at 100 kV will happily arc several centimetres to whatever is nearest — your rig, your mains lead, a radiator, you. Left coiled on the operating desk, an «unplugged» coax is not a precaution. It is a high-voltage electrode pointed at everything you own.
ch4_3.checklistP1: Everything above was mechanism, because if you understand the reasons, you can apply them to situations no rulebook covers. But mechanism is no use at the moment you are tired, the amplifier is open, and you want to get one more contact in before bed. For that moment you need a list.
ch4_3.checklistP2: Nothing in it is new. Every line is one of this chapter's arguments, compressed to the size of something you can check.
ch4_3.quiz_q1: Why is the «dry skin is 100 kΩ» figure useless for judging a 230 V shock?
ch4_3.quiz_q1_a: Because body resistance is measured between the hands, not the feet
ch4_3.quiz_q1_b: Because 100 kΩ applies only to alternating current, not to direct current
ch4_3.quiz_q1_c: Because at mains voltage the skin breaks down and stops insulating
ch4_3.quiz_q1_d: Because the figure describes the skin only while the person is sweating
ch4_3.quiz_q1_explanation: IEC 60479-1 is explicit that skin impedance collapses at higher voltages. Measured hand-to-hand at 220 V (the nearest voltage the standard tabulates), even dry, a typical body is about 1 350 Ω — so 230 V drives roughly 170 mA, not the 2.3 mA the 100 kΩ figure predicts.
ch4_3.quiz_q2: Roughly what current can put the heart into ventricular fibrillation?
ch4_3.quiz_q2_a: About 40 mA, if it flows for more than a second or two
ch4_3.quiz_q2_b: About 400 mA, and only if the skin is broken or wet
ch4_3.quiz_q2_c: About 4 mA, which is why any shock at all is lethal
ch4_3.quiz_q2_d: About 4 A, which is why fuses are rated where they are
ch4_3.quiz_q2_explanation: IEC 60479-1 puts the fibrillation threshold near 40 mA for sustained contact. A 230 V socket drives well over 100 mA through even the most resistant dry-skinned person, which is why mains is not a marginal hazard.
ch4_3.quiz_q3_a: The current at which a fuse is guaranteed to release the fault
ch4_3.quiz_q3_b: The current above which your muscles clamp and you cannot release the conductor
ch4_3.quiz_q3_c: The voltage below which a shock cannot be felt at all
ch4_3.quiz_q3_d: The time after which a residual-current device disconnects the supply
ch4_3.quiz_q3_explanation: Above roughly 5–10 mA the current drives your flexor muscles harder than you can fight them. The figure is a band rather than a line because it varies between people, and is lower for women and children.
ch4_3.quiz_q4: What is the protective earth conductor actually for?
ch4_3.quiz_q4_a: It carries static charge off the equipment case continuously
ch4_3.quiz_q4_b: It carries the return current in place of the neutral conductor
ch4_3.quiz_q4_c: It provides a low-resistance path for radio-frequency currents
ch4_3.quiz_q4_d: It makes a fault current big enough to blow the fuse quickly
ch4_3.quiz_q4_explanation: The earth wire is a trigger, not an escape route. A live-to-case fault through it draws hundreds of amps and clears the fuse in milliseconds. With no earth, the case just sits at 230 V and the fuse never notices — until someone touches it.
ch4_3.quiz_q5: You find a blue wire in an old building. Can you assume it is the neutral?
ch4_3.quiz_q5_a: Yes — under the harmonised code, blue is always the neutral
ch4_3.quiz_q5_b: Yes, but only alongside a brown live conductor
ch4_3.quiz_q5_c: No — in old wiring the colour proves nothing; test it
ch4_3.quiz_q5_d: No — in old installations blue is the protective earth
ch4_3.quiz_q5_explanation: A colour code is reliable only in wiring installed to it. In an old building the cores may be any colour, or all the same, and a blue wire can be a live phase. Never trust colour alone — test every conductor before you touch it.
ch4_3.quiz_q6: Under IEC 60127, what rating should a fuse have?
ch4_3.quiz_q6_a: About the equipment's normal running current
ch4_3.quiz_q6_b: About 125–150 % of the normal running current
ch4_3.quiz_q6_c: About half the normal running current, for a margin
ch4_3.quiz_q6_d: About ten times the normal running current
ch4_3.quiz_q6_explanation: The 125–150 % rule is a UL convention: a UL fuse is meant to run at about 75 % of its marked number, so you size it up. An IEC fuse may run at its full marked number, so the rating simply is the running current, rounded up to the nearest standard value.
ch4_3.quiz_q7: Why does a linear power supply need a T (time-lag) fuse rather than an F?
ch4_3.quiz_q7_a: Because a transformer draws less current than a switch-mode supply
ch4_3.quiz_q7_b: Because the transformer's switch-on inrush would blow a quick fuse
ch4_3.quiz_q7_c: Because T fuses have a higher breaking capacity at mains voltage
ch4_3.quiz_q7_d: Because F fuses cannot be used on alternating current at all
ch4_3.quiz_q7_explanation: Magnetising inrush runs ten to twelve times the running current for the first few cycles, and the empty reservoir capacitor looks like a short. At ten times its rating an F fuse clears in 20–40 ms — inside that window. A T fuse tolerates up to 300 ms and rides it out.
ch4_3.quiz_q8: You take hold of the line in one hand and the neutral in the other. Your 30 mA RCD will:
ch4_3.quiz_q8_a: trip in under 40 ms, because 30 mA is its threshold
ch4_3.quiz_q8_b: trip, but only once the current exceeds 300 mA
ch4_3.quiz_q8_c: trip only if the equipment case is also earthed
ch4_3.quiz_q8_d: not trip at all, because nothing is out of balance
ch4_3.quiz_q8_explanation: An RCD compares the line and neutral currents and acts on the difference. Hand-to-hand, your current goes out on the line and returns on the neutral — perfectly balanced. To the device you are just another load. This is exactly the case it cannot see.
ch4_3.quiz_q9: A meter across a series capacitor bank reads zero. What does that prove?
ch4_3.quiz_q9_a: Nothing — each capacitor can still hold lethal energy individually
ch4_3.quiz_q9_b: That the bleeder resistors have done their job correctly
ch4_3.quiz_q9_c: That the bank is discharged, provided the meter is a good one
ch4_3.quiz_q9_d: That the bank was wired with its capacitors in parallel, not series
ch4_3.quiz_q9_explanation: Two 400 µF capacitors at +300 V and −300 V with an earthed midpoint read zero across the string, and each still holds 18 J. Discharge every capacitor individually and clip a shorting jumper on each before moving to the next.
ch4_3.quiz_q10: Where are the ICNIRP exposure limits at their strictest, and why?
ch4_3.quiz_q10_a: At HF, because those wavelengths penetrate the body most deeply
ch4_3.quiz_q10_b: Across 30–400 MHz, because the body is resonant at about those frequencies
ch4_3.quiz_q10_c: Above 2 GHz, because the energy per photon is highest there
ch4_3.quiz_q10_d: Below 1 MHz, because the body cannot dissipate the heat at all
ch4_3.quiz_q10_explanation: Whole-body resonance for a standing adult is measured near 70 MHz — about 35 MHz if they are standing on conductive ground — so the body absorbs VHF fields far more efficiently. The reference level bottoms out at a flat 27.7 V/m from 30 to 400 MHz, and the 4 m and 2 m bands sit right in that trough.
ch4_3.quiz_q11: You run 100 W PEP and switch from SSB to FM. Your time-averaged exposure:
ch4_3.quiz_q11_a: falls by about half, because FM spreads its power more widely
ch4_3.quiz_q11_b: stays the same, because the meter still reads 100 W
ch4_3.quiz_q11_c: rises about fivefold, because a constant carrier never lets up
ch4_3.quiz_q11_d: rises about a hundredfold, because FM is a wideband mode
ch4_3.quiz_q11_explanation: Ordinary SSB speech has a duty cycle near 20 %; FM, RTTY and every digital mode including FT8 run at 100 %. Same amplifier, same meter reading, five times the averaged power. The mode matters more than the amplifier.
ch4_3.quiz_q12: Why are lightning conductors made heavy, when a stroke's average current is only a few hundred amps?
ch4_3.quiz_q12_a: To survive the mechanical shock of the strike without snapping
ch4_3.quiz_q12_b: To keep their resistance low enough to hold the earth near zero volts
ch4_3.quiz_q12_c: To carry the peak current of 30 kA without melting through
ch4_3.quiz_q12_d: To lower their inductance, which sets the voltage at those frequencies
ch4_3.quiz_q12_explanation: A stroke's energy spans kilohertz to over 10 MHz, so it is the inductance and the sheer rate of change of the current, not resistance, that develops voltage along the conductor. One metre of round wire is about a microhenry — tens of kilovolts against a current rising at tens of kiloamps per microsecond.
ch4_3.quiz_q13: Thirty kiloamps into a heroically good 1 Ω earth rod raises it to about:
ch4_3.quiz_q13_a: 30 kV — you cannot make the rise small by improving the earth
ch4_3.quiz_q13_b: 30 V — which is why a good earth solves the problem
ch4_3.quiz_q13_c: 300 V — enough to notice, not enough to matter
ch4_3.quiz_q13_d: 3 kV — safe, provided the rod is bonded to the mast
ch4_3.quiz_q13_explanation: <var>V</var> = <var>I</var> · <var>R</var> gives 30 kV even at 1 Ω, and a typical 25 Ω rod reaches 750 kV. No achievable earth resistance holds the ground near zero — which is why the strategy is bonding, not bleeding it away.
ch4_3.quiz_q14: Why bond the mast, the feedline shield and every chassis to a single point?
ch4_3.quiz_q14_a: So the strike current is shared evenly between several earth rods
ch4_3.quiz_q14_b: So the resistance to earth is lowered by connecting rods in parallel
ch4_3.quiz_q14_c: So the whole station rises together and no difference appears across it
ch4_3.quiz_q14_d: So the arrestor can measure the potential relative to true earth
ch4_3.quiz_q14_explanation: Damage comes from the difference, not the rise. Bonded to one point, everything sits at the same 750 kV during the strike, so nothing appears across the equipment. Two separate rods put the difference across your coax — through your radio.
ch4_3.quiz_q15: What is wrong with unplugging the coax and leaving it coiled on the desk?
ch4_3.quiz_q15_a: Nothing — disconnecting is the single most effective protection there is
ch4_3.quiz_q15_b: The end is still attached to the antenna and can arc to nearby objects
ch4_3.quiz_q15_c: The unterminated cable will radiate the surge into the mains wiring
ch4_3.quiz_q15_d: Coiling the cable adds inductance, which raises the surge voltage
ch4_3.quiz_q15_explanation: Disconnecting is the right instinct, but the far end is still a large elevated conductor. A nearby strike can drive that connector to a hundred kilovolts, and air breaks down at about 3 kV/mm — so it arcs several centimetres to your rig, the mains lead, or you. Put it outside.
ch4_3.labGoal: Find out what your station's earthing actually is, rather than what you assume it is — with everything switched off and nothing above a battery's voltage involved anywhere.
ch4_3.labEquip1: A multimeter with a continuity or resistance range
ch4_3.labEquip2: A torch — the connectors and markings you need to read sit in shadow, behind the gear and under the desk
ch4_3.labStep1: Power off at the breaker. Not standby, not the front-panel switch. This whole activity happens on dead equipment. If you ever think you need it switched on, stop — that is not part of this exercise.
ch4_3.labStep2: Take each piece of equipment in turn and measure from its metal chassis to the earth pin of its own mains plug. You want continuity — near zero ohms. Anything else means that box's protective earth is not connected, and the fuse-blowing mechanism described earlier does not exist for it. Note which boxes fail; do not fix anything yet.
ch4_3.labStep3: Measure from the outer shell of your antenna connector to the chassis of the rig it plugs into. Below about 1 Ω is what you want. A stubbornly high reading here is a corroded connector or a broken braid — an RF problem and an earthing problem at once.
ch4_3.labStep4: Now the question that matters: count your earth electrodes. Where does the mast's earth go, and where does the mains earth go? If they are two separate rods, you have built the left-hand panel of the lightning diagram — and the only thing bridging them during a storm is your coax. Sketch what you find.
ch4_3.labStep5: Look for the capacitors. Any linear supply or valve amplifier has reservoir electrolytics: note the µF and the working voltage printed on the can, and put them into the stored-energy calculator above. Write the answer on a label and stick it on the lid. Do not open anything — the point is to know the number before the day you have a reason to.
ch4_3.labExpected: Almost nobody passes cleanly the first time. The usual findings are one box with a suspect earth, a coax shell reading a few ohms instead of nearly none, and — most commonly — two separate earth electrodes that nobody ever meant to install.
ch4_3.labConnection: Every measurement here is one of the chapter's mechanisms turned into a number. Step 2 tests whether the trigger of the earth wire exists at all. Step 4 tests whether you have built the ground potential rise the lightning section describes into your own house. Step 5 turns ½CV² from a formula into a figure written on your own amplifier.
ch4_3.labTrouble1: Chassis-to-earth-pin reads open on everything: check your meter and leads on a known short first. A flat battery or a broken probe reads «no earth» very convincingly.
ch4_3.labTrouble2: Chassis-to-earth-pin reads open on one box: it may be double-insulated and have no earth by design — look for the double-square symbol on the rating plate. If it has a metal case and three-core mains lead and still reads open, that is a genuine fault; stop using it until it is fixed.
ch4_3.labTrouble3: The coax shell reads a few ohms: try a different connector or cable to find out whether it is the lead or the socket. Braid corrodes invisibly under the outer jacket, and a cable that still «works» can have lost most of its shield.
ch4_3.heroAria: An operator at a workbench with four hazards converging on them — a mains plug, a charged capacitor, a radiating antenna and a lightning cloud — each stopped short by a barrier before it reaches them.

phonetics.title: Call sign speller
phonetics.description: Type a call sign and read it back in the ITU phonetic alphabet. Tick «hide the words» and the letters stay while the words disappear — say them yourself, then untick to check.
phonetics.emptyNote: Type letters or digits to see them spelled out.
phonetics.digitNote: Digits are spoken as plain numbers. Appendix 14 does define a figure code — Nadazero, Unaone, Bissotwo — but it belongs to maritime and aeronautical practice, and it is not what you will hear on the amateur bands.

qcodes.title: Q-code flashcards
qcodes.description: Fifteen Q-codes in everyday use. Each one is both a question and an answer — the same three letters, with a question mark or without one. Work the deck in whichever direction you need: recognising a code you just heard, or recalling the code for something you want to say.
qcodes.q_qrk: What is the readability of my signals?
qcodes.q_qsy: Shall I change to transmission on another frequency?
qcodes.a_qrk: The readability of your signals is …
qcodes.a_qrx: I will call you again at … hours.

rst.title: RST report builder
rst.description: Move the sliders and watch the report change. Each digit has a written definition — the report is a description, not a score out of nine.
rst.judgementNote: Readability and tone are judged by ear, so two operators can hear the same signal and send different numbers. Strength has an instrument behind it — the S-meter — but those are calibrated differently from radio to radio, so a reading on one set is not a reading on another.
rst.r2: Barely readable — the odd word gets through.
rst.r3: Readable, but only with considerable difficulty.
rst.t2: Very rough note, no trace of musicality.
rst.t6: Modulated note, slight trace of whistle.
rst.t8: Good pure note, just a trace of ripple.
rst.t9: Purest note — no trace of ripple or modulation.

decoder.title: Call sign decoder
decoder.description: Type a call sign and see it taken apart. The same three-part shape — prefix, digit, suffix — is used worldwide, but what each part carries is decided nationally, and the two systems below put the geography in different places.
decoder.invalid: That is not a call sign shape. A call sign is one or two characters, a digit, then a suffix.
decoder.countryUnknown: This prefix is not in the widget's table. Every block is allocated in Appendix 42 of the ITU Radio Regulations, which is the full list.
decoder.uaOblastLead: The first letter of the suffix gives the oblast:
decoder.uaRepeater: UR0 is set aside for repeaters and beacons rather than for an operator.
decoder.uaIndividual: The second letter of the suffix is in the A–V range, which marks an individual station.
decoder.uaCollective: The second letter of the suffix is in the W–Z range, which marks a collective (club) station.
decoder.uaDigitNote: The digit carries no geography here — it is issued in sequence as blocks fill up.
decoder.usAreaLead: The digit is the call area:
decoder.usSuffixNote: The suffix carries no geography. A licensee who moves keeps the call sign they already hold.
decoder.indicatorNote: The «{{indicator}}» part is an added indicator, not part of the issued call sign.
decoder.tableNote: The country table here covers a selection of administrations, enough to show how the prefix works. Ukraine and the United States are broken down in full because the chapter teaches those two systems side by side.
