qsoTimeline.aria: A contact read from top to bottom in two lanes, as three mirrored pairs. The calling station and the answering station take turns, and whatever one offers the other returns: the general call and its answer, a signal report with name and location each way, and thanks with 73 from both before signing.
qsoTimeline.cqSaid: CQ CQ CQ, this is UR5HAA
qsoTimeline.cqWhy: I want a contact — and here is who I am
qsoTimeline.replyWhy: who I am calling, then who I am
qsoTimeline.exchangeSaid: W1AW, you are 5 and 9. Ivan, QTH Poltava
qsoTimeline.exchangeWhy: report, name and location in one turn
qsoTimeline.exchangeBackSaid: UR5HAA, you are 5 and 7. John, QTH Boston
qsoTimeline.closeSaid: Thanks John, 73! W1AW this is UR5HAA
qsoTimeline.closeWhy: thanks, 73 — and both call signs again
qsoTimeline.closeBackWhy: thanks and 73 in return, then my call

callsignAnatomy.aria: Two call signs broken into lettered boxes. Both have a prefix, a digit and a suffix, but the highlighted box is in a different place: for the Ukrainian call sign it is the first letter of the suffix, which gives the oblast, while for the United States call sign it is the digit, which gives the call area.
callsignAnatomy.uaNote1: The digit is issued in sequence as blocks fill up.
callsignAnatomy.uaNote2: It marks no place at all.
callsignAnatomy.usNote2: A licensee who moves keeps the call sign they hold.

ch4_4.heroAria: Two operators facing each other across a radio link. The one on the left is speaking into a hand microphone; the one on the right is wearing headphones. In front of each of them lies the same sheet of paper, ruled with the same lines — both are working from an identical script.
ch4_4.intro1: You can build a transmitter that is clean to the last <db>decibel</db>, hang it on an antenna that is matched to perfection, and still fail to complete a contact — because the last link in the chain is not electrical. It is language, spoken into a channel that is shared with everyone else on the band, that fades without warning, and that drops whole syllables on the way.
ch4_4.intro2: This chapter is about the small fixed vocabulary that was built for exactly that channel: a spelling alphabet, a set of three-letter codes, a three-number signal report, and a shape that a contact follows from first call to sign-off. None of it is difficult. All of it is worth knowing before you first press the button, because it is what the operator at the other end is expecting to hear.
ch4_4.intro3: The word for all of this is procedure, which makes it sound like paperwork. It is closer to error correction.
ch4_4.whyP1: Start with what the channel is actually like. A telephone call gives you a private line, both ends talking at once, and near-perfect audio. A contact on the bands gives you none of those. The frequency is shared with anyone else who can hear it. Only one station can transmit at a time, so every exchange is a series of turns. The signal fades, and static crashes land on top of it. And there is no handshake underneath telling you that anything arrived.
ch4_4.whyP2: Under those conditions a listener does not hear every sound and then work out the meaning. They hear some of the sounds and reconstruct the rest from what they were expecting. That is the whole mechanism, and once you see it, the fixed vocabulary stops looking like ritual: every part of it exists to make the listener's expectation as sharp as possible.
ch4_4.whyP3: A worked case. If you say a letter and half of it is eaten by a static crash, the letter is gone. If you say a whole word instead, the listener can lose a syllable and still know which word it was, because no other word in the set is close to it. The redundancy is deliberate: you are sending more sound than the information strictly needs, so that damage can be absorbed.
ch4_4.whyKey: On-air procedure is not etiquette. It is redundancy, added on purpose, so that a listener who misses part of what you said can still recover the whole of it.
ch4_4.whyP4: That also explains why the vocabulary is shared rather than merely sensible. A private set of words could be clearer to you and still be useless, because the value is not in the words themselves — it is in the other operator already knowing which words are coming.
ch4_4.phonP1: Say the letters B, D, E, P, T and V out loud. In a quiet room they are six different sounds. Put them through a narrow receiver <flt>filter</flt> with static underneath and they collapse towards a single one: a short vowel with a consonant in front that the channel has largely removed. Reading a call sign letter by letter is therefore the least reliable thing you can do with it.
ch4_4.phonP2: The fix is to replace each letter with a whole word, chosen so that no two words in the set are close to one another. Bravo, Delta, Echo, Papa, Tango and Victor cannot be confused even when the channel has taken a bite out of each of them. That substitution is what a <ph>phonetic alphabet</ph> is, and the set in international use is published as Appendix 14 of the <rr>Radio Regulations</rr> of the <itu>International Telecommunication Union</itu> (ITU). Here it is in full:
ch4_4.phonP3: The spellings Alfa and Juliett look like mistakes and are not. Alfa drops the «ph» spelling because a speaker whose language does not read those letters that way would otherwise say the word wrong. Juliett doubles its final consonant so that a French speaker does not leave it silent. The set was built to survive being spoken by people who do not share a first language, and those two spellings are where that shows.
ch4_4.phonP4: Type any call sign into the speller below and it comes back word by word. The «hide the words» switch turns it into a drill: the letters stay, the words disappear, and you say them before checking.
ch4_4.phonP5: Now the part that is easy to miss: for amateur contacts, nobody actually requires this. Appendix 14 says its table «shall be used», but the heading scopes that to the articles covering safety and maritime radiotelephony — Article 25, which covers the amateur service, contains no phonetics requirement at all. The United States rule says only that use of a phonetic alphabet «is encouraged», and does not even name which one. Ukraine's regulation likewise recommends rather than compels it.
ch4_4.phonKey: The phonetic alphabet is near-universal because it works, not because a rule compels it. That is a stronger reason to use it, not a weaker one.
ch4_4.phonP6: Tune across a busy band and you may hear other words: Ontario, Santiago, Quebec, Uruguay, Victoria, Yokohama, Denmark, Italy. These are not inventions. They come from the international phonetic alphabet as the Washington radiotelegraph convention set it down in 1927, directing that «the following well-known names must be used» and then listing a set built almost entirely from place names. Later conventions revised which names were on the list, but the geographic style stayed until the modern set replaced it.
ch4_4.phonP7: Other words you may hear on air — Japan, Germany, Norway, Kilowatt, Radio — never appeared in that 1927 table and came later. So the geographic words are a mixture: some genuinely are a former standard, others are not, and no version of the mixture is standardised today.
ch4_4.phonOnair: Guidance adopted by the International Amateur Radio Union (IARU) Administrative Council is direct about this: use only the international phonetic alphabet, «No fantasies!». Its reasoning is the mechanism from the first section. When one rare station is being called by dozens at once — a pileup — the operator is listening for a specific expected word with a known number of syllables, and an unexpected substitute removes exactly the redundancy that lets them reconstruct it through the interference. Substituting a longer word on a repeat, when the first attempt did not get through, is a widely practised repair; opening with one is not.
ch4_4.phonUa: Ukraine's own regulation carries a phonetic table as Додаток 28, and it has two columns rather than one. The right-hand column is the international set — A for Alpha through to Z for Zulu — so the regulation does tell you how to spell a call sign aloud, in the same words used everywhere else. The left-hand column pairs the Cyrillic alphabet with Ukrainian words (В as Василь, Ж as Жук, Щ as Щука), and that is the column for spelling out a Ukrainian word or a name rather than a call sign, since call signs are always written and logged in Latin letters. The Latin-to-Ukrainian tables that circulate in clubs borrow those same Ukrainian words and re-map them onto Latin letters; that re-mapping is not in the regulation and varies between sources. Two details worth carrying away: the table is recommended rather than mandatory, and it spells the first word Alpha where Appendix 14 of the Radio Regulations spells it Alfa.
ch4_4.qcodeP1: The <qc>Q-code</qc> was born on telegraph keys, where a message was paid for by the character and the operator at the other end might share no language with you at all. A three-letter group starting with Q solved both problems at once: it is short, and its meaning is fixed by international agreement rather than by translation.
ch4_4.qcodeP2: Each code does double duty. Sent with a question mark it asks; sent without one it answers. QTH? means «what is your location»; QTH means «my location is». That symmetry is why the codes survived onto voice long after the economic argument for them disappeared: one short group still carries a whole sentence, and it carries it identically to an operator anywhere in the world.
ch4_4.qcodeP3: Fifteen of them cover almost everything a contact needs. Two are worth separating before you meet them in the deck: <qrm>QRM</qrm> is interference from another transmitter, while <qrn>QRN</qrn> is natural static from atmospherics — the first will often yield to a change of frequency, the second will not. Work the deck below in both directions, because recognising a code you have just heard is a different skill from recalling the code for something you want to say.
ch4_4.qcodeP4: Alongside the Q-codes sits a smaller set of plain abbreviations, mostly inherited from telegraphy and mostly still in use: CQ for a general call to anyone, DE for «from» separating the two call signs, K as an invitation to transmit, BK to break into a transmission in progress, PSE for please, R for received, UR for your, MSG for message, and RX and TX for receiver and transmitter.
ch4_4.qcodeCaution: A few Q-codes have drifted into use as nouns, which is worth knowing before you meet them in a <lb>logbook</lb>. «A <qso>QSO</qso>» means a contact, «a <qsl>QSL</qsl>» means a confirmation card, and «<qrp>QRP</qrp>» has come to mean low-power operating in general rather than the instruction to reduce power. The original question-and-answer meanings are still the ones that matter on air.
ch4_4.rstP1: Somewhere near the start of almost every contact, each station tells the other how well they are being received. The <rst>RST</rst> report is three numbers — or two on voice — and each digit has a written definition rather than being a mark on a scale.
ch4_4.rstP2: The three letters stand for Readability, Strength and Tone. Readability runs from 1 to 5 and answers one question: how much of what you sent can actually be made out? A 5 is perfectly readable; a 1 means the transmission is there but nothing in it can be recovered. Strength runs from 1 to 9 and describes how strongly the signal reaches you, from faint and barely perceptible up to very strong. Those two make the everyday voice report, and «5 and 9» is the one you will hear most.
ch4_4.rstP3: Tone is the third digit and it describes the purity of a Morse note — whether it is a clean steady pitch or has hum and roughness riding on it. A voice signal has no note to describe, which is why voice reports carry two digits and telegraphy reports carry three. Move the mode switch below and the third digit appears and disappears for exactly that reason.
ch4_4.rstNote: In contests the exchange is often a fixed 59 or 599 for everyone, because the score depends on the serial numbers or zones that follow, not on the report. That is a deliberate convention of contest operating rather than a signal report in the ordinary sense — outside a contest, a report that describes what you actually hear is far more use to the other station.
ch4_4.rstKey: Readability is how much got through, strength is how strongly it arrived, tone is how clean the note was. Only telegraphy has a tone to report.
ch4_4.qsoP1: A contact has a shape, and the shape is doing work. Because only one station transmits at a time, every turn has to end in a way that hands control over cleanly, and every turn has to say who it is from and — a general call aside, which is addressed to anyone — who it is for — otherwise a third station listening cannot tell whether the frequency is busy.
ch4_4.qsoP2: It starts before you transmit at all. Listen first, long enough to be sure nothing is already happening on the frequency — a contact can be in progress with only one end audible to you. Then ask whether the frequency is in use. On voice that is plain words; on telegraphy there is a code for exactly this question, QRL? Listen again, and only then call.
ch4_4.qsoP3: A general call is CQ: an invitation to anyone at all, as opposed to a call directed at one station. Send it, give your call sign, and stop to listen. Calling for a long time without pausing is the one reliable way to miss the station that was answering you.
ch4_4.qsoP4: From there the exchange follows the pattern below. The words change from contact to contact; the order does not, and that is what makes the next transmission predictable to the operator waiting for it.
ch4_4.qsoP5: One word carries the turn-taking. Over means «I have finished, your turn», and it belongs mid-contact. It is not combined with out: «over and out» would mean handing over and leaving at the same time, and international guidance is explicit that you should not say it. The last transmission normally names both stations and signs off — «UR5HAA, this is W1AW clear» — with 73 from each operator. 73 means «best regards» — a leftover from a numbered telegraph code.
ch4_4.qsoP6: Everything above assumes <sx>simplex</sx> — both stations on one frequency, taking turns. Working through a <rp>repeater</rp> changes the mechanics but not the shape. Because the repeater listens on one frequency and retransmits on another — working <dx2>duplex</dx2> — you leave a short gap after keying up before you speak, so the repeater is fully open by the time your first word arrives. On a repeater, a CQ is usually replaced by simply giving your call sign and saying you are listening.
ch4_4.qsoKey: Listen, ask, listen again, then call. The opening exchange names both stations, every turn ends in a way that says whether you want an answer, and your own call sign goes out on the clock your licence sets.
ch4_4.csP1: A <cs>call sign</cs> is how a station says which station it is, and it is the one thing every transmission has to carry. You do not invent it: it is issued by the national administration out of blocks that the <itu>ITU</itu> hands to each country by treaty, in Appendix 42 of the Radio Regulations.
ch4_4.csP2: That treaty allocation is why a <cp>prefix</cp> tells you the country before the operator has said anything about where they are. Ukraine holds UR to UZ together with EM, EN and EO; the United States holds AA to AL together with K, N and W. The blocks cover every radio service rather than just the amateur one, which is why some broadcast stations carry the same leading letters.
ch4_4.csP3: Almost every call sign then reads as three parts: a prefix of one or two characters, a single digit, and a suffix. What the digit and the suffix mean, though, is a national decision — and two systems that look identical on paper can put the same information in completely different places.
ch4_4.csP4: In the United States the digit is the call area, a geographic division of the country. The suffix carries no place at all, and a licensee who moves keeps the call sign they already hold. Formats are described by the count of letters either side of the digit — 1×2, 2×1, 1×3, 2×3 — and the default is that the next call sign in sequence is issued. A licensee may instead apply for a particular one, but only from the formats their licence class allows and only if it is not already held. That makes the format a weak hint about class rather than a reliable indicator, because an operator may keep a call sign issued under earlier rules or a different class.
ch4_4.csP5: In Ukraine the arrangement is inverted. The digit carries no geography — it is issued in sequence as blocks fill up. The oblast lives in the first letter of the suffix, from a table of twenty-five letters covering twenty-five regions. The second letter of a three-letter suffix marks the kind of station: A to V for an individual station, W to Z for a collective one. UR0 is set aside for repeaters and beacons rather than for operators, and the EM, EN and EO prefixes are reserved for special event and contest call signs.
ch4_4.csP6: Call signs and operating documents in Ukraine are issued by УДЦР, under the Regulation of the Amateur Radio Service approved by the regulator НКЕК in 2023. That regulation also replaced the older numbered categories with three licence classes: A, B and C.
ch4_4.csP7: Type a call sign into the decoder below and it will take it apart.
ch4_4.csP8: Two more marks appear attached to call signs. An indicator added after a slash says something about how or where you are operating — in Ukraine, /A for a temporary location worked from a fixed installation, /P for one worked in the field, /M from a land vehicle, /MM from a vessel and /AM from an aircraft. And an operator working in another country puts that country's prefix before their own call sign, separated by a slash: a German operator in Ukraine signs UT/DL1ABC, and an American in Germany signs DL/W1AW.
ch4_4.csIdent: How often you must identify is set nationally, and the international baseline barely constrains it: the Radio Regulations say only that amateur stations shall transmit their call sign «at short intervals», leaving every administration to define that one word. Ukraine requires the call sign at the start of a contact, at the end, and at least once every ten minutes in between. The United States requires it at the end and at least every ten minutes — with no requirement to identify at the start at all. Same ten-minute clock, different anchor points.
ch4_4.csKey: The prefix names the country by international treaty. Everything after it — what the digit means, what the suffix means, how often you identify — is decided nationally, and differs.
ch4_4.conP1: Almost every rule about what may go out over an amateur station follows from one phrase in the definition of the service itself: it exists for self-training, intercommunication and technical investigation, carried on «solely with a personal aim and without pecuniary interest». Read that phrase carefully and most of the rest is predictable.
ch4_4.conP2: No business traffic. If a transmission serves someone's commercial interest — yours, your employer's, or a third party's — it does not belong on the amateur bands. The narrow exceptions that exist in national rules are things like notifying other amateurs that equipment is for sale, and they are narrow on purpose.
ch4_4.conP3: No broadcasting. Amateur transmissions are addressed to other stations, not to the general public. This is why a one-way transmission aimed at whoever happens to be listening is treated differently from a contact, and why relaying a broadcast station's programme is not permitted.
ch4_4.conP4: No music, and nothing intended to obscure meaning. The second half of that is more interesting than it first looks. The test is purpose, not encoding: a digital mode whose specification is published is entirely fine, however unintelligible it sounds, because anyone can decode it. What is prohibited is a code chosen so that others cannot follow — which is also why telemetry and published data modes are explicitly carved out in national rules.
ch4_4.conP5: Third-party traffic — passing a message on behalf of somebody who is not a licensed operator at either end — is restricted internationally by default, which is easy to miss. The Radio Regulations permit it across borders only for emergencies and disaster relief, and leave anything beyond that to bilateral agreement between the two administrations. That is why the list of countries you may exchange such traffic with is a patchwork rather than a rule.
ch4_4.conP6: Inside those limits, where on a band you transmit is guided by the <bp>band plan</bp>: the agreement on which segment carries telegraphy, which carries narrow digital modes, which carries voice, and which is set aside for beacons. In most countries band plans are drawn up by amateur organisations rather than imposed by the regulator, which makes them voluntary in law and near-universal in practice. A wide signal landing in a narrow-mode segment can be entirely legal and still wipe out several contacts.
ch4_4.conOnair: The habits that make a band pleasant to use are short and mostly obvious once stated. Listen before transmitting, every time. Identify when you are supposed to. Do not transmit without identifying at all, even to test — an unidentified carrier is untraceable to anyone else on the frequency. Leave gaps, so a station with urgent traffic can break in. Keep the power to what the contact needs. And when someone asks for the frequency because they have an emergency, give it to them without discussion.
ch4_4.conKey: The service is defined as personal and non-commercial — «solely with a personal aim and without pecuniary interest» — and nearly every content rule descends from that one phrase.
ch4_4.labGoal: Make one contact deliberately, with every part of it planned in advance, and then look back at what you actually said. The goal is not a new contact in the log — it is noticing the gap between the shape you intended and the shape that came out.
ch4_4.labEquip1: A transceiver you are licensed to operate, on any band and mode you hold privileges for
ch4_4.labEquip2: Optionally a phone or recorder, to play your own transmissions back
ch4_4.labComp1: A logbook or a sheet of paper for the entry
ch4_4.labComp2: Your written script for each part of the exchange, prepared before you transmit
ch4_4.labComp3: A quiet frequency, or a local repeater at a time when it is not busy
ch4_4.labStep1: Write it out first. Before you key up, write down what you will say for each part: the call, the answer you expect, the signal report, your name and location, and the closing. Putting it on paper is how you find out which parts you had not actually thought about.
ch4_4.labStep2: Listen, then ask. Listen on the frequency for a good while. Ask whether it is in use, and listen again. Only then call.
ch4_4.labStep3: Make the contact. Give a signal report that describes what you are really hearing, rather than a reflex 59. Note the report you receive.
ch4_4.labStep4: Write the log entry immediately. Date, time in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), band or frequency, mode, the call sign worked, and both reports. Doing it from memory an hour later is where the errors come from.
ch4_4.labStep5: Review. Which parts went as planned, and which did not? Two things are the easiest to lose: the other station’s call sign, if it was not written down as it arrived, and the phonetics, which tend to go the moment the script is set aside. Repeat the next day, on a different band or mode if your licence covers one.
ch4_4.labExpected: By the third or fourth contact the script stops being necessary, because the shape has moved from something you are reading to something you are expecting. That is the same shift that happens on the receiving side, and it is the whole reason the vocabulary is fixed.
ch4_4.labConnection: Everything in this chapter is a claim about what survives a noisy shared channel. A recorder settles those claims faster than any amount of reading: play back your own transmission and you will hear immediately which words came through and which did not.
ch4_4.labTrouble1: Nobody answers your call. That is ordinary, not failure — try a different time of day, a different band, or answer somebody else's call instead of making your own.
ch4_4.labTrouble2: You lose the other station's call sign halfway through. Write it down as it arrives, character by character, and read it back to confirm. Asking for a repeat is normal and costs nothing.
ch4_4.labTrouble3: On a repeater your first word is missing. Leave a longer gap between keying up and speaking — the repeater needs a moment to open before it is carrying your audio.
ch4_4.labNote: This is the one activity in the course that needs another person. Not holding a licence yet need not stop you: in Ukraine an operator of class A may let someone who holds no qualification of their own work their station for training, provided that operator is present and supervising throughout, and a club station runs on the same basis under its responsible operator. If there is nobody about, the substitute is a recorder: run the whole script into it and play it back. It catches dropped phonetics and rushed call signs surprisingly well.
ch4_4.quiz_q1: Why does a whole word survive interference better than a single spoken letter?
ch4_4.quiz_q1_a: A word is louder, so more of it gets above the noise floor
ch4_4.quiz_q1_b: A word is longer, so it occupies a wider slice of the band
ch4_4.quiz_q1_c: A word keeps enough spare sound that a lost syllable still identifies it
ch4_4.quiz_q1_d: A word is spoken more slowly, so the receiver has longer to settle
ch4_4.quiz_q1_explanation: The redundancy is the point. Losing part of «Bravo» still leaves something no other word in the set matches; losing part of «B» leaves nothing. Loudness and bandwidth are not what changes.
ch4_4.quiz_q2: Why is the first letter of the alphabet spelled «Alfa» rather than «Alpha»?
ch4_4.quiz_q2_a: So speakers whose language reads those letters differently still say it correctly
ch4_4.quiz_q2_b: Because the shorter spelling fits the column width of the original table
ch4_4.quiz_q2_c: To keep every word in the set to exactly two syllables when spoken
ch4_4.quiz_q2_d: Because an older maritime code had already claimed the longer spelling
ch4_4.quiz_q2_explanation: The set was designed to be spoken by people who share no first language. «Juliett» doubles its final consonant for the same kind of reason — so a French speaker does not leave it silent.
ch4_4.quiz_q3: What is the status of the international spelling alphabet for an amateur contact?
ch4_4.quiz_q3_a: Mandatory worldwide under Article 25 of the Radio Regulations
ch4_4.quiz_q3_b: Recommended internationally, but mandatory under national licence conditions
ch4_4.quiz_q3_c: Mandatory only when working a station in another ITU region
ch4_4.quiz_q3_d: Recommended rather than required, in both national and international rules
ch4_4.quiz_q3_explanation: Article 25, which covers the amateur service, has no phonetics requirement. National rules encourage rather than compel it. It is near-universal because it works, which is a stronger reason than compulsion.
ch4_4.quiz_q4: What is the difference between sending «QTH?» and sending «QTH»?
ch4_4.quiz_q4_a: The first is telegraphy usage, the second is voice usage
ch4_4.quiz_q4_b: The first asks for a location, the second states your own
ch4_4.quiz_q4_c: The first requests a repeat, the second acknowledges receipt
ch4_4.quiz_q4_d: The first is a question to one station, the second to all stations
ch4_4.quiz_q4_explanation: Every Q-code works both ways: with a question mark it asks, without one it answers. That symmetry is why one short group can replace a whole sentence in either direction.
ch4_4.quiz_q5: A station reports QRM. What are they telling you?
ch4_4.quiz_q5_a: Another transmitter is interfering with them
ch4_4.quiz_q5_b: Atmospheric static is making you hard to copy
ch4_4.quiz_q5_c: Your signal is fading up and down at their end
ch4_4.quiz_q5_d: They want you to reduce your transmitter power
ch4_4.quiz_q5_explanation: QRM is interference from other transmitters; QRN is natural static. The distinction is practical — QRM will often yield to a change of frequency, QRN usually will not.
ch4_4.quiz_q6_a: You are calling one specific station you have just heard
ch4_4.quiz_q6_b: You are asking whether the frequency is currently in use
ch4_4.quiz_q6_c: You are inviting a contact from any station that hears you
ch4_4.quiz_q6_d: You are announcing that you are about to leave the frequency
ch4_4.quiz_q6_explanation: CQ is the general call. Asking whether a frequency is in use is a separate step that comes before it, and leaving is signalled by thanks, 73 and both call signs.
ch4_4.quiz_q7: In a signal report, what does the first number describe?
ch4_4.quiz_q7_a: How strong the signal is at the receiver
ch4_4.quiz_q7_b: How much of the transmission can actually be made out
ch4_4.quiz_q7_c: How clean and steady the Morse note sounds
ch4_4.quiz_q7_d: How far the signal has travelled to reach you
ch4_4.quiz_q7_explanation: Readability runs 1 to 5 and answers only «how much got through». Signal strength is the second number, and tone — the purity of the note — is the third.
ch4_4.quiz_q8: Why does a voice contact exchange two digits rather than three?
ch4_4.quiz_q8_a: Because voice signals are too wide for a tone judgement to be meaningful
ch4_4.quiz_q8_b: Because the third digit is reserved for contest serial numbers
ch4_4.quiz_q8_c: Because the third digit is only exchanged between different ITU regions
ch4_4.quiz_q8_d: Because tone describes a Morse note, and a voice signal has none
ch4_4.quiz_q8_explanation: Tone describes the purity of a telegraphy note. A voice transmission has no note to describe, so the digit would carry no information.
ch4_4.quiz_q9: A contact is finished. Which closing is correct?
ch4_4.quiz_q9_a: 73 and both call signs, because the exchange is finished
ch4_4.quiz_q9_b: «Over», because control passes back to the other station
ch4_4.quiz_q9_c: «Over and out», because both handing over and leaving apply
ch4_4.quiz_q9_d: «Break», because the frequency is released to other stations
ch4_4.quiz_q9_explanation: «Over» hands the turn over mid-contact, so it belongs inside a contact rather than at its end. «Over and out» combines handing over with leaving, which is why international guidance says not to say it. In practice a contact closes with thanks, 73 and both call signs.
ch4_4.quiz_q10: Why leave a short gap after keying up before speaking on a repeater?
ch4_4.quiz_q10_a: To let the other station adjust their squelch to your signal
ch4_4.quiz_q10_b: To confirm that nobody else has started transmitting first
ch4_4.quiz_q10_c: To give the repeater time to open before your first word arrives
ch4_4.quiz_q10_d: To allow the repeater to switch its antenna from receive to transmit
ch4_4.quiz_q10_explanation: The repeater needs a moment to come up and start retransmitting. Speaking immediately means the opening word goes out while nothing is carrying it.
ch4_4.quiz_q11: What does the prefix of a call sign tell you?
ch4_4.quiz_q11_a: The licence class held by the operator using it
ch4_4.quiz_q11_b: The country whose administration issued it
ch4_4.quiz_q11_c: The region of the country the operator lives in
ch4_4.quiz_q11_d: The year in which the call sign was first assigned
ch4_4.quiz_q11_explanation: Prefix blocks are allocated to countries by treaty in Appendix 42 of the Radio Regulations. Everything after the prefix is decided nationally and varies.
ch4_4.quiz_q12: In a Ukrainian call sign, which part identifies the oblast?
ch4_4.quiz_q12_a: The first letter of the suffix
ch4_4.quiz_q12_b: The digit between prefix and suffix
ch4_4.quiz_q12_c: The second letter of the two-letter prefix
ch4_4.quiz_q12_d: The final letter of the three-letter suffix
ch4_4.quiz_q12_explanation: Ukraine puts the geography in the first suffix letter, from a table of twenty-five letters. The digit there carries no geography at all — it is issued in sequence as blocks fill up.
ch4_4.quiz_q13: In a United States call sign, what does the digit indicate?
ch4_4.quiz_q13_a: The licence class the holder qualified for
ch4_4.quiz_q13_b: The number of letters that follow it in the suffix
ch4_4.quiz_q13_c: The sequence in which the call sign was issued
ch4_4.quiz_q13_d: The call area, a geographic division of the country
ch4_4.quiz_q13_explanation: The United States puts geography in the digit and none in the suffix. A licensee who moves keeps the call sign they already hold, so the digit reflects where it was issued.
ch4_4.quiz_q14: A German operator working from Ukraine signs which of these?
ch4_4.quiz_q14_a: DL1ABC/UT, with the home call sign first
ch4_4.quiz_q14_b: UT/DL1ABC, with the visited country first
ch4_4.quiz_q14_c: UT1ABC, replacing the home prefix entirely
ch4_4.quiz_q14_d: DL1ABC/P, with a portable indicator only
ch4_4.quiz_q14_explanation: The visited country's prefix goes before the operator's own call sign, separated by a slash. An American operating in Germany signs the mirror image: DL/W1AW.
ch4_4.quiz_q15: What does the international default permit for third-party traffic?
ch4_4.quiz_q15_a: Any message, provided both operators hold a licence
ch4_4.quiz_q15_b: Any message, provided the content is logged at both ends
ch4_4.quiz_q15_c: Only messages concerning emergencies and disaster relief
ch4_4.quiz_q15_d: Only messages between stations inside the same ITU region
ch4_4.quiz_q15_explanation: The Radio Regulations allow it internationally for emergencies and disaster relief, and leave anything wider to agreement between the two administrations — which is why the list of countries involved is a patchwork.
ch4_4.qsoTimelineCaption: A complete contact, read downward. Whatever one station offers — a report, a name and location, thanks — the other returns, and nobody transmits twice in a row.
ch4_4.callsignAnatomyCaption: The same three-part shape, and the geography in a different place. Ukraine puts the oblast in the first letter of the suffix; the United States puts the call area in the digit.
ch4_4.alphabetTableCaption: The complete ITU spelling alphabet — the twenty-six words in international use. They are the same words in every country and every language, which is exactly what makes them work.

alphabetTable.aria: A reference table of the twenty-six letters of the Latin alphabet, each paired with its ITU spelling word, from A for Alfa through to Z for Zulu.

ch4_5.regionsAria: Three bars on one frequency axis showing the 40-metre amateur allocation in each ITU Radio Region: Region 2 reaches 7.300 megahertz, while Regions 1 and 3 both stop at 7.200.
ch4_5.regionsCaption: The 40-metre band in each of the three ITU Radio Regions, on one axis. Ukraine is in Region 1, along with the rest of Europe. Region 1 is Europe, Africa, the Middle East and northern Asia; Region 2 is the Americas; Region 3 is the rest of Asia and the Pacific. The rows run 2, 1, 3 because that is where a world map puts them, left to right. The region numbers are not a west-to-east sequence: Region 1 is Europe, Region 2 the Americas. Only Region 2 reaches 7.300 MHz: in Region 1 the stretch above 7.200 MHz carries broadcasting instead, which is why a station in the Americas can hold a relaxed conversation on 7.250 MHz that you may listen to but not answer.
ch4_5.allocAria: Three bars on one frequency axis for the 40-metre band: the span the ITU allocates to the amateur service, the way the IARU band plan divides that span by mode, and how far each Ukrainian licence class may actually go.
ch4_5.allocCaption: The 40-metre band read three times over. The ITU allocation is a treaty; the band plan is an agreement between amateurs; the licence conditions are law — and only the third one stops short, at 7.100 MHz, for classes B and C. Two simplifications, so that the three layers stay legible: the band plan subdivides its top segment further into contest-preferred stretches and centres of activity, and each class bar shows only how far that class may transmit and at what power — the Regulations also vary which modes each class may use inside that span.
ch4_5.heroAria: A radio wave running unbroken across a dashed border, with a different rule book standing on each side of it.
ch4_5.intro1: Everything in this course so far has been about making a signal: getting a current to do what you want, folding a voice onto a carrier, feeding an antenna without wasting half the power in the cable. This chapter is about being allowed to send it.
ch4_5.intro2: The reason a hobby has a rule book at all is that the spectrum is shared and finite. Two stations transmitting on one frequency do not get half a contact each — they get none. And unlike almost every other shared resource, this one ignores borders completely: a signal that leaves an antenna in Kyiv is a fact in Warsaw and Ankara a few milliseconds later, whether or not anyone there agreed to it.
ch4_5.intro3: So the rules arrive in three layers, and most confusion about them comes from mistaking one layer for another. A treaty divides the spectrum between services worldwide. Amateurs themselves agree how to use their share. And a national regulator decides what you, holding your qualification, may actually transmit. This chapter takes them in that order, and then looks at what Ukraine's own rules say.
ch4_5.sectionWhy: Why radio has a rule book
ch4_5.whyP1: Chapter 4.2 dealt with interference as an engineering problem: a harmonic landing where it should not, a switching supply filling the band with hash. The same phenomenon has a second face. Interference is also the reason radio is one of the most tightly coordinated technologies there is — and the coordination is old, older than broadcasting.
ch4_5.whyP2: The argument is short. Radio spectrum cannot be fenced, stacked or stored. Two transmissions occupying the same frequency in the same place at the same time destroy each other rather than sharing. And a transmission travels as far as physics allows, not as far as its operator intends, so the people affected by a badly chosen frequency are usually not the people who chose it.
ch4_5.whyP3: That is why the rules are agreed internationally before they are made nationally, rather than the other way round. A country that assigned frequencies purely to suit itself would be assigning its neighbours' frequencies too. What each administration keeps for itself is the narrower question: who among its own citizens may use the allotted space, with how much power, and after what examination.
ch4_5.whyKey: Spectrum is shared, finite, and indifferent to borders. Those three facts, together, are the whole reason an amateur licence exists.
ch4_5.sectionItu: The ITU and the Radio Regulations
ch4_5.ituP1: The <itu>International Telecommunication Union</itu> is the United Nations agency that divides the radio spectrum between services. Its instrument is the <rr>Radio Regulations</rr> — not guidance but a treaty, binding on the states that have signed it, revised every few years at a World Radiocommunication Conference. Ukraine is a member state, so the Radio Regulations sit above everything else in this chapter.
ch4_5.ituP2: Two of the services the treaty defines are ours. The amateur service, whose definition Chapter 4.4 already leaned on, exists for self-training, intercommunication and technical investigation, carried on «solely with a personal aim and without pecuniary interest». Alongside it sits the <ams>amateur-satellite service</ams>: the same purposes, the same people, carried out through space stations on satellites. It is a separate service with its own allocations, which is why an amateur satellite is not simply a <rp>repeater</rp> that happens to be high up.
ch4_5.ituP3: Article 25 is the part of the Radio Regulations written specifically about these two services, and it is remarkably short. Four of its provisions are worth knowing by heart:
ch4_5.ituArt1: Contacts between amateur stations of different countries are permitted — unless the administration of one of the two has notified that it objects.
ch4_5.ituArt2: Such transmissions must not be encoded to obscure their meaning, with one explicit exception: the command signals sent from earth stations to satellites.
ch4_5.ituArt3: The maximum power an amateur station may use is left to each administration to fix.
ch4_5.ituArt4: Everything in the article applies to the amateur-satellite service as well as the amateur service.
ch4_5.ituP4: Notice what Article 25 does not do: it sets no power figure, prescribes no examination, and names no bands for you personally. It establishes that the service exists, that it may cross borders, and that it must stay intelligible. Every number you will actually obey comes from further down the stack.
ch4_5.ituP5: The treaty also splits the world into three Radio Regions, and hands the same slice of spectrum to a different mix of services in each. This is why a band can end in one place and continue in another:
ch4_5.ituKey: The Radio Regulations are a treaty, and Article 25 is its amateur chapter. It guarantees that amateur radio may cross borders and stay unencoded — and deliberately leaves power, bands and examinations to each country.
ch4_5.ceptP1: Between the treaty and your national rules sits a European layer. <cept>CEPT</cept> — the European Conference of Postal and Telecommunications Administrations — is the body through which European administrations harmonise their telecommunications rules, and for amateurs it solved a problem that used to be genuinely tiresome: before it, taking a radio across a border meant applying for a temporary licence in each country, in each country's language, weeks in advance.
ch4_5.ceptP2: It did so with two ideas. The first is a harmonised examination: if every country tests the same syllabus to the same standard, a pass in one is meaningful in all of them. The second is a harmonised licence: a document that other countries agree to honour without paperwork of their own.
ch4_5.ceptP3: The examination side comes in three levels, and Ukraine's three qualifications are built directly on them. The entry level follows Report 089 of CEPT’s Electronic Communications Committee (ECC). The novice level follows Report 32 of the European Radiocommunications Committee (ERC) — which is the syllabus this course has been working through, so the qualification it prepares you for is class B. The full level follows CEPT Recommendation T/R 61-02 and earns the HAREC (Harmonised Amateur Radio Examination Certificate), which is recognised across the CEPT membership.
ch4_5.ceptP4: The licence side is CEPT Recommendation T/R 61-01, and Ukraine's own harmonised operating document — issued by УДЦР, the state radio-frequency centre — says so on its face, in four languages. On a visit of up to three months to any country that applies the recommendation, that document is enough on its own — no local application, no fee, no waiting. You sign with your own <cs>call sign</cs> and the visited country's prefix in front of it, and the arrangement is symmetric:
ch4_5.ceptP5: Past three months it stops being a visit, and you apply to the country you are in, attaching your HAREC or novice certificate so you do not sit their examination again. The same applies in reverse: a visitor to Ukraine works on their CEPT licence for up to three months, and after that applies to УДЦР like anyone else.
ch4_5.ceptKey: CEPT harmonised two things: the exam, so a pass travels; and the licence, so the operator does. Three months is the line between visiting on your own document and applying locally.
ch4_5.layersP1: Ask where you may transmit and you will be given three different answers, all correct, because three different questions are hiding inside that one. They come from different authorities, cover different spans, and — the part that matters — only one of them binds you personally: the licence conditions. Those are the ones you answer for.
ch4_5.layersP2: An allocation is what the treaty gives the amateur service in your region. It also comes with a rank. A <prim>primary allocation</prim> means the service has first claim: other users must not interfere with it, and must accept interference from it. A <sec>secondary allocation</sec> means the opposite — you must not disturb the primary users, and you have no protection from them. Several amateur bands are secondary, which is a fact about your legal standing rather than about your equipment.
ch4_5.layersP3: A <bp>band plan</bp> is an agreement among amateurs about how to use that space: which stretch carries telegraphy (<cw>CW</cw>), which carries narrow digital modes, which carries voice. In most countries it is drawn up by amateur societies, coordinated worldwide by the <iaru>IARU</iaru>, rather than imposed by the regulator, so it is voluntary in law and near-universal in practice. Chapter 4.4 made the practical point: a wide signal landing in a narrow-mode segment can be perfectly legal and still wipe out several contacts.
ch4_5.layersP4: Licence conditions are the third layer and the only one carrying legal force over you personally. They say which bands your class may use, at what power, in which modes — Ukraine letters its three qualifications A, B and C, and the next section explains them. They are never wider than the allocation and often narrower, and they are what an inspector measures you against. Read on one axis, the three layers look like this:
ch4_5.layersP5: The figure is worth staring at for a moment, because the shape of the answer is the lesson: the class B and class C bars stop short of the other two. A class B operator on 40 metres is not restricted by physics, nor by the treaty, nor by the band plan. They are restricted by the line in their own operating document, and that line moves only by sitting another examination.
ch4_5.layersKey: Allocation is what the treaty gives your region; the band plan is what amateurs agree among themselves; licence conditions are what the law permits you. Only the third one binds you personally — and only the third one is measured.
ch4_5.uaP1: In Ukraine two bodies share the work. НКЕК is the regulator: it makes the rules and supervises compliance. УДЦР is the state radio-frequency centre: it runs the examinations through regional qualification commissions, assigns call signs, and issues the operating documents. The rules themselves live in one document — the Regulations of the Amateur Radio Service, approved by НКЕК decision № 173 of 10 May 2023 and registered with the Ministry of Justice. They replaced a 2010 predecessor.
ch4_5.uaP2: That replacement matters more than a date usually would, because it changed the vocabulary. The old Regulations numbered operators first, second and third category; the current ones letter them by qualification. A is the full qualification and corresponds to HAREC. B is the novice qualification. C is a new entry level with no equivalent in the old scheme. The Regulations publish the mapping themselves — A covers the former first and second categories, B the former third — and permits issued under the old rules stay valid until they expire. Both vocabularies are therefore alive, and a great deal of what you will read online still uses the retired one.
ch4_5.uaP3: Each qualification has its own examination programme — one per CEPT level — and its own power ceiling:
ch4_5.uaP4: The examination is run by a qualification and technical commission drawn from УДЦР and the amateur societies. It must be held within thirty days of your application; a pass needs three quarters of the questions right; a failed attempt can be retaken after thirty days. For classes B and C the theory is taken as an interview rather than a paper. The Regulations also require the commission to accommodate candidates with disabilities — papers in Braille, extra time, examination at home where mobility makes travel impractical.
ch4_5.uaP5: What you get at the end is the harmonised operating document. It is valid for at least ten years. It has to be replaced within thirty days if certain things change — your name or address, the station's location, your qualification, or the equipment's technical characteristics — and an operating document that should have been replaced and was not is simply invalid.
ch4_5.uaP6: Two provisions deserve to be better known than they are. Home-built equipment is expressly allowed, and amateur equipment does not need mandatory conformity assessment: you file a declaration that it matches the characteristics of typical amateur systems, and the commission may ask you about anything you designed yourself. And an operator holding class A may let someone with no qualification of their own work their station for training, provided they are present and supervising throughout. A club station runs on the same basis, and the age of its operators is not regulated at all.
ch4_5.uaP7: So the honest answer to «when can I get on the air?» is: possibly before you are licensed, from someone else's station, with a class A operator beside you. What the licence buys is the right to do it alone, on your own call sign — and, band by band, this much:
ch4_5.uaOnair: Two numbers from the table are worth carrying in your head, because they surprise people who learned on foreign material. The shortwave ceiling is 200 W even at the full qualification — a kilowatt amplifier is legal equipment in some countries and not here. And on 144 and 430 MHz every class is held to 5 W, which is why so much Ukrainian activity above 30 MHz runs through repeaters rather than station to station.
ch4_5.uaKey: НКЕК makes the rules, УДЦР runs the exams and issues the documents. The qualifications are A, B and C; the old first, second and third categories map onto them and are still in circulation.
ch4_5.logP1: Nearly every book on amateur radio tells you to keep a log. In Ukraine that is advice rather than law: the Regulations recommend keeping a station log rather than obliging you to. What they do fix is the content, if you keep one, and how long it lives.
ch4_5.logP2: The required content is short: — names, locations, equipment, the weather, how the contact felt — is at your discretion and no less valuable for being optional.
ch4_5.logField2: the date, the time, the band or frequency, and the mode;
ch4_5.logP3: Two conventions are recommended alongside: keep the time in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) and write call signs in Latin letters. Both exist to remove ambiguity. UTC is one clock for everybody, so an entry means the same moment whatever time zone you are in and whether or not summer time is running — a local time does not. And call signs are issued in Latin letters, so written that way a call sign has exactly one spelling — the same one the station at the other end wrote down. An electronic log is explicitly allowed. Repeaters and beacons have one extra obligation, to record when they were switched on and off, and mobile stations are exempt from logging altogether.
ch4_5.logP4: The log has to be produced if authorised officials ask to see it, and kept for at least a year after its last entry. A confirmation card — a <qsl>QSL</qsl> — is likewise optional, may be paper or electronic, and has no prescribed form; the Regulations only say what it should contain if you send one.
ch4_5.logKey: Keeping a log is recommended, not required. What is required is what goes in it if you do keep one, and that it survives a year past its last line.
ch4_5.rulesP1: Most of the operating rules are things a considerate operator would do anyway, which is a good sign about how they were written. Use the lowest power that gives the contact the quality it needs. Check the frequency is clear before you transmit. If your station interferes with another service, stop — the Regulations say «even to the point of ceasing emission».
ch4_5.rulesP2: Frequencies are not owned. Whoever started a contact on a clear frequency has priority on it, but nobody may claim a frequency permanently or demand it be vacated for them. Identification follows the rule Chapter 4.4 already gave: your call sign at the start of a contact, at the end, and at least once every ten minutes in between.
ch4_5.rulesP3: The prohibitions are worth reading once in full. You may not:
ch4_5.rulesBan1: use codes or ciphers that conceal the meaning of what you send;
ch4_5.rulesBan2: transmit at all without sending your call sign — not even to test;
ch4_5.rulesBan3: use a band, a mode or a power beyond your qualification;
ch4_5.rulesBan4: cause deliberate interference, or interference with television reception;
ch4_5.rulesBan5: play recorded music, or relay broadcast programmes;
ch4_5.rulesBan6: change frequency without stopping transmission, dragging a live carrier across other people’s contacts;
ch4_5.rulesBan7: use a transmitter whose <spur>spurious emissions</spur> exceed the limits, or whose note would be reported below T6 — the tone digit of the signal report from Chapter 4.4 runs from 1 to 9 and is cleanest at 9.
ch4_5.rulesP4: Content is limited to amateur subjects, in plain language, and the Regulations list topics that are outside them: political, ethnic, religious and gender questions, commercial matters, and calls to change the state order or to military action. The choice of language itself is explicitly free.
ch4_5.rulesP5: There is one circumstance in which the ordinary limits give way. A distress signal — SOS or MAYDAY — may be answered even from a station that is not an amateur station at all, and every other station on that frequency must stop transmitting and keep listening so the traffic can get through. Ukraine also maintains an amateur emergency service with agreed frequencies, and it is in emergencies and disaster relief that <tp>third-party traffic</tp> — passing messages for people licensed at neither end — becomes expressly permitted, having been restricted by default up to that point.
ch4_5.rulesOnair: Two of the emergency service's agreed frequencies, 7090 and 7110 kHz, are the same ones the IARU Region 1 band plan marks as the <qrp>QRP</qrp> (low-power) calling frequency and the Region 1 emergency centre of activity. That is not coincidence: the national list was built on the international one, which is the band plan doing exactly the job it exists for.
ch4_5.rulesKey: Nearly every operating rule follows from two ideas: do not obscure what you are sending, and do not take more of the shared resource than the contact needs. The exception is distress traffic, which outranks everything.
ch4_5.nextP1: That is the end of the course. It began with what a volt is and ends with a treaty, and the thread running through it is that everything in radio is a consequence of something simpler: a band plan is a consequence of <bw>bandwidth</bw>, an output <flt>filter</flt> on a transmitter is a consequence of harmonics, a power limit is a consequence of a shared spectrum.
ch4_5.nextP2: The syllabus these chapters follow is ERC Report 32, which in Ukraine is the programme for the class B qualification — the novice level. Sitting it means applying to the qualification commission for your area; for class B the theory is an interview, and you will be asked to declare that your equipment matches the characteristics of typical amateur systems.
ch4_5.nextP3: After that the useful next steps are not more reading. Listen for a few evenings before you call. Make the first contacts short. Find an operator of class A who will let you work their station under supervision, because an hour beside an experienced operator settles more than a chapter can. And when the novice qualification stops being enough, the same commission examines for HAREC — the syllabus is broader, but it is the same subjects, taken further.
ch4_5.bands.title: What your qualification may use
ch4_5.bands.description: Pick a qualification and read the bands it opens. Every number is from the Regulations' own table of permitted bands, powers and modes.
ch4_5.bands.summary: This qualification opens {{count}} of the {{total}} bands listed, with a ceiling of {{watts}} W.
ch4_5.bands.footnote: One row per band, showing the stretch this qualification may use and the highest power it may run anywhere on it. Inside that stretch the permitted modes still vary segment by segment, so check the Regulations' own table before operating near a band edge.
ch4_5.log.title: A log entry, field by field
ch4_5.log.description: Keeping a log is recommended in Ukraine rather than required — but if you keep one, these six fields are the part the Regulations fix. Fill them in and watch one line assemble.
ch4_5.log.footnote: Keep the log at least a year after its last entry, and produce it if authorised officials ask. UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) and Latin letters are recommended; an electronic log is allowed. Mobile stations need not keep one at all.
ch4_5.ladderAria: Three columns whose heights are the highest shortwave power each Ukrainian amateur qualification permits: 40 watts for class C, 100 for class B, 200 for class A.
ch4_5.ladderCaption: The three Ukrainian qualifications, drawn to the highest shortwave power each one permits. On 144 and 430 MHz the picture is flat instead — every class is limited to 5 W there — so the ceiling shown is the shortwave one. Each level is examined against the CEPT document named under it.
ch4_5.ladder_a_exam: examined on CEPT T/R 61-02; earns HAREC
ch4_5.ladder_b_exam: examined on ERC Report 32 — this course's syllabus
ch4_5.ladder_c_exam: examined on Electronic Communications Committee Report 089
ch4_5.ceptAria: Two directions of travel: a Ukrainian call sign signing with a foreign prefix in front of it abroad, and a foreign call sign signing with UT in front of it in Ukraine.
ch4_5.ceptCaption: The harmonised document working in both directions — a Ukrainian operator in Germany signs DL in front of their call sign, a German visitor to Ukraine signs UT. On a visit of up to three months, no local application is needed either way — the operator simply puts the visited country's prefix in front of their own call sign.
ch4_5.quiz_q1: Why are amateur radio rules agreed internationally before they are made nationally?
ch4_5.quiz_q1_a: Because radio equipment is manufactured for a single worldwide market
ch4_5.quiz_q1_b: Because a signal travels as far as physics allows, not as far as a border
ch4_5.quiz_q1_c: Because the ITU owns the radio spectrum and licenses it to states
ch4_5.quiz_q1_d: Because amateur societies negotiate directly with foreign governments
ch4_5.quiz_q1_explanation: Spectrum cannot be fenced. A country assigning frequencies purely to suit itself would be assigning its neighbours' frequencies at the same time, so the division has to be agreed first and narrowed afterwards.
ch4_5.quiz_q2: What kind of document are the ITU Radio Regulations?
ch4_5.quiz_q2_a: A recommendation that member states may adopt at their discretion
ch4_5.quiz_q2_b: A technical standard published by equipment manufacturers
ch4_5.quiz_q2_c: A code of conduct drawn up by amateur radio societies
ch4_5.quiz_q2_d: A treaty that binds the states which have signed it
ch4_5.quiz_q2_explanation: They are revised at World Radiocommunication Conferences and are binding on member states, which is why they sit above every other rule in this chapter.
ch4_5.quiz_q3: Under Article 25, when may an amateur station contact one in another country?
ch4_5.quiz_q3_a: Whenever neither administration has objected to such contacts
ch4_5.quiz_q3_b: Only where the two countries hold a bilateral agreement
ch4_5.quiz_q3_c: Only on bands that are primary in both of the regions involved
ch4_5.quiz_q3_d: Whenever both operators hold the full HAREC qualification
ch4_5.quiz_q3_explanation: The default is permission. Article 25 allows contacts between amateur stations of different countries unless one of the administrations concerned has notified that it objects.
ch4_5.quiz_q4: Article 25 forbids encoding a transmission to obscure its meaning. What is carved out?
ch4_5.quiz_q4_a: Digital modes whose specification has been published openly
ch4_5.quiz_q4_b: Contest exchanges using abbreviations agreed in advance
ch4_5.quiz_q4_c: Command signals sent from earth stations to amateur satellites
ch4_5.quiz_q4_d: Emergency traffic passed on behalf of a rescue service
ch4_5.quiz_q4_explanation: The test is purpose, not encoding: a published digital mode is fine however unintelligible it sounds. The one explicit exception in the article is satellite command and control.
ch4_5.quiz_q5: Your band is a secondary allocation. What does that mean in practice?
ch4_5.quiz_q5_a: You may use it only after notifying the regulator of each session
ch4_5.quiz_q5_b: You must not disturb the primary users and get no protection from them
ch4_5.quiz_q5_c: You may use half the power that a primary allocation would allow
ch4_5.quiz_q5_d: You share it equally with the primary users on a first-come basis
ch4_5.quiz_q5_explanation: Secondary status is a statement about legal standing, not about equipment. Interference from the primary service is something you have to accept.
ch4_5.quiz_q6: Who draws up a band plan in most countries, and what force does it carry?
ch4_5.quiz_q6_a: Amateur societies, and it is voluntary in law but near-universal in practice
ch4_5.quiz_q6_b: The national regulator, and breaking it is an administrative offence
ch4_5.quiz_q6_c: The ITU at each conference, and it binds every member state equally
ch4_5.quiz_q6_d: Equipment manufacturers, and it is enforced through type approval rules
ch4_5.quiz_q6_explanation: That is exactly why a wide signal in a narrow-mode segment can be entirely legal and still ruin several contacts for other people.
ch4_5.quiz_q7: A Ukrainian operator visits Germany for two weeks. What do they need?
ch4_5.quiz_q7_a: A temporary German licence applied for at least a month in advance
ch4_5.quiz_q7_b: Nothing at all — the harmonised document is not valid outside Ukraine
ch4_5.quiz_q7_c: A HAREC certificate lodged with the German regulator before travelling
ch4_5.quiz_q7_d: Only their harmonised document, signing DL in front of their call sign
ch4_5.quiz_q7_explanation: CEPT Recommendation T/R 61-01 is what makes this work: up to three months, no local application, and the visited country's prefix goes in front of the operator's own call sign.
ch4_5.quiz_q8: Which CEPT document is the syllabus this course has been following?
ch4_5.quiz_q8_a: CEPT Recommendation T/R 61-01, the harmonised licence
ch4_5.quiz_q8_b: CEPT Recommendation T/R 61-02, the HAREC syllabus
ch4_5.quiz_q8_c: ERC Report 32, the novice syllabus behind class B
ch4_5.quiz_q8_d: Report 089 of the Electronic Communications Committee
ch4_5.quiz_q8_explanation: Ukraine's Regulations name ERC Report 32 as the examination programme for the novice qualification, which is class B.
ch4_5.quiz_q9: Which Ukrainian body assigns call signs and issues operating documents?
ch4_5.quiz_q9_c: The Ministry of Justice, which registers the Regulations
ch4_5.quiz_q9_d: The regional amateur society for the operator's area
ch4_5.quiz_q9_explanation: НКЕК makes the rules and supervises compliance; УДЦР runs the examinations through the qualification commissions and issues the documents.
ch4_5.quiz_q10: A source describes a Ukrainian operator as «third category». What does that correspond to?
ch4_5.quiz_q10_a: Nothing — the category system was abolished without any equivalent
ch4_5.quiz_q10_b: Class B, the novice qualification in the current Regulations
ch4_5.quiz_q10_c: Class C, the entry level introduced by the current Regulations
ch4_5.quiz_q10_d: Class A, since the old first three categories all merged into it
ch4_5.quiz_q10_explanation: The Regulations publish the mapping: class A covers the former first and second categories, class B the former third, and class C is new. Permits issued under the old rules stay valid until they expire.
ch4_5.quiz_q11: What is the maximum transmitter power for the full qualification on 40 metres?
ch4_5.quiz_q11_a: 1000 W, the usual ceiling for a full amateur licence
ch4_5.quiz_q11_b: 400 W, matching the limit common across western Europe
ch4_5.quiz_q11_c: 100 W, the output of a typical shortwave transceiver
ch4_5.quiz_q11_d: 200 W, as set in the Regulations' table of bands and powers
ch4_5.quiz_q11_explanation: It is a genuine surprise to readers who learned on foreign material: the shortwave ceiling is 200 W even at class A, and on 144 and 430 MHz every class is limited to 5 W.
ch4_5.quiz_q12: What do Ukraine's Regulations say about keeping a station log?
ch4_5.quiz_q12_a: It is required of every station without exception
ch4_5.quiz_q12_b: It is required on shortwave and optional above 30 MHz
ch4_5.quiz_q12_c: It is recommended, but its contents are fixed if you keep one
ch4_5.quiz_q12_d: It is optional, and its contents are entirely up to the operator
ch4_5.quiz_q12_explanation: Recommended rather than obliged. What is fixed is the content — correspondent's call sign, date, time, band, mode, report — and that it survives a year past the last entry.
ch4_5.quiz_q13: How long must a station log be kept?
ch4_5.quiz_q13_a: Until the contacts in it have been confirmed by QSL
ch4_5.quiz_q13_b: At least one year after the last entry made in it
ch4_5.quiz_q13_c: At least ten years, matching the operating document
ch4_5.quiz_q13_d: For as long as the operator holds the same call sign
ch4_5.quiz_q13_explanation: It also has to be produced for inspection if authorised officials ask to see it.
ch4_5.quiz_q14: A distress call reaches you on an amateur frequency. What does the operator do?
ch4_5.quiz_q14_a: Stop transmitting, keep listening, and help the traffic through
ch4_5.quiz_q14_b: Log the call and change frequency to avoid adding congestion
ch4_5.quiz_q14_c: Answer only if the calling station is itself an amateur station
ch4_5.quiz_q14_d: Continue the contact quietly at the lowest usable power
ch4_5.quiz_q14_explanation: Distress outranks everything else, including the rule that amateur stations work only other amateur stations: SOS or MAYDAY may be answered whatever the calling station is.
ch4_5.quiz_q15: When may an amateur pass a message on behalf of somebody who is not licensed?
ch4_5.quiz_q15_a: Never — third-party traffic is prohibited without exception
ch4_5.quiz_q15_b: Whenever both operators agree in advance to accept the message
ch4_5.quiz_q15_c: In emergencies and disaster relief, where it is permitted
ch4_5.quiz_q15_d: Only within one country, never across an international border
ch4_5.quiz_q15_explanation: Internationally it is restricted by default under the Radio Regulations and otherwise depends on agreement between the two administrations. Emergencies are the standing exception.
